knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\). The function \(f\) is submodular if, for every \(A,B\subseteq V\), \[f(A)+f(B)\ge f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B).\] Equivalently, it has diminishing marginal returns: whenever \(A\subseteq B\subseteq V\) and \(e\in V\setminus B\), \[f(A\cup\{e\})-f(A)\ge f(B\cup\{e\})-f(B).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set function is submodular when unions and intersections satisfy the submodular inequality, equivalently when each element's marginal gain decreases as the chosen set grows.
knowledge_statements.title: Submodular Function Classes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Submodular Set Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard lattice-inequality definition for a real-valued set function on the power set of V.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set function \(F:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is submodular if and only if, for every \(A,B\subseteq V\), \[F(A)+F(B)\geq F(A\cup B)+F(A\cap B).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued set function is submodular exactly when, for any two subsets, the sum of its values on those subsets is at least the sum of its values on their union and intersection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is submodular}\iff \forall A,B\subseteq V,\;F(A)+F(B)\geq F(A\cup B)+F(A\cap B).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-element local characterization of submodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes submodularity through the inequality obtained by adding two distinct elements to a common subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set function \(f:\mathcal P(S)\to\mathbb R\) is submodular if and only if, for every \(U\subseteq S\) and all distinct \(s,t\in S\setminus U\), \[f(U\cup\{s\})+f(U\cup\{t\})\ge f(U)+f(U\cup\{s,t\}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set function is submodular exactly when the two-element inequality holds for every subset and every pair of distinct elements outside that subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is submodular}\iff \forall U\subseteq S,\ \forall s\ne t\in S\setminus U,\ f(U\cup\{s\})+f(U\cup\{t\})\ge f(U)+f(U\cup\{s,t\}).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\). The function \(f\) is supermodular if, for every \(A,B\subseteq V\), \[f(A)+f(B)\le f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B).\] Equivalently, \(-f\) is submodular, and marginal returns are increasing: if \(A\subseteq B\subseteq V\) and \(e\in V\setminus B\), then \[f(A\cup\{e\})-f(A)\le f(B\cup\{e\})-f(B).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set function is supermodular when the submodular inequality is reversed; equivalently, its negative is submodular and its marginal returns increase with the set.
knowledge_statements.title: Supermodular Function Classes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supermodular Set Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the normalized one-sided extended-real convention stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(\mu:2^V\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) is supermodular if \(-\mu\) is submodular. Under the stated convention, \(\mu(\varnothing)=0\) and \(\mu(V)>-\infty\); equivalently, \(-\mu\in\mathcal S[\mathbb R]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set function that may take negative-infinite values is supermodular when its negation is submodular. It is normalized at the empty set and has a finite ground-set value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu\text{ is supermodular}\iff -\mu\in\mathcal S[\mathbb R]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive representation of finite real-valued modular set functions.

source_refs.locator: 8.1 Minimizing Submodular Functions p. 194

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\). The function \(f\) is modular exactly when \[f(A)+f(B)=f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B)\] for all \(A,B\subseteq V\). This holds exactly when there are weights \(w_e\in\mathbb{R}\), one for each \(e\in V\), such that \[f(S)=f(\varnothing)+\sum_{e\in S}w_e\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V.\] The weights are uniquely determined by \(w_e=f(\{e\})-f(\varnothing)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite set function is modular exactly when it is a constant plus the sum of fixed element weights, or equivalently when the lattice inequality always holds with equality.
knowledge_statements.title: Modular Function Classes

source_witnesses.locator: 8.1 Minimizing Submodular Functions p. 194

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additive Representation of Normalized Modular Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of normalized modular set functions by additive element weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(F(\varnothing)=0\). Then \(F\) is modular, equivalently both submodular and supermodular, if and only if there exists \(s\in\mathbb{R}^p\) such that, for every \(A\subseteq V\), \[F(A)=\sum_{k\in A}s_k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set function with F(empty set) = 0 is modular, meaning both submodular and supermodular, exactly when its value on every subset is the sum of fixed weights assigned to that subset's elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is modular}\iff \exists s\in\mathbb{R}^p\;\forall A\subseteq V,\;F(A)=\sum_{k\in A}s_k.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite ground set \(V\) and a function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\), the following are equivalent: \(f\) is both submodular and supermodular; the lattice relation holds with equality, \[f(A)+f(B)=f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B)\qquad\text{for all }A,B\subseteq V;\] and \(f\) is modular. Consequently, the intersection of the submodular and supermodular function classes is precisely the modular function class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set function belongs to both the submodular and supermodular classes exactly when it is modular, meaning every lattice inequality is an equality.
knowledge_statements.title: Class Intersections

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\). The set function \(f\) is normalized if \[f(\varnothing)=0.\] Every set function admits a normalized translate \(f_0:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \[f_0(S)=f(S)-f(\varnothing)\qquad\text{for all }S\subseteq V.\] Translation by this constant preserves submodularity, supermodularity, modularity, and both directions of inclusion monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set function is normalized when its value at the empty set is zero. Subtracting the empty-set value normalizes any function without changing its modularity or monotonicity class.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Set Functions

assumptions_latex: V\text{ is a finite ground set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\subseteq B\Rightarrow f(A)\le f(B)\text{ or }A\subseteq B\Rightarrow f(A)\ge f(B)

notation.meaning: marginal increment from adding e to S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Increasing, decreasing, and unrestricted inclusion-monotonicity regimes.

source_refs.locator: 8. Optimizing Submodular Functions p. 194

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\). The function \(f\) is nondecreasing if \(A\subseteq B\) implies \(f(A)\le f(B)\), and nonincreasing if \(A\subseteq B\) implies \(f(A)\ge f(B)\). Equivalently, with \(\Delta_e f(S)=f(S\cup\{e\})-f(S)\), nondecreasing functions satisfy \(\Delta_e f(S)\ge0\), while nonincreasing functions satisfy \(\Delta_e f(S)\le0\), for every \(S\subseteq V\) and \(e\in V\setminus S\). Functions satisfying neither predicate form the nonmonotone regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inclusion can make a set function never decrease, never increase, or behave nonmonotonically. The first two regimes are equivalently characterized by the signs of all one-element marginal increments.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Sign Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise sign classes on the entire power set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\). The function \(f\) is nonnegative if \[f(S)\ge 0\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V,\] and it is nonpositive if \[f(S)\le 0\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V.\] It is sign-changing if there exist \(A,B\subseteq V\) such that \[f(A)<0<f(B).\] A function is sign-changing exactly when it belongs to neither weak-sign class. The nonnegative and nonpositive classes intersect precisely in the identically zero function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set function is nonnegative when all its values are at least zero, nonpositive when all its values are at most zero, and sign-changing when it takes both a negative and a positive value. The two weak-sign classes overlap only at the zero function.
assumptions_latex: V\text{ is a finite ground set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall S\subseteq V,\ f(S)\ge 0),\quad (\forall S\subseteq V,\ f(S)\le 0),\quad\text{or}\quad (\exists A,B\subseteq V,\ f(A)<0<f(B))

children.title: Regime Interactions
children.top_down_role: Structural interactions among normalization, monotonicity, and sign restrictions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and suppose \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is normalized. If \(f\) is nondecreasing, then \[f(S)\ge f(\varnothing)=0\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V,\] so \(f\) is nonnegative. If \(f\) is nonincreasing, then \[f(S)\le f(\varnothing)=0\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V,\] so \(f\) is nonpositive. Neither converse holds in general: pointwise sign restrictions alone do not order values on nested nonempty sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalization turns increasing set functions into nonnegative functions and decreasing set functions into nonpositive functions. Sign restrictions alone do not imply monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.title: Regime Interactions

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite. A function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is a symmetric submodular function if it is submodular and invariant under complementation: \[f(S)=f(V\setminus S)\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V.\] Symmetry implies \(f(\varnothing)=f(V)\). Moreover, for any \(A,B\subseteq V\), its values depend on an unordered bipartition rather than on the choice of shore, while submodularity retains the inequality \(f(A)+f(B)\ge f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric submodular function is submodular and assigns the same value to every set and its complement, so it naturally measures an unordered bipartition.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Submodular Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric submodular functions and nontrivial minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines symmetric submodularity and identifies the boundary that makes its minimization problem nontrivial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A submodular function \(f:2^U\to\mathbb{R}\) is symmetric if \(f(A)=f(U\setminus A)\) for every \(A\subseteq U\). Every such function satisfies \(f(\varnothing)=f(U)\le f(A)\) for all \(A\subseteq U\). Hence unrestricted minimization is trivial, and the nontrivial problem minimizes \(f(A)\) over \(\varnothing\ne A\subsetneq U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A submodular set function is symmetric when every set and its complement have equal values. The empty set and the whole ground set are global minimizers, so the nontrivial minimization problem is restricted to nonempty proper subsets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(\varnothing)=f(U)\le f(A)\quad\forall A\subseteq U;\qquad \min_{\varnothing\ne A\subsetneq U}f(A)\text{ is the nontrivial variant.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric set functions and the unrestricted submodular minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complement-symmetry definition together with its elementary consequence for unrestricted minimization of a submodular function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set function \(f:2^S\to\mathbb R\) is symmetric if \[f(U)=f(S\setminus U)\qquad(\forall U\subseteq S).\] If \(f\) is also submodular, then for every \(U\subseteq S\), \[2f(U)=f(U)+f(S\setminus U)\ge f(\varnothing)+f(S)=2f(\varnothing),\] so \(\varnothing\) is an unrestricted minimizer of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set function is symmetric when each set and its complement have equal value. If the function is also submodular, the empty set attains its unrestricted minimum.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is submodular for the minimization conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall U\subseteq S,\ f(U)\ge f(\varnothing),\quad \varnothing\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{U\subseteq S}f(U)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegativity and trivial minimizers of normalized symmetric submodular functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry and its consequences under the normalization used in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $F:2^V\to\mathbb{R}$ be submodular, normalized by $F(\varnothing)=0$, and symmetric in the sense that $F(V\setminus B)=F(B)$ for every $B\subseteq V$. Then $F(B)\geq 0$ for every $B\subseteq V$, and both $\varnothing$ and $V$ are global minimizers of $F$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a normalized submodular set function assigns the same value to every set and its complement, then it is nonnegative, and both the empty set and the ground set attain its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall B\subseteq V,\;F(B)\geq 0,\qquad \varnothing,V\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{A\subseteq V}F(A).

assumptions_latex: V\text{ is a finite ground set}

source_refs.locator: 8. Optimizing Submodular Functions p. 194

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite. A set function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is integer-valued if \[f(S)\in\mathbb{Z}\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V.\] Integer-valuedness is an arithmetic restriction independent of submodularity, supermodularity, modularity, normalization, and monotonicity. Thus an integer-valued submodular function is precisely a function satisfying both the pointwise integrality condition and the submodular lattice inequality; neither condition alone implies the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer-valued set function takes an integer value on every subset. This arithmetic condition can be combined independently with submodularity, normalization, monotonicity, and related classes.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Valued Regimes

children.title: Rational-Valued Regimes
children.top_down_role: Rational data regimes and denominator-sensitive structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Rational-Valued Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rational codomain restriction for finite set functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite. A set function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is rational-valued if \[f(S)\in\mathbb{Q}\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V.\] Every integer-valued set function is rational-valued, but the converse fails: the constant function \[f(S)=\frac{1}{2}\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V\] is rational-valued and modular but not integer-valued. Rational-valuedness is otherwise independent of submodularity, monotonicity, normalization, and the weak-sign predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational-valued set function takes rational values on every subset. Every integer-valued function is rational-valued, while the constant modular function with value one half shows that the converse fails.
assumptions_latex: V\text{ is a finite ground set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(2^V)\subseteq\mathbb{Q}

children.title: Arithmetic Scaling Relations
children.top_down_role: Scaling links between rational-valued and integer-valued formulations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}:qf(2^V)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-denominator scaling on a finite power-set domain.

source_refs.locator: 8. Optimizing Submodular Functions p. 194

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{Q}\). Because \(2^V\) is finite, there exists a positive integer \(q\) divisible by the denominator of every value \(f(S)\), and hence \[(qf)(S)=qf(S)\in\mathbb{Z}\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V.\] Multiplication by any positive scalar preserves submodularity, supermodularity, modularity, both monotonicity directions, and weak sign. It also preserves normalization. Thus positive common-denominator scaling converts every rational-valued member of any such class into an integer-valued member of the same class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite ground set, one common positive denominator scales every rational-valued function to an integer-valued one while preserving modularity, monotonicity, sign, and normalization classes.
knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic Scaling Relations

children.title: Matroid Rank Models
children.top_down_role: Rank-function representations arising from matroid structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_M\) is an integer-valued, normalized, monotone, submodular rank model with \(0\le r_M(S)\le |S|\).

notation.meaning: family of independent sets of the matroid

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroids represented by their rank functions.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\subseteq E\), define \(r_M(S)=\max\{|I|:I\subseteq S,\ I\in\mathcal I\}\). Then \(r_M(\varnothing)=0\), \(0\le r_M(S)\le |S|\), and \(S\subseteq T\) implies \(r_M(S)\le r_M(T)\). Moreover, for all \(S,T\subseteq E\), \[r_M(S)+r_M(T)\ge r_M(S\cup T)+r_M(S\cap T).\] Thus a finite matroid is represented by an integer-valued normalized, monotone, submodular set function whose value is the maximum size of an independent subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid rank assigns each set the largest size of an independent subset; it is integer-valued, normalized, monotone, submodular, and bounded by cardinality.
knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Rank Models

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Induced by a Submodular Function on a Set Lattice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matroid construction and rank formula from a nonnegative integer-valued lattice-submodular function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal E\) be a lattice of subsets of \(E\) that is closed under intersection and contains \(\varnothing\) and \(E\). Let \(f:\mathcal E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) be submodular with \(f(\varnothing)=0\), and define
\[
\mathcal I(\mathcal E,f)=\{X\subseteq E:|X\cap T|\le f(T)\text{ for every }T\in\mathcal E\}.
\]
Then \(\mathcal I(\mathcal E,f)\) is the family of independent sets of a matroid on \(E\). For every \(X\subseteq E\), its rank is
\[
r(X)=\min\{f(T)+|X\setminus T|:T\in\mathcal E\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized, nonnegative integer-valued submodular function on an intersection-closed lattice containing the empty set and ground set induces a matroid through the stated intersection bounds. Its rank is the minimum of f(T) plus the number of elements outside T.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal E\subseteq 2^E\text{ is a lattice under inclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal I(\mathcal E,f)\text{ is a matroid independence family and }\forall X\subseteq E,\ r(X)=\min\{f(T)+|X\setminus T|:T\in\mathcal E\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representation of Polymatroids by Unions of Matroid Flats
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of polymatroid set functions through matroid-rank representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be a function on \(2^E\). Then \(f\) is a polymatroid if and only if there exist a matroid \(M\) and a map \(\varphi:E\to\mathcal F(M)\) into the flats of \(M\) such that, for every \(X\subseteq E\),
\[
f(X)=r_M\!\left(\bigcup_{x\in X}\varphi(x)\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set function is a polymatroid exactly when it can be represented as the matroid rank of the union of flats assigned to its ground-set elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a polymatroid}\iff\exists M\,\exists\varphi:E\to\mathcal F(M)\,\forall X\subseteq E,\ f(X)=r_M\left(\bigcup_{x\in X}\varphi(x)\right)

children.title: Coverage Models
children.top_down_role: Set functions generated by weighted or unweighted coverage structure.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite set of selectable items and \(U\) is a finite universe.
\(C_e\subseteq U\) for each \(e\in E\), and \(a_u\ge0\) for each \(u\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The weighted coverage function \(f\) is normalized, monotone, and submodular.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weighted union coverage is a canonical submodular construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite nonnegative weighted set-union coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each selected set \(S\subseteq E\), define \[f(S)=\sum_{u\in\bigcup_{e\in S}C_e}a_u.\] Equivalently, \(f(S)=\sum_{u\in U}a_u\mathbf 1\{S\cap D_u\ne\varnothing\}\), where \(D_u=\{e\in E:u\in C_e\}\). Then \(f(\varnothing)=0\), \(f\) is monotone, and for all \(S,T\subseteq E\), \[f(S)+f(T)\ge f(S\cup T)+f(S\cap T).\] Each universe element contributes once whenever at least one selected item covers it, producing diminishing marginal coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted coverage sums the weights of universe elements covered by at least one selected item and is normalized, monotone, and submodular.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted-coverage construction and its submodularity are standard and precise, but the record supplies no inspectable citation.

children.title: Facility-Location Models
children.top_down_role: Set functions generated by facility-selection and client-value structure.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite facility set and \(D\) is a finite client set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The facility-location objective \(F\) is normalized, monotone, and submodular.

notation.meaning: nonnegative service score of facility j for client i
facility-location value of the selected facilities

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sums of clientwise maximum service scores are canonical facility-location submodular functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite nonnegative maximum-similarity facility-location objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq E\), define \[F(S)=\sum_{i\in D}\max_{j\in S}s_{ij},\] using the convention \(\max_{j\in\varnothing}s_{ij}=0\). Then \(F(\varnothing)=0\), \(F\) is monotone, and \(F\) is submodular. Equivalently, whenever \(A\subseteq B\subseteq E\) and \(e\in E\setminus B\), \[F(A\cup\{e\})-F(A)\ge F(B\cup\{e\})-F(B).\] The marginal value of a facility is the sum of improvements it provides beyond each client's best currently selected service score.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facility location sums each client's best score among selected facilities; nonnegative scores make this objective normalized, monotone, and submodular.
knowledge_statements.title: Facility-Location Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximum-service facility-location representation and diminishing-returns formula are mathematically consistent, but no authoritative source with a locator is supplied.

children.title: Coverage–Location Overlap
children.top_down_role: Shared representational territory and separation boundaries between the model families.

assumptions_latex: \(s_{ij}\ge0\) takes finitely many values for every client \(i\in D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Facility-location functions are nonnegative weighted sums of threshold-coverage functions, and binary-score facility location is exactly weighted coverage.

notation.meaning: facilities serving client i at threshold t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite layer-cake decomposition gives the coverage representation directly
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite threshold decomposition linking coverage and facility location.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(i\in D\), list the distinct positive scores as \(0=t_{i,0}<t_{i,1}<\cdots<t_{i,m_i}\) and set \(C_{i,k}=\{j\in E:s_{ij}\ge t_{i,k}\}\). Then \[F(S)=\sum_{i\in D}\max_{j\in S}s_{ij}=\sum_{i\in D}\sum_{k=1}^{m_i}(t_{i,k}-t_{i,k-1})\mathbf 1\{S\cap C_{i,k}\ne\varnothing\}.\] Hence every finite nonnegative facility-location model is a weighted sum of coverage indicators. If \(s_{ij}\in\{0,a_i\}\), the formula reduces exactly to weighted coverage of clients with weights \(a_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facility location decomposes into weighted threshold-coverages; with binary service scores, it is exactly a weighted coverage function.
knowledge_statements.title: Coverage–Location Overlap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite threshold decomposition is algebraically consistent and fits the overlap leaf, including the binary-score specialization, but it lacks an inspectable source.

children.title: Entropy Models
children.top_down_role: Submodular set functions arising from entropy quantities.

assumptions_latex: \((X_e)_{e\in E}\) are jointly distributed discrete random variables on finite alphabets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The joint-entropy set function \(h(S)=H(X_S)\) is normalized, monotone, and submodular.

notation.meaning: tuple of random variables indexed by S
joint entropy as a set function

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Shannon entropy submodularity is the standard strong-subadditivity model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shannon entropy of finite-alphabet variable subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(h:2^E\to\mathbb R_+\) by \(h(S)=H(X_S)\), with \(X_\varnothing\) constant and hence \(h(\varnothing)=0\). For \(S\subseteq T\subseteq E\), \(h(S)\le h(T)\). For all \(S,T\subseteq E\), Shannon's strong subadditivity gives \[h(S)+h(T)\ge h(S\cup T)+h(S\cap T).\] Equivalently, conditioning cannot increase the marginal entropy of an additional variable. Thus joint entropies form normalized, monotone, submodular set-function models, subject to further information inequalities not shared by arbitrary polymatroid ranks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint Shannon entropy of selected finite-alphabet variables is a normalized, monotone, submodular set function, though entropy vectors satisfy additional constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Entropy Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Entropy submodularity is standard, but no source is supplied. The additional claim about information inequalities should also be sourced and qualified by the number of variables and the distinction between entropic and almost-entropic regions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Entropy and Gaussian log-determinant submodular models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete joint-entropy set functions, their symmetrization as mutual information, and the nondegenerate Gaussian log-determinant specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let V=\{1,\ldots,p\}. If X_1,\ldots,X_p are finite-valued random variables and F(A)=H(X_A), then F is nonnegative, nondecreasing, and submodular. Moreover, G(A)=F(A)+F(V\setminus A)-F(V)=I(X_A;X_{V\setminus A}) is symmetric and submodular. If X\in\mathbb R^p is Gaussian with covariance Q\succ0, then H(X_A)=\tfrac12\log\det(2\pi e\,Q_{AA}), and hence A\mapsto\log\det Q_{AA} is submodular. Discrete entropic set functions satisfy restrictions not shared by all submodular functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint entropy of subsets of finitely valued random variables is a nonnegative, nondecreasing submodular set function. Its symmetrization is the mutual information between a subset and its complement and is symmetric and submodular. For a Gaussian vector with positive-definite covariance, the principal-submatrix log-determinant function is submodular. Entropic functions obey additional restrictions beyond ordinary submodularity.
assumptions_latex: X_1,\ldots,X_p\text{ are finite-valued for the discrete-entropy claims}
X\in\mathbb R^p\text{ is Gaussian with covariance }Q\succ0\text{ for the log-determinant claim}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(A)=H(X_A)\text{ is nonnegative, nondecreasing, and submodular};\quad G(A)=I(X_A;X_{V\setminus A})\text{ is symmetric and submodular};\quad A\mapsto\log\det Q_{AA}\text{ is submodular}.

children.title: Information-Gain Models
children.top_down_role: Submodular models based on information gain and uncertainty reduction.

assumptions_latex: \(Y\) and \((X_e)_{e\in E}\) are discrete random variables on finite alphabets.
The variables \((X_e)_{e\in E}\) are conditionally independent given \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The information-gain function \(g(S)=I(Y;X_S)\) is normalized, monotone, and submodular.

notation.meaning: information gained about Y from variables indexed by S
tuple of observations indexed by S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conditional independence makes conditional entropy modular, yielding the standard submodular information-gain model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Submodular mutual information under conditional independence of observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq E\), define \[g(S)=I(Y;X_S)=H(X_S)-H(X_S\mid Y)=H(Y)-H(Y\mid X_S).\] Then \(g(\varnothing)=0\) and \(g\) is monotone. Conditional independence given \(Y\) implies \(H(X_S\mid Y)=\sum_{e\in S}H(X_e\mid Y)\), which is modular in \(S\). Since \(H(X_S)\) is submodular, \(g\) is submodular. Without the conditional-independence assumption, mutual information \(I(Y;X_S)\) remains monotone but need not be submodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Information gained about a target is monotone and becomes submodular when observations are conditionally independent given that target; without this assumption submodularity can fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Information-Gain Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional-independence hypothesis yields the stated modular conditional entropy and submodular information gain, while monotonicity holds generally. An authoritative source is required for the exact hypothesis and failure boundary.

children.title: Log-Determinant Models
children.top_down_role: Matrix-derived submodular models based on log-determinant objectives.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and \(A_e\) is a real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix for each \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized log-determinant function \(f\) is monotone and submodular.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: log determinant of a positive-definite baseline plus selected positive-semidefinite increments is a standard submodular matrix model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefinite additive matrix increments with a positive-definite baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\subseteq E\), define \[f(S)=\log\det\!\left(A_0+\sum_{e\in S}A_e\right)-\log\det(A_0).\] The positive-definite baseline makes every determinant positive and gives \(f(\varnothing)=0\). Nonnegative positive-semidefinite increments make \(f\) monotone. Moreover, for \(S\subseteq T\subseteq E\) and \(e\in E\setminus T\), \[f(S\cup\{e\})-f(S)\ge f(T\cup\{e\})-f(T),\] so \(f\) is submodular. This supplies a canonical matrix-valued diminishing-returns model used for information accumulation and experimental design.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normalized log determinant of a positive-definite baseline plus selected positive-semidefinite increments is a monotone submodular set function.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Determinant Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-definite baseline and positive-semidefinite additive increments support the stated normalized, monotone log-determinant model, but the exact noncommutative matrix hypotheses and submodularity claim require an authoritative citation.

children.title: Information–Matrix Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between informational and matrix-derived constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Information–Matrix Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-Gaussian information gain represented by positive-semidefinite measurement information matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the unknown vector have positive-definite prior precision \(\Lambda_0\), and let measurement \(i\in V\) contribute a positive-semidefinite information matrix \(M_i\). For \(S\subseteq V\), the Gaussian information gain is represented by
\[F(S)=\frac12\log\frac{\det\!\left(\Lambda_0+\sum_{i\in S}M_i\right)}{\det(\Lambda_0)}.\]
Thus \(F(\varnothing)=0\), and the posterior precision is \(\Lambda_S=\Lambda_0+\sum_{i\in S}M_i\). The function \(F\) is monotone and submodular: for \(A\subseteq B\subseteq V\) and \(i\notin B\), \(F(A\cup\{i\})-F(A)\ge F(B\cup\{i\})-F(B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent Gaussian measurement information adds at the matrix level, while its log-determinant information gain forms a normalized, monotone submodular set function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(S)=\tfrac12[\log\det(\Lambda_0+\sum_{i\in S}M_i)-\log\det\Lambda_0]\) is normalized, monotone, and submodular.

children.title: Submodular Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reduction operations that produce smaller or specialized submodular systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Submodular Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination of auxiliary ground-set elements by partial minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) and \(U\) be disjoint finite sets, and let \(f:2^{V\cup U}\to\mathbb{R}\) be submodular. Define the reduced function on \(V\) by
\[g(S)=\min_{T\subseteq U}f(S\cup T),\qquad S\subseteq V.\]
Then \(g\) is submodular on \(2^V\). If a normalized reduction is required, replacing \(g\) by \(g-g(\varnothing)\) preserves submodularity and gives value zero at the empty set. This operation eliminates the auxiliary variables indexed by \(U\) without leaving the class of finite-valued submodular functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a submodular function over auxiliary Boolean variables produces a submodular function on the retained variables.
assumptions_latex: \(V\cap U=\varnothing\) and both sets are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(S)=\min_{T\subseteq U}f(S\cup T)\) is submodular on \(2^V\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind fits this closure result, and partial minimization over a finite auxiliary Boolean ground set does preserve submodularity. A specific authoritative source is nevertheless required to support the theorem and confirm that this operation is the intended local meaning of submodular reduction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Restriction of a Submodular Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Submodularity, Lovász-extension, and polyhedral behavior under restriction to a subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:2^V\to\mathbb{R} be submodular with F(\varnothing)=0, and let A\subseteq V. Define F_A:2^A\to\mathbb{R} by F_A(B)=F(B) for B\subseteq A. Then F_A is submodular. If f is the Lovász extension of F, the Lovász extension of F_A is f_A(w_A)=f(w_A,0_{V\setminus A}). Moreover, s\in P(F_A) if and only if there exists t\in\mathbb{R}^{V\setminus A} such that (s,t)\in P(F).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restriction to a subset preserves submodularity. The restricted Lovász extension is obtained by setting outside coordinates to zero, and the restricted submodular polyhedron is the coordinate projection of the original polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_A\text{ is submodular},\quad f_A(w_A)=f(w_A,0_{V\setminus A}),\quad P(F_A)=\operatorname{proj}_A P(F).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedra of a vector reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the submodular polyhedron of a vector-reduced system and, under the superbase condition, its base polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contraction of a Submodular Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Submodularity, Lovász-extension, and polyhedral behavior under contraction by a subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:2^V\to\mathbb{R} be submodular with F(\varnothing)=0, and let A\subseteq V. Define F^A:2^{V\setminus A}\to\mathbb{R} by F^A(B)=F(A\cup B)-F(A). Then F^A is submodular. If f is the Lovász extension of F, the Lovász extension of F^A is f^A(w_{V\setminus A})=f(1_A,w_{V\setminus A})-F(A). Moreover, t\in P(F^A) if and only if there exists s\in P(F) such that s(A)=F(A) and s_{V\setminus A}=t.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contraction by A preserves submodularity. Its Lovász extension fixes the A-coordinates to one and subtracts F(A), while its polyhedron is the projection of the tight face s(A)=F(A) onto the remaining coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F^A\text{ is submodular},\quad f^A(w_{V\setminus A})=f(1_A,w_{V\setminus A})-F(A),\quad P(F^A)=\operatorname{proj}_{V\setminus A}\bigl(P(F)\cap\{s:s(A)=F(A)\}\bigr).

children.title: Ground-Set Restrictions
children.top_down_role: Restriction operations on selected portions of the ground set.

knowledge_statements.title: Ground-Set Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction of a set function to subsets of a retained ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) and let \(W\subseteq V\). The ground-set restriction of \(f\) to \(W\) is the function
\[f|_W:2^W\to\mathbb{R},\qquad (f|_W)(S)=f(S)\quad(S\subseteq W).\]
If \(f\) is submodular on \(2^V\), then \(f|_W\) is submodular on \(2^W\). Normalization, monotonicity, and integer-valuedness are also inherited whenever they hold for \(f\). In minor terminology, restricting to \(W\) deletes the elements of \(V\setminus W\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restriction keeps only subsets of a chosen ground set and preserves submodularity and the usual inherited properties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f|_W)(S)=f(S)\) defines a submodular function on \(2^W\).

notation.meaning: restriction of f to ground set W

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind and restriction convention fit the leaf, and the stated inherited properties are standard and internally consistent. The record supplies no inspectable source or locator, so it requires an authoritative citation before acceptance.

children.title: Ground-Set Contractions
children.top_down_role: Contraction operations relative to fixed ground-set elements.

knowledge_statements.title: Ground-Set Contractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized contraction by conditioning a set function on a fixed subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) and fix \(C\subseteq V\). The contraction of \(f\) by \(C\) is the function on \(V\setminus C\) defined by
\[(f/C)(S)=f(S\cup C)-f(C),\qquad S\subseteq V\setminus C.\]
If \(f\) is submodular, then \(f/C\) is submodular, since adjoining the same fixed set preserves the submodular inequality. Moreover, \((f/C)(\varnothing)=0\), regardless of whether \(f\) was normalized. Monotonicity and integer-valuedness are inherited when present.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contraction fixes a subset as already selected, subtracts its value, and yields a normalized submodular function on the remaining elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f/C)(S)=f(S\cup C)-f(C)\) is normalized and submodular on \(2^{V\setminus C}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the leaf, and the normalized contraction formula correctly preserves submodularity, monotonicity, and integer-valuedness. Because contraction normalization conventions vary, an authoritative source with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Minor-Type Relations
children.top_down_role: Structural relations generated by successive restrictions and contractions.

knowledge_statements.title: Minor-Type Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minor relation generated by ground-set deletion and contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a submodular function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\), choose disjoint sets \(C,D\subseteq V\) and put \(W=V\setminus(C\cup D)\). A normalized minor of \(f\) obtained by contracting \(C\) and deleting \(D\) is the function \(g:2^W\to\mathbb{R}\) given by
\[g(S)=f(S\cup C)-f(C),\qquad S\subseteq W.\]
The result is submodular. The minor-type relation is reflexive and transitive: any finite sequence of restrictions and contractions can be consolidated into disjoint contracted and deleted sets, up to the additive normalization used above.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A submodular minor results from contracting some elements and deleting others; such operations preserve submodularity and compose transitively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(S)=f(S\cup C)-f(C)\) is a submodular minor on \(V\setminus(C\cup D)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits a minor-type relation, and the displayed deletion-contraction form is coherent with the prerequisite records. The normalization convention and the reflexive, transitive, and consolidation claims have no cited support and require an authoritative source.

children.title: Function Translations
children.top_down_role: Translations of function values or arguments within submodular systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Function Translations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertical translation of a set function by a constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) be submodular and let \(c\in\mathbb{R}\). Define the vertical translation \(g:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) by
\[g(S)=f(S)+c,	\qquad S\subseteq V.\]
Then \(g\) is submodular, because the two copies of \(c\) cancel from every submodular inequality. All marginal differences are unchanged: for \(S\subseteq V\) and \(i\notin S\), \(g(S\cup\{i\})-g(S)=f(S\cup\{i\})-f(S)\). Translation preserves minimizers and maximizers but preserves normalization only when \(c=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding one constant to every function value preserves submodularity, marginal values, and optimizers, though generally not normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g=f+c\) is submodular and has the same marginal differences and optimizers as \(f\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind fits the stated invariance result, and vertical translation preserves submodularity, marginals, and optimizer sets as claimed. A source is needed both for the result and to confirm that vertical translation, rather than another translation operation, is the intended local sense of the title.

children.title: Submodular Sums
children.top_down_role: Additive combinations of submodular functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Submodular Sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of submodular functions under nonnegative linear combinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_j:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) be submodular for \(j=1,\ldots,m\), and let \(\lambda_j\ge0\). Then
\[F(S)=\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j f_j(S),\qquad S\subseteq V,\]
is submodular. If every \(f_j\) is normalized, monotone, or integer-valued, then \(F\) is respectively normalized, monotone, or integer-valued in the last case when every \(\lambda_j\) is a nonnegative integer. Allowing a negative coefficient does not preserve submodularity in general, because it reverses the corresponding submodular inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative linear combination of submodular functions on the same ground set is submodular; negative weights can destroy the property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j f_j\) is submodular.

notation.meaning: weighted sum of the component functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind fits the closure statement. The nonnegative-combination result, the qualifications concerning monotonicity and integer values, and the warning about negative coefficients are mathematically consistent, but no inspectable source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decomposable Submodular Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The component property called “simple” is source-relative and is not defined in this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A submodular function \(F\) on \(2^V\) is decomposable if there exist submodular functions \(F_1,\ldots,F_r\), regarded as simple components, such that \[\forall A\subseteq V,\qquad F(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{r}F_i(A).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A submodular function is decomposable when it is the pointwise sum of finitely many submodular component functions regarded as simple.
assumptions_latex: F_i\text{ is a submodular function on }2^V\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,r
F_1,\ldots,F_r\text{ belong to a source-dependent class regarded as simple}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall A\subseteq V,\quad F(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{r}F_i(A)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-set marginal perturbation yields monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A particular constant and modular perturbation preserves submodularity and makes the resulting function monotone nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $U$ be finite, let $f:2^U\to\mathbb R$ be submodular, and let $\beta\in\mathbb R$. Define $g:2^U\to\mathbb R$ by
\[
g(X)=f(X)-\beta+\sum_{e\in X}\bigl(f(U\setminus\{e\})-f(U)\bigr).
\]
Then $g$ is submodular and monotone nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the specified modular correction formed from full-set deletion marginals, together with an arbitrary constant shift, preserves submodularity and makes the function monotone nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is submodular and monotone nondecreasing}

children.title: Modular Perturbations
children.top_down_role: Modification of submodular functions by modular terms.

knowledge_statements.title: Modular Perturbations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Addition of a modular function to a submodular function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) be submodular and let \(m\) be modular, equivalently
\[m(S)=c+\sum_{i\in S}w_i\]
for constants \(c,w_i\in\mathbb{R}\). Then \(g=f+m\) is submodular. More precisely, its submodular slack is unchanged:
\[g(A)+g(B)-g(A\cup B)-g(A\cap B)=f(A)+f(B)-f(A\cup B)-f(A\cap B).\]
Thus modular perturbations preserve every submodular inequality, although arbitrary weights \(w_i\) can change monotonicity and the sets minimizing or maximizing the function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding element weights and a constant leaves all submodular slacks unchanged, but may alter monotonicity and optimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f+m\) is submodular and has the same submodular slack as \(f\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind fits the leaf, and addition of a modular function leaves every submodular slack unchanged. The notation and qualifications are consistent, but an authoritative citation with a specific locator is absent.

children.title: Perturbation Equivalence Classes
children.top_down_role: Structural equivalence induced by translations and modular modifications.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Equivalence Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of set functions modulo additive modular terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For functions \(f,g:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\), define \(f\sim g\) when \(g-f\) is modular; equivalently, there exist \(c\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(w\in\mathbb{R}^V\) such that
\[g(S)=f(S)+c+\sum_{i\in S}w_i\qquad(S\subseteq V).\]
This relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Functions in one equivalence class have identical submodular slacks for every pair of subsets. Consequently, either every representative is submodular or none is, although representatives need not share normalization, monotonicity, or optimizer sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two set functions are perturbation-equivalent when their difference is modular; equivalence preserves all submodular slacks and hence submodularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\sim g\iff g-f\) is modular, and \(f\) is submodular if and only if \(g\) is submodular.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the leaf, and equivalence modulo modular functions is an equivalence relation preserving submodular slack. The proposed equivalence convention and its consequences require a specific authoritative source before acceptance.

children.title: Ordinary Truncation
children.top_down_role: Standard truncation of submodular functions and rank systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Truncation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-capping truncation for normalized monotone submodular functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) be normalized, monotone, and submodular, and let \(\alpha\ge0\). The ordinary truncation of \(f\) at level \(\alpha\) is
\[T_\alpha f(S)=\min\{f(S),\alpha\},\qquad S\subseteq V.\]
The function \(T_\alpha f\) is again normalized, monotone, and submodular. Its values agree with \(f\) below the truncation level and equal \(\alpha\) above it. The monotonicity hypothesis is essential for this general value-capping closure statement; capping an arbitrary submodular function need not preserve submodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capping a normalized monotone submodular function at a nonnegative level yields another normalized monotone submodular function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\alpha f(S)=\min\{f(S),\alpha\}\) is normalized, monotone, and submodular.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits ordinary value-capping truncation, and the hypotheses are sufficient for the stated closure properties. The naming convention and the claim that monotonicity is essential to the general closure statement need support from an authoritative source with a precise locator.

children.title: Dilworth Truncation
children.top_down_role: Partition-based truncation associated with Dilworth-type structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Dilworth Truncation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition-envelope truncation of an intersecting-submodular set function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(f(\varnothing)=0\) and be intersecting submodular: the submodular inequality holds whenever \(A\cap B\ne\varnothing\). Its Dilworth truncation is defined by \(Df(\varnothing)=0\) and, for nonempty \(S\subseteq V\),
\[Df(S)=\min_{\mathcal P\in\Pi(S)}\sum_{X\in\mathcal P}f(X),\]
where \(\Pi(S)\) is the set of partitions of \(S\) into nonempty blocks. Then \(Df\) is fully submodular and \(Df(S)\le f(S)\). It is the greatest submodular function dominated by \(f\) that agrees with \(f\) on singleton sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dilworth truncation minimizes total block value over partitions and converts an intersecting-submodular function into a fully submodular one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Df(S)=\min_{\mathcal P\in\Pi(S)}\sum_{X\in\mathcal P}f(X)\) is submodular and satisfies \(Df\le f\).

notation.meaning: partitions of S into nonempty blocks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The partition-envelope definition is a plausible fit for the Dilworth truncation leaf, but the record also asserts full submodularity and a greatest-dominated-function characterization. Those nontrivial claims, especially the maximality clause under exactly the stated hypotheses, require an authoritative theorem-level citation before their reliability can be established.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concerns the optimization problem denoted by (48.2); its formulation is inherited from the surrounding source context.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a submodular set function on S, problem (48.2) has an optimal solution whose positive-support sets form a laminar family.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists y\in\operatorname{Opt}(48.2)\text{ such that }\{U\in\mathcal P(S)\setminus\{\varnothing\}:y(U)>0\}\text{ is laminar}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dilworth truncation, bi-truncation, and crossing-submodular slices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The truncation formulas and bi-truncation terminology refer to the preceding constructions. The constant-sum slice assertion is a separate geometric property retained with its nonemptiness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{The partition function }f_{\mathrm p}\text{ defined for an intersecting-submodular or crossing-submodular function }f:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\text{ by minimizing }\sum_{i\in I}f(X_i)\text{ over admissible partitions }\{X_i:i\in I\}\text{ is called the Dilworth truncation of }f.\text{ In the crossing-case construction, }\widehat f_2^{\#}\text{ is the Dilworth truncation of the intersecting-supermodular function }(f_{\mathrm p})^{\#},\text{ and }f_2\text{ is called the bi-truncation of }f.\text{ Because }B(f)=B(f^{\#}),\text{ a dual formula for }f_2\text{ can be obtained by beginning with }f^{\#}.\text{ If }f\text{ is crossing-submodular on a crossing family, }P(f)\text{ need not be a submodular polyhedron; nevertheless, for every constant }k,\ P(f)\cap\{x:x(E)=k\}\neq\varnothing\Longrightarrow P(f)\cap\{x:x(E)=k\}\text{ is a base polyhedron.}
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The partition-minimum construction for an intersecting- or crossing-submodular function is called its Dilworth truncation. In the crossing-case construction, applying Dilworth truncation to the relevant dual intersecting-supermodular function yields the dual of the bi-truncation; an equivalent formula can start from the dual function because the two base polyhedra agree. A crossing-submodular polyhedron need not itself be submodular, but every nonempty constant-total-value slice of it is a base polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\text{ is intersecting-submodular or crossing-submodular on the corresponding intersecting or crossing family }\mathcal F.
\text{The terms }\widehat f_2^{\#}\text{ and }f_2\text{ use the preceding crossing-case construction.
\text{For the slice property, }f\text{ is crossing-submodular on a crossing family and }P(f)\cap\{x:x(E)=k\}\neq\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_{\mathrm p}\text{ is the Dilworth truncation of }f;\qquad f_2\text{ is the bi-truncation of }f;\qquad P(f)\cap\{x:x(E)=k\}\neq\varnothing\Longrightarrow P(f)\cap\{x:x(E)=k\}\text{ is a base polyhedron.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dilworth-truncation rank formulas and crossing-case base feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The induced systems and their notation are inherited from Theorem 2.5. The crossing-case rank formula applies only when the associated base polyhedron is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{(i) Let }f:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\text{ be intersecting-submodular on an intersecting family }\mathcal F\subseteq2^E,\ \varnothing,E\in\mathcal F,\ f(\varnothing)=0.\text{ Define }f_{\mathrm p}(Y)=\min\left\{\sum_{i\in I}f(X_i):\{X_i:i\in I\}\text{ partitions }Y,\ X_i\in\mathcal F\right\},\text{ taking }f_{\mathrm p}(Y)=+\infty\text{ if no admissible partition exists. Then }\mathcal D_1=\{Y\subseteq E:f_{\mathrm p}(Y)<+\infty\}\text{ and }f_1=f_{\mathrm p}|_{\mathcal D_1}.\quad\text{(ii) Let }f\text{ be crossing-submodular on a crossing family }\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\text{ with the same normalization, and define }f^{\#}(X)=f(E)-f(E\setminus X)\text{ when }E\setminus X\in\mathcal F.\text{ Then }B(f)\neq\varnothing\iff f(E)=f_{\mathrm p}(E)=(f^{\#})_{\mathrm p}(E),\text{ equivalently }\sum_{j\in J}f^{\#}(Y_j)\le f(E)\le\sum_{i\in I}f(X_i)\text{ for every pair of partitions }\{X_i\}_{i\in I},\{Y_j\}_{j\in J}\text{ of }E\text{ such that }X_i\in\mathcal F\text{ and }E\setminus Y_j\in\mathcal F.\text{ If }B(f)\neq\varnothing,\text{ let }\mathcal F_{\mathrm p}=\{X\subseteq E:f_{\mathrm p}(X)<+\infty\},\ (f_{\mathrm p})^{\#}(X)=f(E)-f_{\mathrm p}(E\setminus X),\text{ and define }\widehat f_2^{\#}(Y)=\max\left\{\sum_{i\in I}(f_{\mathrm p})^{\#}(X_i):\{X_i:i\in I\}\text{ partitions }Y,\ E\setminus X_i\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm p}\right\}.\text{ Then }f_2=\widehat f_2|_{\mathcal D_2},\quad \mathcal D_2=\{X\subseteq E:\widehat f_2(X)<+\infty\},\text{ where an empty minimum is }+\infty\text{ and an empty maximum is }-\infty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a normalized intersecting-submodular function, its partition minimum is the rank function of the induced submodular system on the sets admitting an admissible partition. For a normalized crossing-submodular function, the associated base polyhedron is nonempty exactly when the primal partition minimum and dual partition maximum both equal the total value, equivalently when all admissible primal and dual partitions satisfy the stated two-sided inequality. Conditional on nonemptiness, a second dual partition construction gives the bi-truncated rank function on its finite domain.
assumptions_latex: \text{In (i), }\mathcal F\text{ is intersecting and }f\text{ is intersecting-submodular on }\mathcal F.
\text{In (ii), }\mathcal F\text{ is crossing and }f\text{ is crossing-submodular on }\mathcal F.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_1=f_{\mathrm p}|_{\mathcal D_1};\qquad B(f)\neq\varnothing\iff f(E)=f_{\mathrm p}(E)=(f^{\#})_{\mathrm p}(E);\qquad B(f)\neq\varnothing\Longrightarrow f_2=\widehat f_2|_{\mathcal D_2}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dilworth truncation of a submodular function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the partition formula and records the source's maximal characterization of the resulting function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a submodular set function on \(S\). Its Dilworth truncation \(\widehat f:\mathcal P(S)\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \[\widehat f(U):=\min\left\{\sum_{P\in\mathcal Q}f(P)\;\middle|\;\mathcal Q\text{ is a partition of }U\text{ into nonempty sets}\right\}\quad(U\subseteq S).\] Thus \(\widehat f(\varnothing)=0\). Moreover, \(\widehat f\) is the unique largest submodular function \(g\) satisfying \(g(U)\le f(U)\) for every nonempty \(U\subseteq S\) and \(g(\varnothing)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Dilworth truncation of f is the minimum, over partitions of U into nonempty parts, of the sum of f on those parts. It is zero at the empty set and is the unique largest submodular function bounded above by f on nonempty subsets and equal to zero at the empty set.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is a submodular set function on }S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat f(U)=\min_{\mathcal Q\text{ partition of }U\text{ into nonempty sets}}\sum_{P\in\mathcal Q}f(P),\quad \widehat f(\varnothing)=0,\quad \widehat f=\max\{g:g\text{ is submodular},\ g(\varnothing)=0,\ g(U)\le f(U)\ \forall U\ne\varnothing\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Truncation Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of ordinary and Dilworth truncations on polymatroid rank functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) be normalized, monotone, and submodular. Because submodularity and \(f(\varnothing)=0\) imply \(f(S)\le\sum_{X\in\mathcal P}f(X)\) for every partition \(\mathcal P\) of \(S\), its Dilworth truncation satisfies \(Df=f\). Hence, for every \(\alpha\ge0\),
\[T_\alpha f(S)=\min\{f(S),\alpha\}\le Df(S)=f(S).\]
Pointwise equality holds exactly when \(f(S)\le\alpha\); equality on every subset holds exactly when \(f(V)\le\alpha\). Thus ordinary truncation may lower a polymatroid rank function, whereas unshifted Dilworth truncation does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polymatroid rank function, Dilworth truncation changes nothing, while ordinary truncation caps values and is therefore no larger.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\alpha f\le Df=f\), with global equality if and only if \(f(V)\le\alpha\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind fits a truncation comparison. Under the record's unshifted partition-envelope definition, the conclusion that a normalized submodular function satisfies Df=f is mathematically coherent, as is the comparison with ordinary truncation. A source is still required to verify that these are the intended two truncation conventions and to support the exact equality claims.

knowledge_statements.title: Submodular Convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infimal convolution of finite-valued set functions over disjoint decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be finite and let \(f,g:2^V\to\mathbb R\). Their submodular convolution, or infimal convolution, is the set function \(f\mathbin{\square}g:2^V\to\mathbb R\) defined by
\[
(f\mathbin{\square}g)(X)=\min_{Y\subseteq X}\bigl(f(Y)+g(X\setminus Y)\bigr),\qquad X\subseteq V.
\]
Equivalently, the minimum ranges over ordered disjoint pairs \((Y,Z)\) satisfying \(Y\mathbin{\dot\cup}Z=X\). The term “submodular convolution” names this operation in the submodular setting; submodularity of both operands alone is not asserted to imply submodularity of the result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convolution assigns each set the minimum total cost of partitioning it into two disjoint parts evaluated by the two operand functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f\mathbin{\square}g)(X)=\min_{Y\subseteq X}\{f(Y)+g(X\setminus Y)\}\) for every \(X\subseteq V\).

notation.meaning: infimal convolution of the two set functions
disjoint union of Y and Z

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convolution with a Modular Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Submodularity and polyhedral representation of convolution with a modular function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:2^V\to\mathbb{R} be submodular with F(\varnothing)=0, and let z\in\mathbb{R}^V, where z(S)=\sum_{i\in S}z_i. Define G(A)=\min_{B\subseteq A}\{F(B)+z(A\setminus B)\}. Then G is submodular, G(\varnothing)=0, and P(G)=P(F)\cap\{s\in\mathbb{R}^V:s\leq z\}. Moreover, G(A)\leq F(A) and G(A)\leq z(A) for every A\subseteq V.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convolution of a normalized submodular function with a modular function remains normalized and submodular. Its submodular polyhedron is the original polyhedron intersected with componentwise upper bounds, and its value does not exceed either input value on any set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is submodular},\quad G(\varnothing)=0,\quad P(G)=P(F)\cap\{s:s\leq z\},\quad G(A)\leq F(A),\ G(A)\leq z(A)\ \forall A\subseteq V.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Modular convolution and coordinate truncation of a polymatroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents coordinate upper-bound truncation through convolution with a modular function and states the normalized maximality property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal P(S)\to\mathbb R\) be submodular and let \(a\in\mathbb R^S\). Define \[(f\mid a)(U):=\min_{T\subseteq U}\bigl(f(T)+a(U\setminus T)\bigr),\qquad U\subseteq S.\] Then \(f\mid a\) is submodular and \[EP_{f\mid a}=\{x\in EP_f:x\le a\},\qquad P_{f\mid a}=\{x\in P_f:x\le a\}.\] Consequently, intersecting an extended polymatroid or polymatroid with coordinate upper bounds again yields an extended polymatroid or polymatroid, respectively. If additionally \(f(\varnothing)=0\), then \(f\mid a\) is the unique pointwise-largest submodular function \(f'\) satisfying \(f'(\varnothing)=0\), \(f'\le f\), and \(f'(U)\le a(U)\) for every \(U\subseteq S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convolving a submodular function with an additive weight function preserves submodularity and imposes coordinate upper bounds on its associated polyhedra. Under normalization, the result is the unique pointwise-largest normalized submodular function dominated by both the original function and the additive bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\mid a\text{ is submodular},\quad EP_{f\mid a}=EP_f\cap\{x:x\le a\},\quad P_{f\mid a}=P_f\cap\{x:x\le a\};\quad f(\varnothing)=0\implies f\mid a\text{ has the stated unique pointwise-maximality property}.

knowledge_statements.title: System Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of submodular systems under nonnegative linear aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be finite, let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be submodular, and let \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m\ge 0\). For any \(c\in\mathbb R\), define
\[
h(X)=c+\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i(X),\qquad X\subseteq V.
\]
Then \(h\) is submodular. If every \(f_i\) is normalized and \(c=0\), then \(h(\varnothing)=0\); if every \(f_i\) is also nondecreasing, then \(h\) is nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative weighted sum of submodular functions remains submodular; normalization and monotonicity are retained under the stated extra conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(A)+h(B)\ge h(A\cup B)+h(A\cap B)\) for all \(A,B\subseteq V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Submodular Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection by partial minimization over a disjoint block of variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) and \(W\) be disjoint finite sets and let \(f:2^{U\cup W}\to\mathbb R\) be submodular. Define the projection of \(f\) onto \(U\) by
\[
g(A)=\min_{B\subseteq W} f(A\cup B),\qquad A\subseteq U.
\]
Because the domain \(2^W\) is finite, each minimum is attained. Then \(g:2^U\to\mathbb R\) is submodular; explicitly, \(g(A)+g(C)\ge g(A\cup C)+g(A\cap C)\) for all \(A,C\subseteq U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a submodular function over an entire block of Boolean variables produces a submodular function on the remaining variables.
assumptions_latex: \(U\cap W=\varnothing\) and both sets are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(A)=\min_{B\subseteq W}f(A\cup B)\) defines a submodular function on \(2^U\).

notation.meaning: projection or partial minimization of f onto U

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partial Minimization of a Submodular Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination of a disjoint auxiliary ground-set block by partial minimization, including continuous and polyhedral representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let V\cap W=\varnothing, |V|=p, |W|=q, and let G:2^{V\cup W}\to\mathbb{R} be submodular with Lovász extension g:\mathbb{R}^{p+q}\to\mathbb{R}. For A\subseteq V define F(A)=\min_{B\subseteq W}G(A\cup B)-\min_{B\subseteq W}G(B). Then F is submodular and F(\varnothing)=0. If \min_{B\subseteq W}G(B)=0, then for every w\in\mathbb{R}_+^p the Lovász extension f of F satisfies f(w)=\min_{v\in\mathbb{R}_+^q}g(w,v), and P(F)=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^p:\exists t\in\mathbb{R}_+^q\text{ such that }(s,t)\in P(G)\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial minimization over a disjoint auxiliary block, followed by normalization, produces a normalized submodular function. If the auxiliary minimum is zero, its Lovász extension is the nonnegative partial minimum of the original extension, and its polyhedron is obtained by eliminating nonnegative auxiliary coordinates.
assumptions_latex: g:\mathbb{R}^{p+q}\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is the Lovász extension of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is submodular and }F(\varnothing)=0;\quad \min_{B\subseteq W}G(B)=0\Rightarrow\left[f(w)=\min_{v\in\mathbb{R}_+^q}g(w,v)\ \forall w\in\mathbb{R}_+^p,\ P(F)=\{s:\exists t\geq0,(s,t)\in P(G)\}\right].

knowledge_statements.title: Composition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar composition boundary for monotone submodular set functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:2^V\to I\) be nondecreasing and submodular, where \(I\subseteq\mathbb R\) is an interval, and let \(\phi:I\to\mathbb R\) be nondecreasing and concave. Then \(h=\phi\circ f\) is submodular. Concavity cannot be replaced by arbitrary convexity: on \(V=\{1,2\}\), take \(f(X)=|X|\) and \(\phi(t)=t^2\). The resulting \(h(X)=|X|^2\) violates submodularity because
\[
h(\{1\})+h(\{2\})=2<4=h(V)+h(\varnothing).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nondecreasing concave scalar composition preserves monotone submodularity, while even squaring a modular cardinality function can destroy submodularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\circ f\) is submodular; unrestricted convex scalar composition is not closure-preserving.

notation.meaning: interval containing the range of f
set function mapping X to φ(f(X))

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Preserving Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic operations preserving finite-set submodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be submodular. For fixed \(D\subseteq V\), both the restriction \(f|_D:2^D\to\mathbb R\), given by \((f|_D)(X)=f(X)\), and the contraction \(f/D:2^{V\setminus D}\to\mathbb R\), given by
\[
(f/D)(X)=f(X\cup D)-f(D),
\]
are submodular. Submodularity is also preserved by adding a modular function and by taking finite nonnegative linear combinations of submodular functions on the same ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restriction, contraction, modular perturbation, and finite nonnegative aggregation preserve submodularity.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) is submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f|_D\) and \(f/D\) are submodular, as are modular perturbations and nonnegative linear combinations.

notation.meaning: restriction of f to subsets of D
fixed subset being restricted to or contracted

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosure Phenomena
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise minimization is not closed within submodular set functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(V=\{1,2\}\), define modular, hence submodular, functions \(f(X)=\mathbf 1_{\{1\in X\}}\) and \(g(X)=\mathbf 1_{\{2\in X\}}\). Their pointwise minimum \(h(X)=\min\{f(X),g(X)\}\) satisfies \(h(\varnothing)=h(\{1\})=h(\{2\})=0\) and \(h(V)=1\). Consequently,
\[
h(\{1\})+h(\{2\})=0<1=h(V)+h(\varnothing),
\]
so \(h\) is not submodular. Thus pointwise minimization, unlike partial minimization over variables, does not preserve submodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise minimum of two modular functions can fail submodularity, already on a two-element ground set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h=\min\{f,g\}\) is not submodular although \(f\) and \(g\) are modular.

notation.meaning: pointwise minimum of f and g

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Boundary Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact universal criterion for an operation to preserve submodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An operation \(T\) on finite-valued set functions is submodularity-preserving precisely when, for every finite ground set \(V\), every admissible submodular input tuple \(\boldsymbol f\), and all \(A,B\subseteq V\), its output \(h=T(\boldsymbol f)\) satisfies
\[
h(A)+h(B)-h(A\cup B)-h(A\cap B)\ge 0.
\]
Accordingly, a closure claim is disproved by one admissible input tuple and one pair \((A,B)\) for which this deficit is negative. If \(T\) changes the ground set, the same criterion is applied on its output ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operation preserves submodularity exactly when every admissible output satisfies every lattice inequality; one negative deficit is a complete failure certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) maps its admissible finite-valued inputs to a set function \(h\).
Every component of \(\boldsymbol f\) required to be submodular is submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is closure-preserving if and only if the displayed deficit is nonnegative for every admissible \(\boldsymbol f,A,B\).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Failure Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smallest ground-set obstruction to closure under pointwise minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair on \(V=\{1,2\}\) given by \(f(X)=\mathbf 1_{\{1\in X\}}\) and \(g(X)=\mathbf 1_{\{2\in X\}}\) is a cardinality-minimal family witnessing failure of closure under pointwise minimum. Both functions are modular, but \(h=\min\{f,g\}\) has values \(h(\varnothing)=h(\{1\})=h(\{2\})=0\) and \(h(V)=1\), violating the sole nontrivial two-element lattice inequality. No smaller ground set can witness failure, because every real-valued function on a ground set of cardinality at most one is submodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two modular indicator functions on two elements form a smallest possible counterexample to closure under pointwise minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are the two singleton-membership indicators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{f,g\}\) is not submodular, and no counterexample exists on a ground set with fewer than two elements.

notation.meaning: pointwise minimum of f and g

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Submodular system and its polyhedron-base pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint definition of a normalized submodular system, its inequality polyhedron, and its full-set equality slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let E be finite, let \mathcal D\subseteq2^E be a distributive lattice with \varnothing,E\in\mathcal D, and let f:\mathcal D\to\mathbf R be submodular with f(\varnothing)=0. Then (\mathcal D,f) is a submodular system on E, with rank f(E). Its submodular polyhedron and base polyhedron are P(f)=\{x\in\mathbf R^E:x(X)\leq f(X)\ \forall X\in\mathcal D\} and B(f)=\{x\in P(f):x(E)=f(E)\}. Elements of P(f) are subbases and elements of B(f) are bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized submodular function on a distributive set lattice containing the empty and full sets defines a submodular system. Its submodular polyhedron satisfies all rank inequalities, and its base polyhedron is the slice on which the full-set inequality is tight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P(f)=\{x\in\mathbf R^E:x(X)\leq f(X)\ \forall X\in\mathcal D\},\qquad B(f)=P(f)\cap\{x:x(E)=f(E)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Submodular and Base Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Jointly defines the submodular polyhedron, its base polyhedron, and the latter's fixed-total slice representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) be submodular with \(F(\varnothing)=0\), and let \(s(A)=\sum_{k\in A}s_k\). Then
\[
P(F)=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^p: s(A)\leq F(A)\text{ for every }A\subseteq V\},
\]
and
\[
B(F)=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^p:s(V)=F(V),\ s(A)\leq F(A)\text{ for every }A\subseteq V\}=P(F)\cap\{s:s(V)=F(V)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a normalized submodular function, the submodular polyhedron contains the vectors whose coordinate sums over every subset do not exceed the function value. The base polyhedron is its slice where the full-set inequality is tight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P(F)=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^p:\forall A\subseteq V,\ s(A)\leq F(A)\},\qquad B(F)=P(F)\cap\{s:s(V)=F(V)\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Submodular Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedron induced by the upper subset-sum inequalities of a normalized submodular function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be finite and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be submodular with \(f(\varnothing)=0\). For \(x\in\mathbb R^V\), write \(x(X)=\sum_{i\in X}x_i\). The submodular polyhedron associated with \(f\) is
\[
P(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x(X)\le f(X)\text{ for every }X\subseteq V\}.
\]
The empty-set inequality is redundant under normalization. In general, \(P(f)\) is nonempty and unbounded in coordinatewise nonpositive directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The submodular polyhedron consists of vectors whose sum over every subset does not exceed the submodular function's value on that subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x(X)\le f(X)\text{ for all }X\subseteq V\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Network-flow representation of a monotone submodular function and its positive submodular polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a sink-set function from capacitated multi-source, multi-sink flows and gives its min-cut representation, submodularity, monotonicity, and positive-polyhedron characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S,V\subseteq W\), let \(c:W\times W\to\mathbb R_+\), and define \(\varphi(A,B)=\sum_{k\in A,\,j\in B}\varphi(k,j)\). Let \(\mathcal F\) be the set of functions \(\varphi:W\times W\to\mathbb R_+\) satisfying \(\varphi\le c\), \(\varphi(W,\{w\})-\varphi(\{w\},W)=0\) for every \(w\in W\setminus(S\cup V)\), \(\varphi(W,\{s\})-\varphi(\{s\},W)\le0\) for every \(s\in S\), and \(\varphi(W,\{t\})-\varphi(\{t\},W)\ge0\) for every \(t\in V\). For \(A\subseteq V\), define \(F(A)=\max_{\varphi\in\mathcal F}\bigl[\varphi(W,A)-\varphi(A,W)\bigr]\). Then \[F(A)=\min_{\substack{X\subseteq W:\,S\subseteq X,\ A\subseteq W\setminus X}}c(X,W\setminus X).\] Consequently, \(F\) is nondecreasing and submodular. Moreover, \[s\in P(F)\cap\mathbb R_+^V\iff \exists\varphi\in\mathcal F\ \text{such that}\ \forall k\in V,\quad s_k=\varphi(W,\{k\})-\varphi(\{k\},W).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a capacitated network with source set S and sink set V, consider nonnegative capacity-feasible flows that conserve flow at all other vertices, have nonpositive net inflow at sources, and nonnegative net inflow at sinks. For each subset A of sinks, its maximum aggregate net inflow equals the minimum capacity of a cut separating every source from A. This defines a nondecreasing submodular function. A nonnegative vector belongs to its submodular polyhedron exactly when its coordinates are the individual sink net inflows of a feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall A\subseteq V:\ F(A)=\min_{X\subseteq W:\,S\subseteq X,\,A\subseteq W\setminus X}c(X,W\setminus X);\quad F\text{ is nondecreasing and submodular};\quad s\in P(F)\cap\mathbb R_+^V\iff\exists\varphi\in\mathcal F\ \forall k\in V:\ s_k=\varphi(W,\{k\})-\varphi(\{k\},W).
