knowledge_statements.statement_title: Associated polymatroid and extended polymatroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines both inequality systems and states their exact nonemptiness conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let E be finite and let f:2^E\to\mathbb{R} be submodular. Writing x(F):=\sum_{e\in F}x_e, define
\[
P_f:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^E:x(F)\le f(F)\ \forall F\subseteq E,\ x\ge0\},
\qquad
EP_f:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^E:x(F)\le f(F)\ \forall F\subseteq E\}.
\]
Then P_f is the polymatroid associated with f and EP_f is its extended polymatroid. Moreover,
\[
EP_f\ne\varnothing\iff f(\varnothing)\ge0,
\qquad
P_f\ne\varnothing\iff f(F)\ge0\ \forall F\subseteq E.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The associated polymatroid consists of the nonnegative vectors satisfying every submodular subset inequality, while the extended polymatroid omits nonnegativity. The extended polymatroid is nonempty exactly when the empty-set value is nonnegative; the polymatroid is nonempty exactly when the function is nonnegative on every subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_f=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^E:x(F)\le f(F)\ \forall F\subseteq E,\ x\ge0\},\quad EP_f=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^E:x(F)\le f(F)\ \forall F\subseteq E\},\quad EP_f\ne\varnothing\iff f(\varnothing)\ge0,\quad P_f\ne\varnothing\iff f\ge0

knowledge_statements.title: Base Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total-sum equality face of a submodular polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be finite and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be submodular with \(f(\varnothing)=0\). Its base polyhedron is
\[
B(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x(X)\le f(X)\text{ for every }X\subseteq V,\;x(V)=f(V)\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(B(f)=P(f)\cap\{x:x(V)=f(V)\}\). For finite-valued normalized submodular \(f\), the set \(B(f)\) is a nonempty bounded polyhedron and hence a polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The base polyhedron is the slice of the submodular polyhedron where the total coordinate sum equals the full-set value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(f)=P(f)\cap\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x(V)=f(V)\}\) is nonempty and bounded.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Base vectors and the base polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the base face of an extended set-function polyhedron and records its coordinate bounds and boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be finite and let \(f:\mathcal P(S)\to\mathbb R\). A vector \(x\in EP_f\) is a base vector of \(f\) if \(x(S)=f(S)\). The set of all base vectors is \[B_f:=\{x\in\mathbb R^S:x(U)\le f(U)\text{ for every }U\subseteq S,\ x(S)=f(S)\}.\] Thus \(B_f\) is the face of \(EP_f\) on which the inequality indexed by \(S\) is tight. For every \(s\in S\), each \(x\in B_f\) satisfies \[f(S)-f(S\setminus\{s\})\le x_s\le f(\{s\}),\] so \(B_f\) is bounded and, when nonempty, is a polytope. A vector in \(P_f\) satisfying \(x(S)=f(S)\) is analogously a base vector of \(P_f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A base vector is feasible for the extended set-function polyhedron and makes the full-ground-set inequality tight. All base vectors form a bounded face described by the subset inequalities together with equality on the ground set; if nonempty, this face is a polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B_f=EP_f\cap\{x:x(S)=f(S)\}\text{ is a bounded face of }EP_f\text{ and, when nonempty, a polytope}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Anti-isomorphism between associated sublattices and base-polyhedron faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete face-poset representation of a submodular base polyhedron by its associated sublattices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\mathbf D$ be the associated collection of sublattices and $\mathbf F$ the collection of all nonempty faces of $B(f)$. Then
\[
\mathbf F=\{F(\mathcal D_0)\mid \mathcal D_0\in\mathbf D\}.
\]
Distinct members of $\mathbf D$ determine distinct faces, and for all $\mathcal D_1,\mathcal D_2\in\mathbf D$,
\[
\mathcal D_1\subseteq\mathcal D_2\iff F(\mathcal D_2)\subseteq F(\mathcal D_1).
\]
Thus $F$ is an anti-isomorphism from $\mathbf D$ onto $\mathbf F$. The face lattice is $\mathbf F$, or $\mathbf F\cup\{\varnothing\}$ when $\mathbf F$ has no unique minimal element.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face is represented uniquely by an associated sublattice, and sublattice inclusion corresponds exactly to reverse face inclusion. The empty face is adjoined when the nonempty-face poset has no unique minimum.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf D\text{ is the associated collection of sublattices}
\mathbf F\text{ is the collection of all nonempty faces of }B(f)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F:(\mathbf D,\subseteq)\to(\mathbf F,\subseteq)\text{ is an anti-isomorphism, with }\mathcal D_1\subseteq\mathcal D_2\iff F(\mathcal D_2)\subseteq F(\mathcal D_1).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when a coordinate box intersects a matroid base polytope through its downward and upward closures.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Base polyhedron and greedy-vertex representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Base-polyhedron geometry for a normalized submodular function, together with the representation used by Schrijver's algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $U$ be finite and let $f:2^U\to\mathbb R$ be submodular with $f(\varnothing)=0$. Define
$B(f)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^U:\sum_{u\in A}x(u)\le f(A)\ \text{for every }A\subseteq U,\ \sum_{u\in U}x(u)=f(U)\right\}$.
For a total order $\prec$ on $U$, define
$b^\prec(u)=f(\{v\in U:v\preccurlyeq u\})-f(\{v\in U:v\prec u\})$.
Then the vertices of $B(f)$ are precisely the vectors $b^\prec$. Schrijver's algorithm maintains its point $x\in B(f)$ as an explicit convex combination $x=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i b^{\prec_i}$, where $\lambda_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The base polyhedron of a finite normalized submodular function is defined by all subset inequalities and equality on the ground set. Its vertices are exactly the greedy marginal vectors induced by total orders. Schrijver's algorithm explicitly maintains its current point as a convex combination of these vertices.
assumptions_latex: Each $\prec$ is a total order on $U$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{vert}(B(f))=\{b^\prec:\prec\text{ is a total order on }U\},\qquad x=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i b^{\prec_i}\in B(f).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Base Polyhedron and Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the base polyhedron associated with a submodular function and its integrality property when the function is integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a submodular function \(\rho:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), its base polyhedron is \[\mathbf{B}(\rho)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^V\mid x(X)\le\rho(X)\ \text{for every proper subset }X\subset V,\ x(V)=\rho(V)\}.\] If \(\rho\) is integer-valued, then \[\mathbf{B}(\rho)=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\mathbf{B}(\rho)\cap\mathbb{Z}^V\bigr),\] and hence every vertex of \(\mathbf{B}(\rho)\) is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The base polyhedron consists of vectors satisfying the submodular upper bounds on every proper subset and equality on the whole ground set. When the submodular function is integer-valued, the polyhedron is the convex hull of its integer points, so all vertices are integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf{B}(\rho)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^V\mid x(X)\le\rho(X)\ (\forall X\subset V),\ x(V)=\rho(V)\};\qquad \rho\text{ integer-valued}\Rightarrow\mathbf{B}(\rho)=\operatorname{conv}(\mathbf{B}(\rho)\cap\mathbb{Z}^V).

children.top_down_role: Geometric relation between a submodular polyhedron and its base region.

knowledge_statements.title: Base-Slice Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-hyperplane and tight-set structure of the base slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For normalized submodular \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\), the base polyhedron is the exposed slice
\[
B(f)=P(f)\cap\{x:x(V)=f(V)\}
\]
taken from the valid inequality \(x(V)\le f(V)\). For \(x\in B(f)\), define \(\mathcal T_x=\{X\subseteq V:x(X)=f(X)\}\). Then \(\varnothing,V\in\mathcal T_x\), and \(\mathcal T_x\) is closed under union and intersection. Thus the subset inequalities active at any base form a lattice of tight sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The base polyhedron is the full-set supporting slice of the submodular polyhedron, and each base's tight subsets form a union-intersection lattice.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) is normalized and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(f)=P(f)\cap\{x:x(V)=f(V)\}\), and \(\mathcal T_x\) is closed under \(\cup\) and \(\cap\).

notation.meaning: family of subsets tight at x

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Orderings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds greedy construction for linear optimization over a base polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n=|V|\). Input a normalized submodular function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) through a value oracle and weights \(w\in\mathbb R^V\). Choose a permutation \(\pi\) of \(V\) with \(w_{\pi(1)}\ge\cdots\ge w_{\pi(n)}\), set \(S_0=\varnothing\), and for \(k=1,\ldots,n\) set
\[
S_k=\{\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(k)\},\qquad x_{\pi(k)}=f(S_k)-f(S_{k-1}).
\]
Output \(x\). Then \(x\in B(f)\) and \(x\) maximizes \(w^\top y\) over \(y\in B(f)\). Ties in the weights may be resolved arbitrarily.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort the elements of the finite ground set by nonincreasing weight and assign successive marginal values; the resulting base maximizes the given linear objective.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite, \(n=|V|\), and \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) is normalized and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in B(f)\) and \(w^\top x=\max\{w^\top y:y\in B(f)\}\).

notation.meaning: cardinality of the finite ground set V
permutation of V sorting weights in nonincreasing order
first k elements of the greedy ordering

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Edmonds greedy characterization of base-polyhedron linear optimization

children.title: Extreme Points
children.top_down_role: Vertex structure of submodular and base polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds’ characterization for the base polyhedron of a normalized finite submodular function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\) be submodular with \(f(\varnothing)=0\), and define \(B(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E,\ x(E)=f(E)\}\). For a permutation \(\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n)\), put \(S_k=\{\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k\}\) and \(x^\pi_{\pi_k}=f(S_k)-f(S_{k-1})\). Then \(x^\pi\) is an extreme point of \(B(f)\). Conversely, every extreme point of \(B(f)\) equals \(x^\pi\) for at least one permutation \(\pi\) of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extreme points of a submodular base polyhedron are exactly the marginal-increment vectors produced by permutations of the ground set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ext} B(f)=\{x^\pi:\pi\text{ is a permutation of }E\}\).

notation.meaning: The sum of coordinates of x indexed by S.
The greedy marginal vector associated with permutation π.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem and content kind fit the Extreme Points leaf, but the record cites no source or inspectable locator for Edmonds’ characterization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme-base recognition and dependence-set construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition of extreme bases through nested tight sets, with construction of element dependence sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a submodular system $(E,\mathcal D,f)$ and $x\in B(f)$, initialize $S\leftarrow\varnothing$. For $i=1,\ldots,|E|$, seek $e_i\in E\setminus S$ such that $S\cup\{e_i\}\in\mathcal D$ and $x(S\cup\{e_i\})=f(S\cup\{e_i\})$. If none exists, stop and declare that $x$ is not an extreme base. Otherwise set $S\leftarrow S\cup\{e_i\}$ and $T\leftarrow S$. In reverse order through $e_{i-1},\ldots,e_1$, remove $e_{i-j}$ from $T$ whenever $x(T\setminus\{e_{i-j}\})=f(T\setminus\{e_{i-j}\})$, and then set $\operatorname{dep}(x,e_i)\leftarrow T$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting with the empty set, extend a nested chain by elements whose extensions belong to the domain and are tight for x. Failure to extend certifies that x is not an extreme base. After each extension, scan earlier elements in reverse order, removing any whose deletion preserves tightness; the remaining set is the dependence set of the new element.
assumptions_latex: (E,\mathcal D,f)\text{ is the submodular system in the surrounding context}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure either certifies that }x\text{ is not an extreme base or completes the ordering and constructs }\operatorname{dep}(x,e_i)\text{ for every }i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme points of a base polyhedron from greedy orderings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy characterization of all extreme points of the base polyhedron of a normalized submodular function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:2^{[p]}\to\mathbb{R} be submodular with F(\varnothing)=0. For a permutation (j_1,\ldots,j_p), let A_k=\{j_1,\ldots,j_k\}, A_0=\varnothing, and set s_{j_k}=F(A_k)-F(A_{k-1}). Then the extreme points of B(F) are exactly the vectors obtained in this way over all permutations of [p].
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extreme points of the base polyhedron are precisely the successive-marginal vectors produced by the greedy construction over all orderings of the ground-set elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ext}B(F)=\left\{s^{\pi}:\pi\text{ is a permutation of }[p],\ s^{\pi}_{j_k}=F(A_k)-F(A_{k-1})\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme-point characterization by maximal chains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the extreme points of a submodular base polyhedron through marginal increments along a maximal lattice chain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in B(f)\). Then \(x\) is an extreme point of \(B(f)\) if and only if there exists a maximal chain \[\varnothing=S_0\subset S_1\subset\cdots\subset S_n=E\] of \(\mathcal D\) such that, with \(\{e_i\}=S_i\setminus S_{i-1}\), \[x(e_i)=f(S_i)-f(S_{i-1})\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A base is an extreme point exactly when its coordinates equal the successive marginal increments of f along some maximal chain of the distributive lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{ext}B(f)\iff \exists\text{ a maximal chain }\varnothing=S_0\subset\cdots\subset S_n=E\text{ with }\{e_i\}=S_i\setminus S_{i-1}\text{ and }x(e_i)=f(S_i)-f(S_{i-1})\ \forall i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme Points of a Base-Polyhedron Face

children.title: Ordering–Vertex Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between greedy orderings and polyhedral vertices.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering–Vertex Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy representation of vertices together with the criterion for an ordering to expose its vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\), \(B(f)\), and \(x^\pi\) be as above. If \(w\in\mathbb R^E\) satisfies \(w_{\pi_1}>\cdots>w_{\pi_n}\), then \(x^\pi\) is the unique maximizer of \(w^Tx\) over \(B(f)\). More generally, a permutation \(\pi\) represents a vertex \(v\) precisely when every prefix \(S_k=\{\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k\}\) is tight at \(v\) and \(v_{\pi_k}=f(S_k)-f(S_{k-1})\) for all \(k\). Thus orderings map surjectively, but not necessarily injectively, onto the vertices of \(B(f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each ordering yields a greedy vertex uniquely exposed by strictly decreasing ordered weights; a vertex may be represented by several orderings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\mapsto x^\pi\) is a surjection from permutations of \(E\) onto \(\operatorname{ext}B(f)\).

notation.meaning: The kth prefix set of π.
A linear objective ordered by π.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the leaf and is mathematically plausible, but neither unique exposure nor the surjective ordering–vertex correspondence has cited support.

children.title: Degenerate Ordering Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nonuniqueness and degeneracy arising from multiple compatible orderings.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Ordering Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjacent-interchange criterion for nonunique ordering representations of a greedy vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi\) contain consecutive elements \(i,j\) after a prefix \(S\), and let \(\pi'\) be obtained by interchanging only \(i\) and \(j\). Their greedy vectors coincide exactly when \[f(S\cup\{i\})+f(S\cup\{j\})=f(S)+f(S\cup\{i,j\}).\] If the inequality is strict, the two greedy vectors are distinct. Consequently, ordering degeneracy occurs along zero submodularity-slack interchanges; permutations representing one vertex are connected through adjacent interchanges satisfying the displayed equality at their current prefixes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adjacent elements may be swapped without changing a greedy vertex exactly when their conditional submodularity inequality is tight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\pi=x^{\pi'}\iff f(S\cup\{i\})+f(S\cup\{j\})=f(S)+f(S\cup\{i,j\})\).

notation.meaning: The prefix preceding the interchanged elements.
The ordering obtained by swapping adjacent i and j.
The greedy vector associated with π.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The adjacent-swap equality is plausible and the property kind fits, but the stronger connectivity assertion for all permutations representing a vertex requires an authoritative source and locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Elementary Exchange Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-exchange feasibility in a submodular base polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in B(f)\) and distinct \(i,j\in E\), consider the elementary exchange \(x'=x+\alpha(\chi_i-\chi_j)\), where \(\alpha\ge0\). Define \[c_{ij}(x)=\min\{f(S)-x(S):S\subseteq E,\ i\in S,\ j\notin S\}.\] Then \(x'\in B(f)\) if and only if \(0\le\alpha\le c_{ij}(x)\). The total coordinate sum is preserved, while precisely the inequalities indexed by sets containing \(i\) and excluding \(j\) restrict the admissible step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elementary exchange increases one coordinate and decreases another; its largest feasible step is the minimum slack over separating sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x+\alpha(\chi_i-\chi_j)\in B(f)\iff 0\le\alpha\le c_{ij}(x)\).

notation.meaning: The exchange capacity from j to i at x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exchange-feasibility representation fits the topic and is internally coherent, but the minimum-slack characterization has no cited source.

children.title: Polyhedral Faces
children.top_down_role: Face families and their tight-set descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposed-face representation using ordered weight blocks and tight prefix sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in B(f)}w^Tx\), and partition \(E=L_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup L_k\) so that \(w\) is constant on each \(L_r\) and strictly decreases from \(L_r\) to \(L_{r+1}\). Put \(A_r=L_1\cup\cdots\cup L_r\). Then \[F=\{x\in B(f):x(A_r)=f(A_r),\ r=1,\ldots,k-1\}.\] Conversely, every nonempty face of \(B(f)\) has such a representation for some ordered partition, after redundant prefix equalities are permitted or removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every face of a submodular base polyhedron is obtained by making the prefix inequalities of an ordered partition tight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=B(f)\cap\bigcap_{r=1}^{k-1}\{x:x(A_r)=f(A_r)\}\) for an ordered partition of \(E\).

notation.meaning: A block of equal objective coefficients.
The union of the first r ordered blocks.
An exposed face of the base polyhedron.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ordered-partition representation matches Polyhedral Faces, but the converse characterization of every nonempty face lacks an authoritative citation and locator.

children.title: Polyhedral Dimensions
children.top_down_role: Dimension and codimension structure of submodular polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Dimensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension formula in terms of inseparable components of a submodular system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Call a nonempty set \(C\subseteq E\) inseparable for \(f\) if no nontrivial partition \(C=C_1\dot\cup C_2\) satisfies \(f(C)=f(C_1)+f(C_2)\), using the appropriate restriction after decomposing \(E\). Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_q\) be the maximal inseparable components of \(f\). Then the affine hull of \(B(f)\) is determined by \(x(C_r)=f(C_r)\) for \(r=1,\ldots,q\), and \[\dim B(f)=|E|-q.\] In particular, \(B(f)\) has dimension \(|E|-1\) exactly when \(f\) is inseparable on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The base-polyhedron dimension equals the ground-set size minus the number of maximal inseparable components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim B(f)=|E|-q\), where \(q\) is the number of maximal inseparable components.

notation.meaning: A maximal inseparable component of f.
The number of maximal inseparable components.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits Polyhedral Dimensions, but “using the appropriate restriction after decomposing E” does not precisely define the components. A source is needed to settle the exact component notion, affine-hull equations, and dimension formula.

children.title: Connected Components
children.top_down_role: Component decompositions associated with submodular systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Connected Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inseparable components governing the affine decomposition of a submodular base polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a normalized submodular function \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\), a nonempty subset \(C\subseteq E\) is inseparable if every partition \(C=C_1\dot\cup C_2\) into nonempty sets satisfies \(f(C)<f(C_1)+f(C_2)\). The connected components of \(f\) are the maximal inseparable blocks in the unique finest partition \(E=C_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup C_q\) satisfying \[f(X)=\sum_{r=1}^q f(X\cap C_r)\qquad\text{for every }X\subseteq E.\] The function is connected, or inseparable, when \(q=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Connected components are the maximal blocks across which the submodular function decomposes additively; one block means the function is inseparable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E=C_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup C_q\) is the unique finest additive decomposition into inseparable blocks.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Connected Components, but the asserted unique finest additive decomposition and its equivalence with maximal inseparable blocks require authoritative support; no source is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dependency-Graph Representation of Connected Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the partition \Pi(\mathcal{D}_0) through the dependency graph associated with any base.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any x\in\mathrm{B}(f), let G(x)=(E,A(x)), where A(x)=\{(e,e')\mid e'\in\operatorname{dep}(x,e)\}. Then \Pi(\mathcal{D}_0) is the set of vertex sets of the connected components of G(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any base x, the blocks of Pi(D0) are exactly the vertex sets of the connected components of the graph whose arcs record the dependency relation dep(x,e).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi(\mathcal{D}_0)=\{V(C)\mid C\text{ is a connected component of }G(x)\}

children.title: Face–Component Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Links among face structure, dimension loss, and component decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Face–Component Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product decomposition and dimension of a face through components of contracted submodular minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a face \(F\) be defined by a tight chain \(\varnothing=A_0\subset A_1\subset\cdots\subset A_k=E\), and put \(L_r=A_r\setminus A_{r-1}\). Define the minor \(f_r:2^{L_r}\to\mathbb R\) by \(f_r(X)=f(A_{r-1}\cup X)-f(A_{r-1})\). Then restriction to the blocks gives an affine isomorphism \[F\cong\prod_{r=1}^k B(f_r).\] If \(q_r\) is the number of inseparable components of \(f_r\), then \(\dim F=\sum_{r=1}^k(|L_r|-q_r)\). Thus face dimension is determined by the component structure of the chain minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face factors into base polyhedra of chain minors, and its dimension is the sum of their sizes minus their component counts.
assumptions_latex: The displayed chain defines a nonempty face \(F\) of \(B(f)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\cong\prod_r B(f_r)\) and \(\dim F=\sum_r(|L_r|-q_r)\).

notation.meaning: The rth difference block of the tight chain.
The number of inseparable components of f_r.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the correspondence leaf, but the affine product decomposition and component-based dimension formula are nontrivial and unsupported by any citation.

children.title: Tangent Cones
children.top_down_role: Local feasible-direction geometry at points of submodular polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inner tangent cone of a base polyhedron at a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in B(f)\), the inner tangent cone is \[T_{B(f)}(x)=\operatorname{cl}\{\lambda(y-x):\lambda\ge0,\ y\in B(f)\}.\] Because \(B(f)\) is polyhedral, equivalently \[T_{B(f)}(x)=\{d\in\mathbb R^E:d(E)=0,\ d(S)\le0\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\text{ with }x(S)=f(S)\}.\] Thus only inequalities tight at \(x\) constrain first-order feasible directions; inequalities having positive slack impose no local homogeneous restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent cone consists of zero-sum directions whose sums over every tight set are nonpositive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{B(f)}(x)=\{d:d(E)=0,\ d(S)\le0\text{ whenever }x(S)=f(S)\}\).

notation.meaning: The inner tangent cone of B(f) at x.
The sum of direction coordinates over S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and tight-inequality characterization fit Tangent Cones and are internally consistent, but no inspectable source supports the polyhedral equivalence.

children.title: Exchange Capacity
children.top_down_role: Capacity structure governing feasible coordinate exchanges.

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange Capacity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum feasible magnitude of a directed coordinate exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in B(f)\) and distinct \(i,j\in E\), the exchange capacity from \(j\) to \(i\) is \[c_{ij}(x)=\sup\{\alpha\ge0:x+\alpha(\chi_i-\chi_j)\in B(f)\}.\] It admits the slack representation \[c_{ij}(x)=\min_{\substack{S\subseteq E\\ i\in S,\ j\notin S}}\bigl(f(S)-x(S)\bigr).\] Since the indexing family is nonempty and finite, the minimum is attained and is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exchange capacity is the largest feasible transfer from coordinate j to coordinate i, equal to the minimum slack of a set separating them.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c_{ij}(x)=\min\{f(S)-x(S):i\in S,\ j\notin S\}\).

notation.meaning: Capacity to increase i while decreasing j.
The slack of the inequality indexed by S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Exchange Capacity, but the equality between the feasible-step supremum and minimum separating-set slack lacks cited support.

children.title: Cone–Exchange Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between local cone directions and admissible exchanges.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone–Exchange Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generation of the tangent cone by positive-capacity elementary exchanges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in B(f)\), form the directed exchange set \(D_x=\{(i,j):i\ne j,\ c_{ij}(x)>0\}\). Then the tangent cone of the base polyhedron at \(x\) is \[T_{B(f)}(x)=\operatorname{cone}\{\chi_i-\chi_j:(i,j)\in D_x\}.\] Hence a directed elementary exchange is a feasible infinitesimal direction exactly when it has positive capacity, and every tangent direction is a nonnegative linear combination of such exchange directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-capacity coordinate exchanges generate the entire tangent cone of a submodular base polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{B(f)}(x)=\operatorname{cone}\{\chi_i-\chi_j:c_{ij}(x)>0\}\).

notation.meaning: The directed positive-capacity exchange pairs at x.
The exchange capacity from j to i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the correspondence leaf, but generation of the entire tangent cone by positive-capacity elementary exchanges is nontrivial and has no source or locator.

children.title: Exchange Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Boundary regimes where exchange capacity vanishes or becomes nonunique.

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tight-set certificate for a zero-capacity directed exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in B(f)\) and let \(i\ne j\). The directed exchange from \(j\) to \(i\) is degenerate when \(c_{ij}(x)=0\). This occurs if and only if there exists a tight set \(S\subseteq E\) satisfying \[i\in S,\qquad j\notin S,\qquad x(S)=f(S).\] Such a set is a verifiable certificate of degeneracy: every positive displacement \(\alpha(\chi_i-\chi_j)\) increases \(x(S)\) above \(f(S)\), so no positive exchange step is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed exchange has zero capacity exactly when a tight set contains its receiving coordinate but excludes its donating coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c_{ij}(x)=0\iff\exists S\subseteq E:\ i\in S,\ j\notin S,\ x(S)=f(S)\).

notation.meaning: The exchange capacity from j to i.
A tight separating set certifying zero capacity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind exactly fits the degeneracy leaf, and the statement follows plausibly from the slack formula, but neither that formula nor the certificate equivalence is cited.

children.title: Polyhedral Integrality
children.top_down_role: Integral vertex and face structure in submodular polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-vertex theorem for base polyhedra of integer-valued submodular functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and let \(f:2^E\to\mathbb Z\) be submodular with \(f(\varnothing)=0\). Define \(x(S)=\sum_{e\in S}x_e\) and the base polyhedron \[B(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E,\ x(E)=f(E)\}.\] If \(B(f)\neq\varnothing\), then every vertex of \(B(f)\) is integral. In particular, \(B(f)\) is an integral polyhedron: \[B(f)=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(B(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty base polyhedron defined by an integer-valued normalized submodular function has only integral vertices and equals the convex hull of its integer points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(f)=\operatorname{conv}(B(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E)\).

notation.meaning: Sum of the coordinates indexed by S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polymatroid intersection integrality with coordinate bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States primal and dual integral-optimum guarantees for two intersecting-family submodular inequality systems with lower and upper coordinate bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\mathcal C_1,\mathcal C_2\subseteq2^E$ be intersecting families, let $f_k:\mathcal C_k\to\mathbb Q$ be submodular on intersecting pairs for $k=1,2$, and consider maximizing $c^Tx$ subject to
$$l(e)\le x(e)\le u(e)\quad(e\in E),$$
$$x(T)\le f_1(T)\quad(T\in\mathcal C_1),\qquad x(T)\le f_2(T)\quad(T\in\mathcal C_2).$$
Assume an optimum is attained. If $l,u,f_1,f_2$ are integral wherever finite, with infinite coordinate bounds allowed, then the problem has an integral optimum solution. If additionally $c\in\mathbb Z^E$, its dual problem has an integral optimum solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an attained linear maximization problem over two intersecting-family submodular systems and coordinate bounds, integral finite bounds and right-hand sides guarantee an integral primal optimum. An integral objective also guarantees an integral dual optimum.
assumptions_latex: f_k:\mathcal C_k\to\mathbb Q\text{ is submodular on intersecting pairs for }k=1,2
\max\{c^Tx:x\text{ satisfies the stated system}\}\text{ has an optimum solution}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ an integral primal optimum};\qquad c\in\mathbb Z^E\Rightarrow\exists\text{ an integral dual optimum}

children.title: Integer Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Decomposition behavior of integer points across scaled polyhedral regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer decomposition property for integral submodular base polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite, let \(f:2^E\to\mathbb Z\) be normalized and submodular, and suppose \(B(f)\neq\varnothing\). For every \(k\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and every \(z\in kB(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E\), there exist \(z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(k)}\in B(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E\) such that \[z=z^{(1)}+\cdots+z^{(k)}.\] Equivalently, the homogenized semigroup generated by \(\{(y,1):y\in B(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E\}\) contains every lattice point \((z,k)\) with \(z\in kB(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every integer point in a positive integer dilation of an integral submodular base polyhedron decomposes into that many integer points of the original polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(kB(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E=(B(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E)+\cdots+(B(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E)\), with \(k\) summands.

notation.meaning: The scalar dilation of the base polyhedron by k.
Integer summands belonging to the original base polyhedron.

children.title: Integrality–Decomposition Link
children.top_down_role: Structural relation between integral polyhedra and integer decomposition behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality–Decomposition Link
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The decomposition property strengthens integrality for lattice polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a rational polytope with the integer decomposition property: for every \(k\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and \(z\in kP\cap\mathbb Z^n\), there exist \(z_1,\ldots,z_k\in P\cap\mathbb Z^n\) satisfying \(z=z_1+\cdots+z_k\). Then \[P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb Z^n),\] so \(P\) is integral. The converse fails for general integral polytopes; thus integer decomposition is strictly stronger than integrality outside special classes such as integral submodular base polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer decomposition implies polyhedral integrality, but an arbitrary integral polytope need not have integer decomposition; submodular base polyhedra possess both properties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb Z^n)\), while the general converse is false.

notation.meaning: The scalar dilation of P by the positive integer k.

children.title: Nonintegral Boundary Regimes
children.top_down_role: Data regimes where integral structure or decomposition behavior fails.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonintegral Boundary Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of integer-valuedness already destroys integrality on a one-element ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{e\}\) and define the normalized submodular function \(f\) by \(f(\varnothing)=0\) and \(f(E)=1/2\). Its base polyhedron is \[B(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x_e=1/2\}.\] Hence its unique vertex is nonintegral and \(B(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E=\varnothing\). Thus submodularity and normalization alone do not imply polyhedral integrality; the integer-valued hypothesis in the integral base-polyhedron theorem cannot be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized submodular function taking value one-half on a singleton has a base polyhedron whose sole vertex is one-half, so integer-valuedness is essential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(f)=\{(1/2)\}\) is not integral.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singleton counterexample is correct and appropriately classified as a counterexample, but it has no evidence record or source locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Lovász Extension Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chain-interpolation representation of a normalized set function on the unit cube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(f(\varnothing)=0\). For \(x\in[0,1]^E\), choose an ordering \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\) with \(x_{e_1}\ge\cdots\ge x_{e_n}\), put \(S_i=\{e_1,\ldots,e_i\}\), and set \(x_{e_{n+1}}=0\). The Lovász extension is \[\widehat f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(x_{e_i}-x_{e_{i+1}}\bigr)f(S_i).\] It is independent of tie-breaking, satisfies \(\widehat f(\mathbf1_S)=f(S)\), and is convex on \([0,1]^E\) if and only if \(f\) is submodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lovász extension linearly interpolates a set function along coordinate chains, agrees at Boolean vertices, and is convex exactly for submodular functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat f(\mathbf1_S)=f(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq E\), and \(\widehat f\) is convex exactly when \(f\) is submodular.

notation.meaning: The ith prefix set of a nonincreasing coordinate ordering.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The chain formula, tie independence, Boolean interpolation, and convexity characterization are standard and correctly stated, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lovász Extension by Threshold Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the extension under the stated set-function conventions and records positive homogeneity, incidence-vector agreement, and the effective-domain criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\rho(\varnothing)=0\), \(\rho(V)\in\mathbb R\), and \(\rho\) has at most one sign of infinite value. For \(p\in\mathbb R^V\), let \(\widehat p_1>\cdots>\widehat p_m\) be its distinct component values and set \(U_i=\{v\in V\mid p(v)\geq\widehat p_i\}\). Then \(p=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}(\widehat p_i-\widehat p_{i+1})\chi_{U_i}+\widehat p_m\chi_{U_m}\), and \(\widehat\rho(p)=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}(\widehat p_i-\widehat p_{i+1})\rho(U_i)+\widehat p_m\rho(U_m)\). The function \(\widehat\rho\) is positively homogeneous, satisfies \(\widehat\rho(\chi_X)=\rho(X)\) for every \(X\subseteq V\), and obeys \(p\in\operatorname{dom}\widehat\rho\iff U_1,\ldots,U_{m-1}\in\operatorname{dom}\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lovász extension is obtained from the upper-level-set decomposition of a vector. It is positively homogeneous, agrees with the set function on incidence vectors, and is finite precisely when every nonterminal upper level set has finite set-function value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat\rho(p)=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}(\widehat p_i-\widehat p_{i+1})\rho(U_i)+\widehat p_m\rho(U_m),\quad \widehat\rho(\chi_X)=\rho(X),\quad p\in\operatorname{dom}\widehat\rho\iff U_1,\ldots,U_{m-1}\in\operatorname{dom}\rho

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Truncated Lovász extension

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lovász extension of a concave-over-modular set function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit sorted-coordinate representation, including the unit-weight cardinality specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{1,\ldots,p\}\), \(s\in\mathbb{R}_+^p\), \(g:\mathbb{R}_+\to\mathbb{R}\) be concave with \(g(0)=0\), and \(F(A)=g(s(A))\), where \(s(A)=\sum_{i\in A}s_i\). If \(w_{j_1}\geq\cdots\geq w_{j_p}\), then the Lovász extension of \(F\) is \[f(w)=\sum_{k=1}^p w_{j_k}\left[g\!\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^k s_{j_\ell}\right)-g\!\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{k-1}s_{j_\ell}\right)\right].\] If \(s=\mathbf 1_V\), then \(f(w)=\sum_{k=1}^p w_{j_k}[g(k)-g(k-1)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After sorting the coordinates of w in nonincreasing order, the Lovász extension is a weighted sum of successive increments of g at cumulative set weights. Under unit weights, the coefficients are g(k) minus g(k−1).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(w)=\sum_{k=1}^p w_{j_k}\left[g\!\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^k s_{j_\ell}\right)-g\!\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{k-1}s_{j_\ell}\right)\right],\qquad s=\mathbf 1_V\implies f(w)=\sum_{k=1}^p w_{j_k}[g(k)-g(k-1)]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lovász Extension of a Normalized Set Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent sorted-increment, telescoping, and threshold-integral representations on a finite ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let V=\{1,\ldots,p\} and F:2^V\to\mathbb R satisfy F(\varnothing)=0. For w\in\mathbb R^p, choose a permutation (j_1,\ldots,j_p) such that w_{j_1}\ge\cdots\ge w_{j_p}, and set S_k=\{j_1,\ldots,j_k\} and S_0=\varnothing. The Lovász extension f:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R is equivalently defined by
\[
f(w)=\sum_{k=1}^p w_{j_k}\bigl(F(S_k)-F(S_{k-1})\bigr),
\]
\[
f(w)=\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}F(S_k)(w_{j_k}-w_{j_{k+1}})+F(V)w_{j_p},
\]
\[
f(w)=\int_{\min_i w_i}^{\infty}F(\{i\in V:w_i\ge z\})\,dz+F(V)\min_i w_i,
\]
and
\[
f(w)=\int_0^{\infty}F(\{i\in V:w_i\ge z\})\,dz+\int_{-\infty}^0\bigl(F(\{i\in V:w_i\ge z\})-F(V)\bigr)\,dz.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a normalized set function on a finite ground set, the Lovász extension is obtained by sorting the coordinates and weighting them by successive set-function increments. It has equivalent telescoping and threshold-integral representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(w)=\sum_{k=1}^p w_{j_k}(F(S_k)-F(S_{k-1}))=\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}F(S_k)(w_{j_k}-w_{j_{k+1}})+F(V)w_{j_p},\text{ together with the two displayed equivalent threshold-integral representations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lovász extension as support function and chain representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Lovász extension for a normalized submodular function on a simple distributive lattice and records its effective domain, homogeneity, and chain evaluation formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D=2^{\mathcal P}\), where \(\mathcal P=(E,\preccurlyeq)\), and let \(f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R\) be submodular with \(f(\varnothing)=0\). Define \(\widehat f(c)=\max\{\langle c,x\rangle:x\in P(f)\}\). Then \(\widehat f\) is convex and satisfies \(\widehat f(\lambda c)=\lambda\widehat f(c)\) for \(\lambda>0\). Moreover, \(\widehat f(c)<+\infty\) if and only if \(c\) is nonnegative and monotone nonincreasing on \(\mathcal P\). Every such \(c\) has a unique representation \(c=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i\chi_{A_i}\), where \(\varnothing\ne A_1\subset\cdots\subset A_k\) are in \(\mathcal D\) and \(\lambda_i>0\), and \(\widehat f(c)=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i f(A_i)\). When \(c=0\), \(k=0\) and both sums are empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lovász extension is the support function of the submodular polyhedron. It is finite exactly on nonnegative order-reversing vectors, whose unique nested-chain decomposition gives the corresponding weighted sum of set-function values; the zero vector has the empty decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat f(c)=\max_{x\in P(f)}\langle c,x\rangle,\quad \widehat f(c)<+\infty\iff c\text{ is nonnegative and monotone nonincreasing},\quad \widehat f(c)=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i f(A_i)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lovász Extension by Ordered Prefix Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered-prefix definition of the Lovász extension for an extended-real-valued set function on a finite ground set, including the stated infinity convention and extension property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}\) be finite and let \(\rho:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\}\). For \(p\in\mathbb{R}^V\), choose an ordering such that \(p_j=p(v_j)\) satisfies \(p_1\ge\cdots\ge p_n\), and put \(V_j=\{v_1,\ldots,v_j\}\). Then \[p=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(p_j-p_{j+1})\chi_{V_j}+p_n\chi_V,\] and the Lovász extension is defined by \[\widehat\rho(p)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(p_j-p_{j+1})\rho(V_j)+p_n\rho(V),\] with the convention \(0\cdot(\pm\infty)=0\). Moreover, \(\widehat\rho(\chi_X)=\rho(X)\) for every \(X\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order the coordinates of a vector nonincreasingly and form the nested prefix subsets. The Lovász extension applies the same coefficients to the set-function values, with zero times either infinity defined as zero. On every characteristic vector it agrees with the original set function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat\rho(p)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(p_j-p_{j+1})\rho(V_j)+p_n\rho(V),\qquad \widehat\rho(\chi_X)=\rho(X)\ \ (\forall X\subseteq V).

knowledge_statements.title: Multilinear Extension Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent-random-set representation of a set function on the unit cube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite set \(E\) and \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\), the multilinear extension \(F:[0,1]^E\to\mathbb R\) is \[F(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq E}f(S)\prod_{e\in S}x_e\prod_{e\notin S}(1-x_e)=\mathbb E[f(R_x)],\] where each \(e\in E\) belongs to \(R_x\) independently with probability \(x_e\). The function \(F\) is affine in each coordinate separately and satisfies \(F(\mathbf1_S)=f(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The multilinear extension is the expected set-function value under independent inclusion with prescribed marginals; it is coordinatewise affine and agrees on Boolean vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(R_x)]\), and \(F(\mathbf1_S)=f(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq E\).

notation.meaning: Random subset with independent inclusion probabilities x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multilinear-extension representation and its stated properties are correct and fit the representation container, but no source is cited.

children.title: Convex Closures
children.top_down_role: Convex-envelope representations of set functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Closures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower convex closure of a set function through distributions with fixed marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\). Its convex closure \(f^-:[0,1]^E\to\mathbb R\) is \[f^-(x)=\min\left\{\sum_{S\subseteq E}\lambda_S f(S):\lambda_S\ge0,\ \sum_S\lambda_S=1,\ \sum_S\lambda_S\mathbf1_S=x\right\}.\] Equivalently, \(f^-(x)\) is the minimum of \(\mathbb E[f(R)]\) over all random subsets \(R\subseteq E\) satisfying \(\mathbb P(e\in R)=x_e\). It is the greatest convex function on \([0,1]^E\) whose Boolean-vertex values do not exceed those of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex closure minimizes expected set-function value over all joint distributions with prescribed marginals and is the greatest convex underestimator at Boolean vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^-(x)=\min\{\mathbb E[f(R)]:\mathbb P(e\in R)=x_e\text{ for all }e\in E\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distributional formula and greatest-convex-underestimator characterization are correct, but the record lacks an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex closure of a set function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise convex-envelope definition based on prescribed upper bounds at hypercube vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite with \(|V|=p\), and let \(F:2^V\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(F(\varnothing)=0\). The convex closure of \(F\) is the pointwise largest convex function \(f:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) such that \(f(\mathbf 1_A)\leq F(A)\) for every \(A\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite ground set V and a set function F normalized by F(empty set) = 0, the convex closure is the largest extended-real-valued convex function on R^p whose value at each subset incidence vector does not exceed F at that subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is the pointwise largest convex }g:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\text{ satisfying }g(\mathbf 1_A)\leq F(A)\quad\forall A\subseteq V

children.title: Concave Closures
children.top_down_role: Concave-envelope representations of set functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Concave Closures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper concave closure of a set function through distributions with fixed marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\). Its concave closure \(f^+:[0,1]^E\to\mathbb R\) is \[f^+(x)=\max\left\{\sum_{S\subseteq E}\lambda_S f(S):\lambda_S\ge0,\ \sum_S\lambda_S=1,\ \sum_S\lambda_S\mathbf1_S=x\right\}.\] Equivalently, \(f^+(x)\) is the maximum of \(\mathbb E[f(R)]\) over all random subsets \(R\subseteq E\) satisfying \(\mathbb P(e\in R)=x_e\). It is the least concave function on \([0,1]^E\) whose Boolean-vertex values dominate those of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The concave closure maximizes expected set-function value over all joint distributions with prescribed marginals and is the least concave overestimator at Boolean vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^+(x)=\max\{\mathbb E[f(R)]:\mathbb P(e\in R)=x_e\text{ for all }e\in E\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distributional formula and least-concave-overestimator characterization are correct, but the record lacks an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concave closure sign duality and its computational and tightness boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-dual representation of the concave closure, together with the stated submodular maximization barrier and vertex-versus-interior boundary for constant-plus-modular upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set function \(F:2^V\to\mathbb R\), its concave closure is the negative of the convex closure of \(-F\). Computing concave closures in general would provide polynomial-time algorithms for submodular-function maximization. For submodular \(F\), at every vertex \(\mathbf 1_A\) of the hypercube there exists a constant-plus-modular upper bound that is tight at \(A\); such tight bounds cannot in general be obtained at an interior point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The concave closure of F is the negative of the convex closure of −F. A general procedure for computing it would imply polynomial-time submodular maximization. For a submodular function, a constant-plus-modular upper bound can be made tight at any selected hypercube vertex, but such interior-point tightness is unavailable in general.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is submodular for the constant-plus-modular upper-bound assertion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F^{\mathrm{ccv}}=-(-F)^{\mathrm{cvx}};\quad \forall A\subseteq V\ \exists\,U=c+m\text{ with }m\text{ modular},\ U(B)\geq F(B)\ \forall B\subseteq V,\ U(A)=F(A),\text{ whereas analogous tightness at interior points fails in general}

children.title: Closure Gap Structure
children.top_down_role: Structural separation between convex and concave envelope values.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Gap Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise width between extremal expectations having identical marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite \(E\), set function \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\), and \(x\in[0,1]^E\), define the closure gap by \(\Gamma_f(x)=f^+(x)-f^-(x)\). Then \[\Gamma_f(x)\ge0,\qquad f^-(x)\le F(x)\le f^+(x),\] where \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(R_x)]\) is the multilinear extension generated by independent marginals. Moreover, \(\Gamma_f(x)=0\) exactly when every probability distribution on \(2^E\) with marginal vector \(x\) has the same expected value of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The concave closure dominates the multilinear extension, which dominates the convex closure; their gap vanishes exactly when dependence cannot change the expectation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le\Gamma_f(x)=f^+(x)-f^-(x)\) and \(f^-(x)\le F(x)\le f^+(x)\).

notation.meaning: Closure gap at marginal vector x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closure inequalities and zero-gap characterization follow from the extremal fixed-marginal definitions and are correctly stated, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Exactness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Function classes or domains where a closure representation becomes exact.

knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global closure exactness characterizes modular set functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\). The following are equivalent: \(f^-(x)=f^+(x)\) for every \(x\in[0,1]^E\); every two distributions on \(2^E\) having the same marginals give the same expectation of \(f\); and \(f\) is modular, meaning that constants \(c\in\mathbb R\) and \(w\in\mathbb R^E\) exist with \[f(S)=c+\sum_{e\in S}w_e\quad(S\subseteq E).\] In this regime, both closures and the multilinear extension equal \(c+w^\top x\) throughout the cube.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex and concave closures coincide everywhere exactly for modular set functions; then every standard continuous extension equals the same affine function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^-=f^+\text{ on }[0,1]^E\iff f(S)=c+\sum_{e\in S}w_e\), and then \(f^-(x)=F(x)=f^+(x)=c+w^\top x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The global exactness characterization by modularity is mathematically correct and appropriately classified as a theorem, but it requires an authoritative source and locator.

children.title: Explicit Representations
children.top_down_role: Direct tabular, algebraic, or coefficient-based encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truth-table encoding and its direct evaluation access model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a ground set \(E\) with \(|E|=n\), an explicit representation of \(f:2^E\to\mathbb Q\) lists the pair \((S,f(S))\) for every \(S\subseteq E\), using fixed finite encodings of subsets and rational numbers. The representation contains \(2^n\) value entries. Given a direct-addressed or suitably indexed table, a value query \(S\mapsto f(S)\) is answered by lookup. A procedure that scans all entries and performs work polynomial in the entry bit length per entry runs in time polynomial in the total explicit encoding length, although that length is exponential in \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit set-function encoding lists all values, enables indexed lookup, and has exponentially many entries in the ground-set size; full-table scans are polynomial in the encoding length when their per-entry work is polynomially bounded.
assumptions_latex: Subsets and rational values use fixed finite encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representation contains \(2^n\) values and supports indexed evaluation of \(f(S)\).

notation.meaning: Stored value associated with subset S.

children.title: Combinatorial Representations
children.top_down_role: Encodings through graphs, matroids, networks, or related discrete structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact graph-cut representation of a submodular function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with nonnegative capacities \(c:A\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and let \(E\subseteq V\). A graph-cut representation of \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\) consists of \(G\), \(c\), auxiliary vertices \(U=V\setminus E\), and a constant \(\kappa\) such that \[f(S)=\kappa+\min_{T\subseteq U}c\bigl(\delta^+(S\cup T)\bigr)\qquad(S\subseteq E).\] This representation is compact when \(|V|+|A|\) and the capacity encoding length are polynomial in \(|E|\). For fixed \(S\), evaluation reduces to a minimum-cut problem in which vertices of \(S\) are constrained to the source side, vertices of \(E\setminus S\) are constrained to the sink side, and auxiliary vertices may lie on either side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph-cut representation encodes a set function by a capacitated directed graph, possibly with auxiliary vertices; evaluating a chosen subset reduces to a minimum cut with selected and unselected ground vertices fixed to opposite sides.
assumptions_latex: Auxiliary vertices may be assigned to either cut side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(S)=\kappa+\min_{T\subseteq V\setminus E}c(\delta^+(S\cup T))\) for every \(S\subseteq E\).

notation.meaning: Total capacity of arcs leaving W.

children.title: Encoding Translations
children.top_down_role: Conversions and succinctness tradeoffs between explicit and combinatorial encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Translations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial translations between explicit encodings of finite combinatorial objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R_1\) and \(\mathcal R_2\) be representation schemes for the same class \(\mathcal C\). A translation from \(\mathcal R_1\) to \(\mathcal R_2\) is a map \(T\) such that every valid encoding \(e\in\mathcal R_1\) of \(C\in\mathcal C\) is mapped to a valid encoding \(T(e)\in\mathcal R_2\) of that same object. The translation is polynomial if \(T(e)\) is computable in time polynomial in \(|e|\) and \(|T(e)|\) is polynomially bounded in \(|e|\). The schemes are polynomially equivalent when polynomial translations exist in both directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An encoding translation preserves the represented object; polynomial equivalence requires polynomial-time, polynomial-size translations in both directions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R_1\) and \(\mathcal R_2\) encode the same finite object class \(\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e\) and \(T(e)\) represent the same \(C\), with polynomial time and output size in the polynomial case.

children.title: Value Oracles
children.top_down_role: Access through evaluations of a set function.

knowledge_statements.title: Value Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact value-query access to a set function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite ground set \(E\) and a function \(f:2^E\to\mathbb Q\), an exact value oracle is a procedure that, on every query set \(S\subseteq E\), returns the rational number \(f(S)\). In the value-oracle model, an algorithm accesses \(f\) only through such queries; its oracle complexity is the number of queries, while arithmetic and bit complexity additionally account for manipulating the returned values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value oracle returns the exact function value for any queried subset; query complexity counts these calls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O_f(S)=f(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq E\).

children.title: Rank Oracles
children.top_down_role: Access through rank evaluations in matroidal or polymatroidal systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rank-query access to a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a matroid with rank function \(r_M:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), where \(r_M(S)=\max\{|I|:I\subseteq S,\ I\in\mathcal I\}\). A rank oracle for \(M\) is a procedure that, for every queried set \(S\subseteq E\), returns \(r_M(S)\). The oracle therefore exposes the maximum cardinality of an independent subset of \(S\) without being required to return such a subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid rank oracle returns the maximum size of an independent subset of each queried set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O_r(S)=r_M(S)=\max\{|I|:I\subseteq S,\ I\in\mathcal I\}\).

children.title: Independence Oracles
children.top_down_role: Access through independence queries in combinatorial systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Independence Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean independent-set access to a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid. An independence oracle is a procedure that, for each query \(S\subseteq E\), returns \(1\) if \(S\in\mathcal I\) and returns \(0\) otherwise. In this oracle model, the family \(\mathcal I\) need not be listed explicitly, and algorithms may learn whether a set is independent only by issuing oracle queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independence oracle answers whether a queried subset is independent in a specified matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O_{\mathcal I}(S)=\mathbf 1\{S\in\mathcal I\}\) for every \(S\subseteq E\).

children.title: Oracle Simulation Relations
children.top_down_role: Information comparisons and simulation boundaries among the oracle types.

assumptions_latex: The value oracle is specifically for the rank function \(r_M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O_r\) simulates \(O_{\mathcal I}\) with one query, and \(O_{\mathcal I}\) simulates \(O_r(S)\) with at most \(|S|\) queries.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query simulations among matroid value, rank, and independence access.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Independence and rank p. 173

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid with rank function \(r_M\). For every \(S\subseteq E\), one rank-oracle query determines whether \(S\in\mathcal I\), since \(S\in\mathcal I\) if and only if \(r_M(S)=|S|\). Conversely, the value \(r_M(S)\) can be determined using at most \(|S|\) independence-oracle queries. A value oracle for the particular set function \(r_M\) is identical to a rank oracle. Hence rank, independence, and rank-value access are polynomially query-equivalent for a specified finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite matroid, rank and rank-value queries are identical, while independence and rank oracles simulate one another with at most linear query overhead.

children.title: Membership Oracles
children.top_down_role: Access through feasibility or set-membership queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Membership Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean membership access to a represented feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). An exact membership oracle for \(K\) is a procedure that, given a query point \(y\in\mathbb Q^d\), returns \(1\) when \(y\in K\) and \(0\) when \(y\notin K\). Its response contains no separating hyperplane or quantitative distance information. For lower-dimensional or numerically represented sets, weak membership must instead specify a tolerance and a boundary convention; that distinct model is not included in this exact definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact membership oracle says only whether a rational query point belongs to the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O_K(y)=\mathbf 1\{y\in K\}\).

children.title: Separation Oracles
children.top_down_role: Access through separating certificates for infeasible points.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact strong separation access to a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty closed convex set. A strong separation oracle, queried at \(y\in\mathbb Q^d\), either certifies \(y\in K\) or returns \((a,\beta)\in\mathbb Q^d\times\mathbb Q\) such that \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y\) for every \(x\in K\). Thus the returned inequality is valid for all of \(K\) and strictly excludes the query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong separation oracle accepts a point in the convex set or returns a valid inequality strictly excluding it.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The requested exact certificate has rational coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in K\), or \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y\) for all \(x\in K\).

children.title: Optimization Oracles
children.top_down_role: Access through linear or structured optimization queries.

source_refs.locator: Section 4.6. Separation and Optimization p. 93

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty and let queries be rational objective vectors \(c\in\mathbb Q^d\). A strong optimization oracle returns a point \(x^\star\in K\) satisfying \(c^{\mathsf T}x^\star=\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in K\}\), whenever this maximum is finite and attained. In a formulation allowing unbounded sets, the oracle must instead report unboundedness when \(\sup_{x\in K}c^{\mathsf T}x=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong optimization oracle maximizes each queried rational linear objective, returning an optimizer or reporting unboundedness.

children.title: Oracle Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Computational reductions and nonequivalence boundaries among the interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong optimization–separation equivalence for well-described rational polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty rational polyhedron equipped with a polynomial facet-complexity bound and the standard rational encoding model. There is an oracle-polynomial-time algorithm for strong linear optimization over \(P\) given a strong separation oracle for \(P\); conversely, strong separation for \(P\) is oracle-polynomial-time reducible to strong linear optimization over \(P\). Hence strong optimization and strong separation are polynomially equivalent in this well-described regime. Exact membership alone is not covered by this equivalence without additional geometric or weak-oracle assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For well-described rational polyhedra, strong separation and strong linear optimization reduce to each other in oracle-polynomial time; membership needs extra assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is a nonempty rational polyhedron.
A polynomial facet-complexity bound and rational encoding are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{SEP}(P)\equiv_{\mathrm{poly}}\mathrm{OPT}(P)\) in the strong oracle model.

children.title: Sampling Oracles
children.top_down_role: Random-sample access to values, outcomes, or induced distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-sample access to a query-dependent distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal Q\) be a query space and let \((\Omega,\mathcal F)\) be a measurable output space. A sampling oracle is specified by a family of probability measures \(\{P_q:q\in\mathcal Q\}\). On each query \(q\), it returns a random variable \(Z\sim P_q\); conditional on the submitted queries, separate calls use independent randomness unless another dependence rule is explicitly stated. The algorithm observes samples, not an exact probability table or exact expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sampling oracle draws from a distribution determined by the query, ordinarily using fresh independent randomness on each call.
assumptions_latex: \(P_q\) is a probability measure on \((\Omega,\mathcal F)\) for every \(q\in\mathcal Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O(q)=Z\) with \(Z\sim P_q\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the sampling-oracle leaf and the formulation is plausible, but no source is supplied. In particular, the conditional independence convention is model-dependent and requires an authoritative locator before this version can be accepted.

children.title: Noisy Oracles
children.top_down_role: Access models with stochastic or adversarial observation error.

knowledge_statements.title: Noisy Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive stochastic-error access to a real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a query space \(\mathcal Q\) and function \(f:\mathcal Q\to\mathbb R\), an additive noisy oracle returns \(Y(q)=f(q)+\xi_q\) on query \(q\). A complete noisy-oracle specification states the conditional law of \(\xi_q\), including its bias, tail or moment bounds, and dependence across calls. A common unbiased sub-Gaussian model requires \(\mathbb E[\xi_q\mid q]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[\exp(\lambda\xi_q)\mid q]\le\exp(\lambda^2\sigma^2/2)\) for every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noisy oracle returns the true value plus random error; its bias, tails, and dependence structure are part of the model.
assumptions_latex: In the displayed common model, the noise is conditionally unbiased and \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y(q)=f(q)+\xi_q\) with the stated conditional noise law.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the noisy-oracle leaf, but no source supports the selected additive, conditionally unbiased sub-Gaussian variant. Because noisy-oracle models differ in bias, adaptivity, tails, and cross-call dependence, an authoritative source is needed to validate this exact specification.

children.title: Approximate Oracles
children.top_down_role: Access models returning controlled approximations to exact responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic additive or multiplicative approximation to value access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal Q\to\mathbb R\). An additive \(\varepsilon\)-approximate value oracle returns \(\widetilde f(q)\) satisfying \(|\widetilde f(q)-f(q)|\le\varepsilon\) for every \(q\in\mathcal Q\). If \(f(q)\ge0\), a multiplicative \(\rho\)-approximate value oracle, with \(\rho\ge1\), returns \(\widetilde f(q)\) satisfying \(f(q)/\rho\le\widetilde f(q)\le\rho f(q)\). The approximation type, parameter, and whether the guarantee is deterministic or probabilistic must be specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate oracle returns values within a declared additive or multiplicative error guarantee for every query.
assumptions_latex: For the multiplicative convention, \(f\) is nonnegative and \(\rho\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\widetilde f(q)-f(q)|\le\varepsilon\), or \(f(q)/\rho\le\widetilde f(q)\le\rho f(q)\), according to the declared model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the approximate-oracle leaf and the displayed additive and symmetric multiplicative conventions are internally consistent. No source is supplied, however, and multiplicative approximation conventions vary, so an authoritative locator is required for this exact formulation.

children.title: Information-Loss Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed by sampling error, noise, or approximation.

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Loss Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An indistinguishability boundary for randomized algorithms using imperfect value information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_0,f_1:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be two instances, and let \(P_i\) be the distribution of the complete oracle transcript observed by an adaptive randomized algorithm on \(f_i\). For an accuracy level \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), define \(S_i=\{X\subseteq V:f_i(X)\le \min_Y f_i(Y)+\varepsilon\}\). If \(S_0\cap S_1=\varnothing\), then the algorithm's average probability of returning an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal set satisfies \[\frac12\Pr_{f_0}(\widehat X\in S_0)+\frac12\Pr_{f_1}(\widehat X\in S_1)\le \frac{1+\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1)}2.\] Thus identical transcript laws force failure probability at least \(1/2\) on one of the two instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two instances are nearly indistinguishable from their oracle transcripts but require disjoint approximate solutions, every algorithm has a correspondingly large failure probability.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm's output is measurable with respect to its transcript and internal randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac12\Pr_{f_0}(\widehat X\in S_0)+\frac12\Pr_{f_1}(\widehat X\in S_1)\le (1+\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1))/2\).

notation.meaning: Family of epsilon-optimal sets for instance i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-instance total-variation bound is mathematically plausible and fits a failure-boundary leaf, but no source or locator supports the exact transcript model and conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Succinct-Representation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A counting lower bound for universal exact encodings of submodular functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider any injective binary encoding capable of representing every labeled matroid rank function on an \(n\)-element ground set, hence a subclass of integer-valued monotone submodular functions. If \(M_n\) denotes the number of labeled matroids, some encoded rank function requires at least \(\lceil\log_2 M_n\rceil\) bits. The standard counting lower bound \[\log_2 M_n\ge \frac1n\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\] for sufficiently large \(n\) therefore gives worst-case length \(2^{\Omega(n)}\). Consequently, no polynomial-length representation can encode all submodular functions exactly, although particular subclasses may admit succinct representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Counting matroid rank functions shows that some submodular functions require exponentially many bits in any universal exact, uniquely decodable representation.
assumptions_latex: The encoding is injective and exact.
All labeled matroid rank functions must be representable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_r \operatorname{length}(\operatorname{enc}(r))\ge \lceil\log_2 M_n\rceil=2^{\Omega(n)}\).

notation.meaning: Number of labeled matroids on an n-element ground set.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits, but the stated labeled-matroid counting inequality, its range of validity, and the resulting encoding lower bound require an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate Recovery on a Distributive Lattice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of submodular and supermodular set-function values from their conjugates, with the failure boundary outside the lattice domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\subseteq 2^E\) be a distributive lattice containing \(\varnothing\) and \(E\), let \(f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R\) be submodular, and let \(g:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R\) be supermodular. For every \(X\in\mathcal D\), \[f(X)=\max_{x\in\mathbb R^E}\{x(X)-f^*(x)\},\qquad g(X)=\min_{x\in\mathbb R^E}\{x(X)-g^*(x)\}.\] For every \(X\in 2^E\setminus\mathcal D\), \(x\mapsto x(X)-f^*(x)\) is unbounded above and \(x\mapsto x(X)-g^*(x)\) is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Values on the lattice are recovered from the corresponding conjugates by maximization or minimization. Outside the lattice, the two expressions are respectively unbounded above and below.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal D\subseteq 2^E\) is a distributive lattice with \(\varnothing,E\in\mathcal D\).
\(f^*\) and \(g^*\) are the conjugates defined on \(\mathbb R^E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(X\in\mathcal D\), \(f(X)=\max_x\{x(X)-f^*(x)\}\) and \(g(X)=\min_x\{x(X)-g^*(x)\}\); for \(X\notin\mathcal D\), the first objective is unbounded above and the second is unbounded below.
