knowledge_statements.title: Set-Function Conjugate Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugacy obtained by embedding subsets as incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be submodular on finite \(V\), and write \(p(X)=\sum_{i\in X}p_i\) for \(p\in\mathbb R^V\). Define its modular conjugate by \[f^\star(p)=\max_{Y\subseteq V}\{p(Y)-f(Y)\}.\] Then every set value has the biconjugate representation \[f(X)=\sup_{p\in\mathbb R^V}\{p(X)-f^\star(p)\},\qquad X\subseteq V.\] Equivalently, this is Fenchel biconjugacy for the convex closure of the vertex data \(f(X)\) on the incidence vectors of subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A submodular set function equals its modular-vector biconjugate when subsets are identified with incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)=\sup_{p\in\mathbb R^V}\{p(X)-f^\star(p)\}\) for every \(X\subseteq V\).

notation.meaning: Modular sum of vector coordinates over X.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the leaf and is internally coherent, but the precise modular-conjugacy convention and biconjugate claim have no cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel-Type Min–Max Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-set Fenchel duality for a submodular–supermodular pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be submodular and \(g:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be supermodular. For \(p\in\mathbb R^V\), define \[f^\star(p)=\max_{X\subseteq V}\{p(X)-f(X)\},\qquad g_\star(p)=\min_{X\subseteq V}\{p(X)-g(X)\}.\] Finite-set Fenchel duality states \[\min_{X\subseteq V}\{f(X)-g(X)\}=\max_{p\in\mathbb R^V}\{g_\star(p)-f^\star(p)\}.\] When \(f\) and \(g\) are integer-valued, an integral maximizing vector \(p\in\mathbb Z^V\) may be chosen.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum difference of a submodular and a supermodular function equals a maximum involving their convex and concave modular conjugates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_X(f(X)-g(X))=\max_p(g_\star(p)-f^\star(p))\), with integral \(p\) available for integer-valued data.

notation.meaning: Sum of coordinates of p indexed by X.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality role fits, but the exact finite-set Fenchel identity and especially integral attainment for integer-valued data require a specific theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel-Type Min–Max Theorem for Set Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min–max duality between a submodular function and a supermodular function on intersecting distributive lattices, including conditional integral dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal D_1\to\mathbb R\) be submodular and \(g:\mathcal D_2\to\mathbb R\) be supermodular, where \(\mathcal D_1,\mathcal D_2\subseteq 2^E\) are distributive lattices satisfying \(\varnothing,E\in\mathcal D_1\cap\mathcal D_2\). Then \[\min_{X\in\mathcal D_1\cap\mathcal D_2}\{f(X)-g(X)\}=\max_{x\in\mathbb R^E}\{g^*(x)-f^*(x)\}.\] If \(f\) and \(g\) are integer-valued, the maximum is attained by some \(x\in\mathbb Z^E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum difference between a submodular and a supermodular function over their common lattice domain equals the maximum difference of their conjugates. If both functions are integer-valued, an integral dual maximizer exists.
assumptions_latex: For the integral-attainment clause, \(f\) and \(g\) are integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{X\in\mathcal D_1\cap\mathcal D_2}\{f(X)-g(X)\}=\max_{x\in\mathbb R^E}\{g^*(x)-f^*(x)\}\), and in the integer-valued case a maximizer can be chosen in \(\mathbb Z^E\).

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The discrete subdifferential of a submodular function at a set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite ground set \(V\), a submodular function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\), and \(A\subseteq V\), the subgradient polyhedron at \(A\) is \[\partial f(A)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^V: f(Y)-x(Y)\ge f(A)-x(A)\text{ for every }Y\subseteq V\right\}.\] Equivalently, \(x\in\partial f(A)\) precisely when the modular function \(Y\mapsto f(A)+x(Y)-x(A)\) is a global lower bound for \(f\) and is tight at \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subgradient polyhedron consists of modular lower bounds to the set function that agree with it at the designated set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(A)=\{x:f(Y)-x(Y)\ge f(A)-x(A)\text{ for all }Y\subseteq V\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise and appropriate for Subgradient Polyhedra, but no source with a definition or section locator is supplied.

children.title: Greedy Chains

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Chains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation-chain construction of a greedy modular vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a submodular function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\), a set \(A\subseteq V\), and a permutation \(\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n)\) whose first \(|A|\) elements are exactly \(A\). Initialize \(S_0=\varnothing\). For \(k=1,\ldots,n\), set \[S_k=S_{k-1}\cup\{\pi_k\},\qquad x^\pi_{\pi_k}=f(S_k)-f(S_{k-1}).\] Output the maximal chain \(S_0\subset S_1\subset\cdots\subset S_n=V\) and the greedy vector \(x^\pi\); the prefix condition gives \(S_{|A|}=A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order the elements with the designated set first, form successive prefixes, and assign each element its marginal value along that chain.
assumptions_latex: The permutation lists all elements of \(A\) before those of \(V\setminus A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output satisfies \(x^\pi(S_k)=f(S_k)-f(\varnothing)\) for every chain prefix \(S_k\).

notation.meaning: The first k elements of the permutation.
Greedy marginal vector associated with the permutation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The permutation-chain construction is correctly classified as an algorithm and matches the leaf, but it lacks supporting evidence and a locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Subgradient in a Maximal-Chain Simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness and chain-increment characterization of the convex extension's subgradient at an interior point of a chain simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[\mathcal C:\varnothing=S_0\subset S_1\subset\cdots\subset S_n=E\]
be a maximal chain of \(\mathcal D\), and let \(c\) be an interior point of \(\mathrm P(\mathcal C)\). Then \(\widetilde f\) has a unique subgradient \(x\) at \(c\), given by
\[x(S_i\setminus S_{i-1})=f(S_i)-f(S_{i-1}),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior point of the simplex induced by a maximal chain, the convex extension has a unique subgradient. Its value on each successive chain difference equals the corresponding increment of the set function.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\widetilde f(c)=\{x\},\qquad x(S_i\setminus S_{i-1})=f(S_i)-f(S_{i-1})\quad(i=1,\ldots,n)

children.title: Extreme Subgradients
children.top_down_role: Extremal points of subgradient polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme points of a discrete subdifferential arise from compatible permutations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be submodular and \(A\subseteq V\). For every permutation \(\pi\) that places all elements of \(A\) before all elements of \(V\setminus A\), the greedy marginal vector \(x^\pi\) belongs to \(\partial f(A)\) and is an extreme point of that polyhedron. Conversely, every extreme point of \(\partial f(A)\) is \(x^\pi\) for at least one such permutation. Distinct compatible permutations can yield the same extreme point when marginal increments are degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The vertices of the discrete subdifferential are exactly greedy marginal vectors from permutations having the designated set as a prefix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ext}(\partial f(A))=\{x^\pi:\pi\text{ places }A\text{ before }V\setminus A\}\) after duplicate vectors are identified.

notation.meaning: Greedy marginal vector of permutation pi.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property matches the leaf, but the converse characterization of every extreme point by a compatible permutation needs an authoritative theorem locator.

children.title: Chain–Subgradient Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural matching between greedy chains and extreme subgradients.

knowledge_statements.title: Chain–Subgradient Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy-chain characterization of discrete subgradients and their extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be submodular, let \(A\subseteq V\), and let \(\pi\) be a permutation whose prefix of length \(|A|\) equals \(A\). If \(x^\pi\) is formed from successive marginal increments along the prefix chain, then \[f(Y)\ge f(A)+x^\pi(Y)-x^\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }Y\subseteq V.\] Hence \(x^\pi\in\partial f(A)\), with equality on every prefix of the chain. Moreover, varying over all compatible permutations generates exactly the extreme points of \(\partial f(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chain passing through the designated set produces a tight subgradient, and all extreme subgradients arise from such chains.
assumptions_latex: The permutation has \(A\) as a prefix.
Greedy coordinates are successive chain marginals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\pi\in\partial f(A)\), every chain prefix is tight, and compatible greedy vectors generate \(\operatorname{ext}(\partial f(A))\).

notation.meaning: Greedy vector generated by permutation pi.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is locally appropriate and its notation is consistent, but the tightness and exhaustive extreme-point assertions lack cited support.

children.title: Degenerate Chain Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nonuniqueness caused by ties or multiple compatible chains.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Chain Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness caused by tied levels or coincident greedy marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be normalized and submodular, and maximize \(w^\top x\) over its base polyhedron. If the coordinates of \(w\) have ties, their strict level sets determine only a partial chain. Every permutation refining the tied blocks produces a compatible greedy base, and the exposed maximizing face is the convex hull of these greedy bases. Thus a tied ordering need not identify a unique chain or extreme subgradient; uniqueness holds only when all compatible refinements yield the same greedy vector, while distinct refinements may still coincide because their marginal increments agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tied weights determine only a partial chain; compatible refinements can expose several greedy vectors, though degeneracy may also make different refinements coincide.
assumptions_latex: The weight vector has at least one tied coordinate block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in B(f)}w^\top x=\operatorname{conv}\{x^\pi:\pi\text{ refines the weak order of }w\}\).

notation.meaning: Greedy base associated with a refining permutation.
Weight vector defining the exposed face.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tied-order phenomenon fits a failure-boundary leaf, but the exposed-face formula and its connection to extreme subgradients require a source-specific formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Tight-Set Lattices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of tight constraints under union and intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be submodular and let \(x\in P(f)=\{z\in\mathbb R^V:z(S)\le f(S)\text{ for all }S\subseteq V\}\). Define the tight-set family \(\mathcal T_x=\{S\subseteq V:x(S)=f(S)\}\). If \(A,B\in\mathcal T_x\), then submodularity and modularity give \[x(A\cap B)+x(A\cup B)=x(A)+x(B)=f(A)+f(B)\ge f(A\cap B)+f(A\cup B).\] Feasibility forces equality throughout, so \(A\cap B,A\cup B\in\mathcal T_x\). Hence \(\mathcal T_x\) is a lattice under intersection and union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible point of a submodular polyhedron, the sets on which constraints are tight are closed under intersection and union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A,B\in\mathcal T_x\Rightarrow A\cap B,A\cup B\in\mathcal T_x\).

notation.meaning: Family of constraints tight at x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lattice property is standard and fits the leaf, but it has no citation and the statement includes a proof-style derivation that must be removed before acceptance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Properties of the Lovász Extension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linearity, level-set representations, translation covariance, positive homogeneity, indicator recovery, symmetry, block-constant evaluation, and threshold expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let V=\{1,\ldots,p\}, let F:2^V\to\mathbb R satisfy F(\varnothing)=0, and let f be its Lovász extension. Then:
(a) if G:2^V\to\mathbb R satisfies G(\varnothing)=0 and has Lovász extension g, then f+g is the Lovász extension of F+G, and for every \lambda\in\mathbb R, \lambda f is the Lovász extension of \lambda F;
(b) for w\in\mathbb R_+^p,
\[f(w)=\int_0^{\infty}F(\{i\in V:w_i\ge z\})\,dz;\]
(c) if F(V)=0, then for every w\in\mathbb R^p,
\[f(w)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F(\{i\in V:w_i\ge z\})\,dz;\]
(d) for every w\in\mathbb R^p and \alpha\in\mathbb R,
\[f(w+\alpha\mathbf1_V)=f(w)+\alpha F(V);\]
(e) for every t\ge0 and w\in\mathbb R^p, \(f(tw)=t f(w)\);
(f) for every A\subseteq V, \(f(\mathbf1_A)=F(A)\);
(g) if F(A)=F(V\setminus A) for every A\subseteq V, then \(f(-w)=f(w)\) for every w\in\mathbb R^p;
(h) if V=A_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}A_m and w=\sum_{i=1}^m v_i\mathbf1_{A_i} with v_1\ge\cdots\ge v_m, then
\[f(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}(v_i-v_{i+1})F(A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_i)+v_mF(V);\]
(i) if w\in[0,1]^p and X\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1], then
\[f(w)=\mathbb E\bigl[F(\{i\in V:w_i\ge X\})\bigr].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lovász-extension operator is linear in the underlying normalized set function. It admits simplified level-set integrals under the stated domain conditions, is translation-covariant along the all-ones direction and positively homogeneous, recovers the set function on indicator vectors, maps symmetric set functions to even functions, has an ordered partition-block formula, and has a uniform-threshold expectation representation on the unit cube.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is the Lovász extension of }F
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Properties (a)--(i) hold with their stated additional hypotheses, including }G(\varnothing)=0,\ w\in\mathbb R_+^p,\ F(V)=0,\ t\ge0,\text{ symmetry of }F,\text{ the ordered partition assumptions, and }w\in[0,1]^p.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between set-function submodularity and convexity of the Lovász extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(f(\varnothing)=0\). knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The Lovász extension as the support function of the base polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be normalized and submodular, and define \[B(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for all }S\subseteq V,\ x(V)=f(V)\}.\] For every \(w\in\mathbb R^V\), the Lovász extension satisfies \[\widehat f(w)=\sigma_{B(f)}(w)=\max_{x\in B(f)}w^\top x.\] If \(\pi\) orders the coordinates of \(w\) nonincreasingly, the greedy vector with coordinates \(x^\pi_{\pi_k}=f(S_k)-f(S_{k-1})\) belongs to \(B(f)\) and attains the maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lovász extension is the support function of the base polyhedron, with a maximizing base obtained by the greedy ordering of weights.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite normalized submodular functions; inequalities use every subset of the ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The base polyhedron associated with \(f\) is
\[
B(f):=\bigl\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{V}:y(A)\le f(A)\text{ for every }A\subseteq V,\quad y(V)=f(V)\bigr\},
\]
where \(y(A):=\sum_{i\in A}y_i\). Thus a base is a modular lower bound on \(f\) that is tight on the full ground set. For finite normalized submodular \(f\), the polyhedron \(B(f)\) is nonempty; its extreme points are obtained from permutations of \(V\) by the greedy marginal-increment construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The base polyhedron consists of modular lower bounds on a normalized submodular function that agree with it on the entire ground set.
knowledge_statements.title: Base-Polyhedron View

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The base-polyhedron definition and accompanying nonemptiness and greedy-extreme-point claims are standard and mathematically consistent, but no inspectable citation supports them. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-function identity on all of \(\mathbb{R}^V\), using the homogeneous Lovász-extension convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^V\), order the coordinates as \(x_{\pi(1)}\ge\cdots\ge x_{\pi(n)}\), put \(S_k=\{\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(k)\}\), and define \(y^\pi_{\pi(k)}=f(S_k)-f(S_{k-1})\). Then \(y^\pi\in B(f)\), and the greedy base maximizes the linear functional in direction \(x\). Consequently,
\[
\widehat f(x)=\langle y^\pi,x\rangle=\max_{y\in B(f)}\langle y,x\rangle.
\]
Ties in the ordering may change the maximizing base but not the maximum value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lovász extension is exactly the support function of the base polyhedron, with a maximizing base produced by greedy coordinate ordering.

notation.meaning: Threshold set of a vector at level \(t\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard threshold-integral interface between submodular and convex minimization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional reduction over the unit cube, not merely a relaxation bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is submodular if and only if its Lovász extension \(\widehat f\) is convex. Moreover, for every \(x\in[0,1]^V\), the threshold sets \(S_t(x):=\{i\in V:x_i\ge t\}\) satisfy
\[
\widehat f(x)=\int_0^1 f(S_t(x))\,dt.
\]
Hence \(\widehat f(x)\ge\min_{S\subseteq V}f(S)\), while every incidence vector obeys \(\widehat f(\mathbf{1}_S)=f(S)\). Therefore
\[
\min_{x\in[0,1]^V}\widehat f(x)=\min_{S\subseteq V}f(S),
\]
and an optimal threshold set of any continuous minimizer is a discrete minimizer for almost every threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a submodular function over subsets is equivalent to minimizing its convex Lovász extension over the unit cube.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Minimization Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimization equivalence and threshold conclusion are mathematically sound, but no source is cited and the statement contains a proof-style derivation that must be removed when sourced.

notation.meaning: Optimal value of the unconstrained program.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical unconstrained finite submodular minimization program and minimizer-lattice property
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued unconstrained submodular minimization over the full power set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unconstrained submodular program associated with \(f\) is
\[
p^*:=\min\{f(S):S\subseteq V\},\qquad
\operatorname{Argmin}f:=\{S\subseteq V:f(S)=p^*\}.
\]
Because \(2^V\) is finite, the minimum is attained. If \(A,B\in\operatorname{Argmin}f\), submodularity gives \(f(A\cap B)+f(A\cup B)\le 2p^*\); minimality forces both terms to equal \(p^*\). Thus the minimizers form a lattice under intersection and union and have unique inclusion-minimal and inclusion-maximal members.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unconstrained submodular program minimizes the set function over all subsets; its minimizers form a lattice under union and intersection.
knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Submodular Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The program definition and minimizer-lattice property are correct, but they lack a citation. The record also embeds a proof and combines a definition with a nontrivial property theorem.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each multiplier \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\), define the Lagrangian set function and its optimal value by
\[
L_\lambda(S):=f(S)+\lambda^\top(g(S)-b),\qquad
q(\lambda):=\min_{S\subseteq V}L_\lambda(S).
\]
Since adding a modular function preserves submodularity, \(L_\lambda\) is submodular and evaluating \(q(\lambda)\) is an unconstrained submodular minimization problem. The Lagrangian dual program is \(d^*:=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda)\); its value supplies a lower bound for the associated constrained minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lagrangian submodular program adds nonnegative prices for modular constraint violations, leaving an unconstrained submodular minimization problem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Breakpoint Structure of Parametric Minimizer Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete breakpoint description when the scalar constraint function \(f_1\) is monotone decreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f_1\) is monotone decreasing. Then there exist \(\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_p\), with \(p\leq|E|\), such that the distinct values of \(\mathcal L(\lambda)\) for \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) are the families \(\mathcal L(\lambda_i)\), \(i=1,\ldots,p\), and the singleton families \(\{S^+(\lambda_i)\}=\{S^-(\lambda_{i+1})\}\), \(i=1,\ldots,p-1\). Furthermore, \(S^-(\lambda_1)=\varnothing\), \(S^+(\lambda_p)=E\), \[\mathcal L(\lambda)=\{S^+(\lambda_i)\}=\{S^-(\lambda_{i+1})\}\quad\text{when }\lambda_i<\lambda<\lambda_{i+1},\] and \[\mathcal L(\lambda)=\begin{cases}\{\varnothing\},&\lambda<\lambda_1,\\\{E\},&\lambda_p<\lambda.\end{cases}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the constraint function is monotone decreasing, the parametric minimizer families have at most |E| breakpoints. Between consecutive breakpoints there is one fixed minimizer, with only the empty set below the first breakpoint and only the ground set above the last.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_p,\quad p\leq|E|,\quad\text{with the stated complete breakpoint, interval, and endpoint description of }\mathcal L(\lambda).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given componentwise resource bounds \(b\), define
\[
\mathcal{F}_b:=\{S\subseteq V:g_j(S)\le b_j\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
The constrained submodular program is
\[
p^*:=\min_{S\in\mathcal{F}_b}f(S).
\]
The value is \(+\infty\) when \(\mathcal{F}_b=\varnothing\); otherwise finiteness of \(V\) ensures attainment. Although \(f\) is submodular, the feasible family need not be closed under union or intersection, so the lattice property of unconstrained minimizers does not automatically survive the constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradient-normal optimality condition on a sublattice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient optimality condition for minimizing a submodular function over a sublattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R\) be submodular, let \(\mathcal D_0\) be a sublattice of \(\mathcal D\), and let \(A\in\mathcal D_0\). Then \[f(A)=\min\{f(X)\mid X\in\mathcal D_0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists a\in\partial f(A)\text{ such that }-a\text{ is normal to }\mathcal D_0\text{ at }A.\]

children.title: Lagrangian Relaxation Interface
children.top_down_role: Structural passage from constrained formulations to parameterized Lagrangian families.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Relaxation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak duality and an exact attained saddle-point criterion for finite set programs with modular upper-bound constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L_\lambda(S):=f(S)+\lambda^\top(g(S)-b)\) and \(q(\lambda):=\min_{S\subseteq V}L_\lambda(S)\) for \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\). For the primal and dual values
\[
p^*:=\min\{f(S):S\subseteq V,\ g(S)\le b\},\qquad d^*:=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m}q(\lambda),
\]
weak duality gives \(d^*\le p^*\). If a feasible set \(S^*\) and a multiplier \(\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) satisfy
\[
S^*\in\operatorname{argmin}_{S\subseteq V}L_{\lambda^*}(S),\qquad \lambda_j^*(g_j(S^*)-b_j)=0\quad(j=1,\ldots,m),
\]
then \(d^*=p^*=f(S^*)\). Conversely, if the primal minimum and dual supremum are attained and \(d^*=p^*\), every primal-dual optimal pair satisfies these conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lagrangian values lower-bound the constrained optimum. A feasible Lagrangian minimizer with complementary slackness certifies equality, and attained zero-gap primal-dual optima satisfy the same conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(g:2^V\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is modular, \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and the primal program is feasible with finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^*\le p^*\), with equality under the stated Lagrangian optimality, feasibility, and complementary-slackness certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V=\{1,2\}\), set \(f(\varnothing)=f(\{1\})=f(\{2\})=0\) and \(f(V)=-1\), and impose \(|S|\le1\). The function \(f\) is submodular and the constrained optimum is \(p^*=0\). For \(\lambda\ge0\),
\[
q(\lambda)=\min_{S\subseteq V}\{f(S)+\lambda(|S|-1)\}
             =\min\{-\lambda,0,-1+\lambda\}.
\]
Thus \(d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda)=-\tfrac12<p^*\). Hence submodularity and modular constraints alone do not guarantee exact Lagrangian relaxation; zero gap requires additional structure or a saddle-point certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Submodularity does not ensure strong Lagrangian duality: a two-element submodular problem with a cardinality bound has a positive relaxation gap.

assumptions_latex: For \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\), \(F_\lambda(S)=f(S)-\lambda|S|\), and \(S^+(\lambda)\) is its inclusion-maximal minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varnothing=S_0\subsetneq S_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq S_r=V\), and \((S_k\setminus S_{k-1})_{k=1}^r\) is the principal partition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-parametric principal partition using inclusion-maximal minimizers and increasing parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The maximal minimizers \(S^+(\lambda)\) are nondecreasing with \(\lambda\). Let \(\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_r\) be the parameter values at which this maximal minimizer changes, and let
\[
\varnothing=S_0\subsetneq S_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq S_r=V
\]
be its successive values, with endpoint values understood for sufficiently small and sufficiently large \(\lambda\). The ordered family
\[
\mathcal{P}(f):=(S_1\setminus S_0,\ldots,S_r\setminus S_{r-1})
\]
is the principal partition of \(f\) under the cardinality parametrization; each block is labeled by the critical value at which it enters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The principal partition is formed by the successive blocks entering the maximal minimizer of a cardinality-parameterized submodular function.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak{S}(f)=\{(\lambda,\mathcal{M}_\lambda):\mathcal{M}_\lambda\text{ changes at }\lambda\}\) records the critical minimizer lattices.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(\lambda\), the family \(\mathcal{M}_\lambda\) is a nonempty distributive sublattice of \(2^V\), with least member \(S^-(\lambda)\) and greatest member \(S^+(\lambda)\). The principal structure of the cardinality-parametric family is the finite critical data
\[
\mathfrak{S}(f):=\bigl\{(\lambda,\mathcal{M}_\lambda):\mathcal{M}_\lambda\text{ changes at }\lambda\bigr\},
\]
together with the monotone extremal minimizers between critical values. It records not only the canonical maximal-minimizer chain but also all alternative minimizers occurring at ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The principal structure records each critical minimizer lattice, including its least and greatest sets and all tied minimizers omitted by the principal partition.

children.title: Partition–Structure Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between partition blocks and the encompassing principal structure.

assumptions_latex: The family \(f(S)-\lambda|S|\) uses inclusion-maximal minimizers to define its principal chain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_k=S_k\setminus S_{k-1}\) are exactly the elements entering the maximal minimizer at the \(k\)-th critical value.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard correspondence between the principal sequence and critical parametric minimizer lattices
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence for the maximal-minimizer convention; critical lattices retain refinements within tied blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_r\) be the critical values and \(\varnothing=S_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq S_r=V\) the successive inclusion-maximal minimizers. Then the ordered principal blocks satisfy
\[
P_k=S_k\setminus S_{k-1}\qquad(k=1,\ldots,r).
\]
Equivalently, \(S_k=P_1\cup\cdots\cup P_k\), so the labeled principal partition reconstructs the entire maximal-minimizer chain. At a critical value \(\lambda_k\), the associated minimizer lattice may contain sets strictly between its least and greatest members; this additional tie structure belongs to the principal structure but is not recoverable from the ordered blocks alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordered principal blocks and critical labels reconstruct the maximal-minimizer chain, while critical minimizer lattices additionally record alternatives created by ties.
knowledge_statements.title: Partition–Structure Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The block-chain correspondence follows the candidate's stated convention, but the convention and the claimed division between principal partition and principal structure are unsupported by a source.

children.title: Degenerate Principal Regimes
children.top_down_role: Ties, collapsed levels, and nonunique structural decompositions.

assumptions_latex: Principal data are generated by minimizing \(f(S)-\lambda|S|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equal critical rates can merge several elements into one principal block and create multiple minimizers at the breakpoint.

notation.meaning: A modular submodular function with element weights \(c_i\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit modular example of degeneracy in cardinality-parametric minimization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy means coincident critical values, not failure of submodularity or monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the modular, hence submodular, function \(f(S)=\sum_{i\in S}c_i\). A set minimizes \(f(S)-\lambda|S|\) by including every element with \(c_i<\lambda\), excluding every element with \(c_i>\lambda\), and choosing tied elements with \(c_i=\lambda\) arbitrarily. Therefore, if several elements share a value \(c\), the minimizer lattice at \(\lambda=c\) contains all choices of those tied elements, while the maximal minimizer adds them simultaneously as one block. In the extreme case \(c_i=c\) for every \(i\in V\), the principal chain jumps directly from \(\varnothing\) to \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coincident critical rates cause tied minimizers and merge several elements into one principal block; equal modular weights produce the extreme single-jump case.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Principal Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The modular tied-weight example and single-jump conclusion are mathematically correct and fit a failure-boundary leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable citation.

children.title: Minimum-Ratio Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Decompositions organized by minimum-ratio subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Ratio Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive minimum-ratio decomposition for a normalized submodular function with positive modular weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite, let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be normalized and submodular, and let \(w(S)=\sum_{i\in S}w_i\) with \(w_i>0\). Set \(A_0=\varnothing\). While \(A_{j-1}\ne V\), define \[\rho_j=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V\setminus A_{j-1}}\frac{f(A_{j-1}\cup S)-f(A_{j-1})}{w(S)}.\] Let \(B_j\) be the inclusionwise maximal minimizer, and put \(A_j=A_{j-1}\cup B_j\). The ordered blocks \((B_1,\ldots,B_k)\), together with their ratios \((\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_k)\), form the minimum-ratio decomposition whenever every maximal minimizer is uniquely determined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successively choose the maximal nonempty block minimizing residual submodular value per unit weight; the resulting ordered partition and ratios constitute the minimum-ratio decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((B_1,\ldots,B_k;\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_k)\) is the minimum-ratio decomposition of \((f,w)\).
review_flags: Exact project-intended convention for minimum-ratio decompositions requires an authoritative submodular-analysis source.
The existence and uniqueness convention for maximal tied minimizers needs source confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Minimum-Ratio Decompositions leaf and is internally coherent, but no cited source supports the intended contraction, ratio, or canonical maximal-minimizer convention. Source uncertainty prevents confirming that this is the exact project-intended decomposition.

children.title: Density Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Layered structures organized by density parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Density Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density formulation reciprocal to the positive-residual minimum-ratio decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the minimum-ratio construction, additionally assume \((f/A_{j-1})(S)>0\) for every nonempty residual set \(S\subseteq V\setminus A_{j-1}\). Define the residual density by \[d_{A_{j-1}}(S)=\frac{w(S)}{(f/A_{j-1})(S)}.\] At stage \(j\), choose the inclusionwise maximal set \(B_j\) maximizing \(d_{A_{j-1}}(S)\), set \(A_j=A_{j-1}\cup B_j\), and continue until \(A_k=V\). The ordered blocks and densities \((B_1,\delta_1),\ldots,(B_k,\delta_k)\), where \(\delta_j=d_{A_{j-1}}(B_j)\), form the density decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursively select the maximal residual block having greatest weight per unit residual submodular value; the blocks and attained densities form the density decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is normalized and submodular on finite \(V\).
\((f/A)(S)>0\) for each nonempty residual set considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((B_1,\delta_1),\ldots,(B_k,\delta_k)\) is the density decomposition of \((f,w)\).

notation.meaning: Density attained by the j-th block.
Union of the first j blocks.

review_flags: Density orientation and positivity convention require confirmation from a source specific to the stated correspondence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Density Decompositions leaf and is mathematically coherent under the stated strict-positivity assumption. An authoritative locator is required to confirm the density orientation, positivity domain, and recursive maximal-tie convention.

children.title: Ratio–Density Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between minimum-ratio and density-based decompositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Ratio–Density Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reciprocal equivalence of minimum residual ratios and maximum residual densities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a residual stage with contracted function \(g=f/A\), and suppose \(g(S)>0\) and \(w(S)>0\) for every nonempty \(S\subseteq V\setminus A\). Then \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V\setminus A}\frac{g(S)}{w(S)}=\operatorname*{argmax}_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V\setminus A}\frac{w(S)}{g(S)},\qquad \delta=\rho^{-1}.\] Consequently, applying the same inclusionwise-maximal tie rule at every contraction stage produces identical ordered blocks in the minimum-ratio and density decompositions, with \(\delta_j=1/\rho_j\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With positive residual values and weights, minimizing value per weight is equivalent to maximizing its reciprocal density; identical tie rules therefore yield identical blocks.
assumptions_latex: Both constructions use the same maximal tie rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_j^{\mathrm{ratio}}=B_j^{\mathrm{density}}\) and \(\delta_j=\rho_j^{-1}\) at every stage.

notation.meaning: Submodular contraction at the current accumulated set.

review_flags: The reciprocal identity is elementary, but the intended decomposition terminology and contraction convention lack a supporting source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reciprocal argmin-argmax identity is correct under strict positivity, and duality is an appropriate knowledge kind for this correspondence leaf. No source supports the named decomposition correspondence or confirms that the two recursive constructions use exactly these conventions.

children.title: Tied-Density Regimes
children.top_down_role: Degeneracies and aggregation effects caused by equal density levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Tied-Density Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lattice structure and canonical resolution of equal-density residual optimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:2^U\to\mathbb R\) be normalized and submodular, let \(w\) be positive modular, and fix \(\rho\in\mathbb R\). The minimizers of \(g(S)-\rho w(S)\) form a lattice: if \(S\) and \(T\) are minimizers, then \(S\cap T\) and \(S\cup T\) are minimizers. Hence, when the minimum value is \(0\), all sets satisfying \(g(S)/w(S)=\rho\) have a unique inclusionwise maximal union. Selecting that union gives a canonical block throughout a tied-density regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal optimal residual ratios are closed under union and intersection; their union is the unique maximal tied block and provides a canonical selection.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and \(g\) is normalized submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{S\subseteq U}(g(S)-\rho w(S))\) is a lattice with a unique maximal member.
review_flags: A source is needed to certify that this lattice-based tie convention matches the intended decomposition framework.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lattice claim for minimizers of the parametric submodular objective is standard, and the unique maximal member follows on a finite ground set. A source is still required to connect this lattice selection rule to the exact Tied-Density Regimes container and intended decomposition framework.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal Duality-Gap Certificate for Submodular Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of a primal-dual gap for the proximal Lovász-extension problem into a discrete submodular-minimization certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((w,s)\in\mathbb R^p\times B(F)\) be primal-dual candidates for minimizing
\[
\frac12\lVert w\rVert_2^2+f(w),
\]
with duality gap
\[
\varepsilon=\frac12\lVert w\rVert_2^2+f(w)+\frac12\lVert s\rVert_2^2.
\]
If \(A\) is a superlevel set of \(w\) having the smallest value of \(F\) among its superlevel sets, then
\[
F(A)-s_-(V)\leq\sqrt{\frac{p\varepsilon}{2}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given primal-dual candidates for the proximal problem, select a superlevel set of the primal vector with minimum submodular value. Its objective value exceeds the dual certificate by at most the square root of p times the duality gap divided by two.
assumptions_latex: F:2^V\to\mathbb R\text{ is submodular and }f\text{ is its associated convex extension}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(A)-s_-(V)\leq\sqrt{\frac{p\varepsilon}{2}}.

knowledge_statements.title: Base-Polyhedron Min–Max Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds-type min–max identity for normalized submodular-function minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be normalized and submodular, and define \[B(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq V,\ x(V)=f(V)\}.\] Then \[\min_{S\subseteq V}f(S)=\max_{x\in B(f)}\sum_{i\in V}\min\{x_i,0\}.\] Thus every base supplies a lower bound on every set value through its negative coordinates, and an optimal base attains the minimum set value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum of a normalized submodular function equals the largest sum of negative coordinates attainable by a vector in its base polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{S\subseteq V}f(S)=\max_{x\in B(f)}\sum_{i\in V}\min\{x_i,0\}\).

notation.meaning: Sum of the negative parts of x.

knowledge_statements.title: Sign Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Base-vector signs provide a universally checkable lower bound for submodular minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in B(f)\), and write \(N(x)=\{i\in V:x_i<0\}\). For every \(T\subseteq V\), \[f(T)\ge x(T)\ge\sum_{i\in N(x)}x_i=\sum_{i\in V}\min\{x_i,0\}.\] Therefore \(x\), together with its coordinate signs, certifies the lower bound \(\sum_i\min\{x_i,0\}\) on \(\min_T f(T)\). If a set attains this bound, the certificate is exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A base vector’s negative-coordinate sum is a certified lower bound on every set value; equality for a set proves that set is optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is normalized and submodular on finite \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(T)\ge\sum_{i\in V}\min\{x_i,0\}\) for every \(T\subseteq V\).

notation.meaning: Indices with strictly negative coordinates in x.

review_flags: An authoritative base-polyhedron certificate source and exact locator are missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-bound calculation is correct for a base vector, and certificate is the correct content kind. The record has no authoritative source or locator for the base-polyhedron certificate framework.

children.title: Tight-Set Certificates
children.top_down_role: Optimality evidence encoded by tight subsets and tight families.

knowledge_statements.title: Tight-Set Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A tight set compatible with base-vector signs certifies global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in B(f)\) and \(S\subseteq V\). Suppose \(S\) is tight for \(x\), meaning \(x(S)=f(S)\), and suppose \[\{i:x_i<0\}\subseteq S\subseteq\{i:x_i\le0\}.\] Then \[f(S)=x(S)=\sum_{i\in V}\min\{x_i,0\}\le f(T)\qquad\text{for every }T\subseteq V.\] Hence the verifiable pair \((x,S)\) certifies that \(S\) globally minimizes \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A base-tight set containing every negative coordinate and no positive coordinate attains the base lower bound and is therefore a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{T\subseteq V}f(T)\).

notation.meaning: Tightness of S for the base vector x.
The base-vector and tight-set certificate pair.

review_flags: The certificate follows from the min–max framework, but a supporting submodular-optimization source is absent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tightness and sign conditions correctly force equality with the negative-coordinate lower bound, and the record fits the Tight-Set Certificates leaf. It cannot pass source review without an authoritative submodular-optimization citation and specific locator.

children.title: Sign–Tightness Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between sign patterns and tight-set organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Sign–Tightness Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence between minimizers and sign-compatible tight bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be normalized and submodular. A set \(S\subseteq V\) minimizes \(f\) if and only if there exists \(x\in B(f)\) such that \[x(S)=f(S),\qquad x_i\le0\ \text{for all }i\in S,\qquad x_i\ge0\ \text{for all }i\in V\setminus S.\] Equivalently, \(S\) is tight and contains every strictly negative coordinate of \(x\) while excluding every strictly positive coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set minimizes a normalized submodular function exactly when some base is tight on it and has nonpositive signs inside and nonnegative signs outside.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\iff\exists x\in B(f):x(S)=f(S),\ x_S\le0,\ x_{V\setminus S}\ge0\).

notation.meaning: Every coordinate indexed by S is nonpositive.

review_flags: The converse direction requires an authoritative base-polyhedron optimality theorem locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated equivalence matches the Sign-Tightness Correspondence leaf and theorem is the correct content kind. The converse existence of a sign-compatible tight base is nontrivial and requires an authoritative theorem locator.

children.title: Certificate Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where one certificate form is incomplete or nonunique.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tightness, sign compatibility, and base feasibility are each essential to the certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: None of the three certificate requirements may simply be omitted. For the modular function \(f(S)=\sum_{i\in S}c_i\), its unique base is \(x=c\). If \(V=\{1,2\}\) and \(c=(-1,1)\), the tight set \(\{2\}\) is not minimizing because it violates sign compatibility, while the sign-compatible set \(\{1\}\) is certified precisely because it is tight. More generally, a vector with the desired signs but outside \(B(f)\) need not provide any valid lower bound. Thus base feasibility, tightness, and sign compatibility are jointly required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tightness alone can select a nonminimizer, signs outside the base polyhedron give no lower bound, and exact certification requires all three conditions together.
assumptions_latex: \(V=\{1,2\}\) and \(c=(-1,1)\) for the explicit tightness example.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\{2\}\) is tight but not minimizing, demonstrating failure without sign compatibility.

notation.meaning: Coefficient vector of the modular counterexample.
Base polyhedron of the modular function.

review_flags: The explicit example is directly checkable, but a source is needed for the claimed general certificate boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit modular example correctly shows that tightness without sign compatibility does not certify minimization, and failure_boundary is the exact mathematical role. The broader assertion about the joint necessity of base feasibility, tightness, and signs has no cited source or fully specified counterexample for each omitted condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Lattice Structure of Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of submodular minimizers under union and intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be submodular, and let \(S,T\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{U\subseteq V}f(U)\). Then \[f(S\cap T)+f(S\cup T)\le f(S)+f(T).\] Since each term on the left is at least the minimum value, equality holds and both \(S\cap T\) and \(S\cup T\) are minimizers. Consequently the minimizer family is a distributive sublattice of \(2^V\), with a unique inclusionwise minimal minimizer and a unique inclusionwise maximal minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intersection and union of any two submodular minimizers are also minimizers, yielding unique smallest and largest minimizers on a finite ground set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S,T\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\implies S\cap T,S\cup T\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\).

notation.meaning: Family of subsets attaining the minimum of f.
Boolean lattice of subsets of V.

review_flags: Standard theorem, but no supplied locator addresses submodular minimizer lattices.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lattice theorem is standard and correctly stated for a finite ground set, but no authoritative locator is supplied. The sentences deriving equality and closure are proof text and must be removed when a sourced replacement is prepared.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lattice of Submodular Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of the global minimizer family under union and intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) be submodular with \(F(\varnothing)=0\). If \(A,B\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{C\subseteq V}F(C)\), then \(A\cup B,A\cap B\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{C\subseteq V}F(C)\). Hence the minimizers of \(F\) form a lattice under union and intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a normalized submodular set function, the union and intersection of any two global minimizers are also global minimizers, so the minimizers form a lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\cup B,A\cap B\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{C\subseteq V}F(C)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimizers of a submodular function form a sublattice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of the full minimizer family under union and intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let E be finite, let \mathcal D\subseteq2^E be a distributive lattice, and let f:\mathcal D\to\mathbf R be submodular. If \mathcal D_0=\{X\in\mathcal D:f(X)=\min_{Y\in\mathcal D}f(Y)\}, then X,Y\in\mathcal D_0\Rightarrow X\cup Y,X\cap Y\in\mathcal D_0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The union and intersection of any two minimizers of a submodular function on a distributive set lattice are also minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal D\subseteq2^E\text{ is closed under union and intersection.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal D_0=\operatorname*{argmin}_{X\in\mathcal D}f(X)\text{ is a sublattice of }\mathcal D.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Norm Base Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The minimum-Euclidean-norm base identifies the extremal minimizers by coordinate signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be normalized and submodular, and let \(x^*\) be the unique solution of \[\min_{x\in B(f)}\frac12\lVert x\rVert_2^2.\] Define \(S^- =\{i\in V:x_i^*<0\}\) and \(S^0=\{i\in V:x_i^*\le0\}\). Then \(S^-\) is the unique inclusionwise minimal minimizer of \(f\), and \(S^0\) is the unique inclusionwise maximal minimizer. Thus the signs of the minimum-norm base certify both extremal optimal sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strictly negative coordinates of the minimum-norm base give the smallest minimizer; nonpositive coordinates give the largest minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^-=\min_{\subseteq}\operatorname*{argmin}f\) and \(S^0=\max_{\subseteq}\operatorname*{argmin}f\).

notation.meaning: Unique minimum-Euclidean-norm point of the base polyhedron.
Set of strictly negative coordinates of x*.
Set of nonpositive coordinates of x*.

review_flags: Fujishige's minimum-norm-base characterization requires an exact authoritative theorem locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict-negative and nonpositive sign characterization is the standard minimum-norm-base result, and certificate fits this terminal container. The nontrivial extremal-minimizer characterization requires an exact authoritative theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Base-polyhedron path-exchange iteration for submodular minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General exact minimization procedure maintaining a short convex decomposition into greedy base vectors; this extract describes the iteration and its no-path optimality certificate but does not itself state a termination bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^S\to\mathbb R\) be submodular with \(f(\varnothing)=0\), and represent \(x\in B_f\) as \(x=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i b^{\prec_i}\), where \(\lambda_i>0\) and \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\). Define \(A=\{(u,v):u\prec_i v\text{ for some }i\}\), \(P=\{v:x(v)>0\}\), and \(N=\{v:x(v)<0\}\). If \(D=(S,A)\) has no path from \(P\) to \(N\), let \(U\) be the vertices that can reach \(N\); then \[f(U)=x(U)\le x(W)\le f(W)\qquad(\forall W\subseteq S),\] so \(U\) minimizes \(f\). Otherwise, select \(s,t\) as prescribed from the distance labels, apply the order-pivot decomposition to one \(b^{\prec_i}\), move along \(\chi^t-\chi^s\) to the specified sign boundary, and compress the resulting convex representation to at most \(|S|\) terms before iterating.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a base-polyhedron point as a convex combination of greedy base vectors. When the union of their order arcs contains no path from a positive coordinate to a negative one, the vertices that can reach a negative coordinate form a minimizing set. Otherwise perform the prescribed order-pivot exchange and reduce the new convex decomposition to at most |S| terms.
assumptions_latex: x\in B_f\text{ has a convex decomposition into greedy base vectors}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The no-path case returns }U\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{W\subseteq S}f(W);\text{ otherwise one iteration produces another point of }B_f\text{ represented by at most }|S|\text{ greedy base vectors}

children.title: Ellipsoid Minimization
children.top_down_role: Exact submodular minimization through ellipsoidal convex-optimization machinery.

knowledge_statements.title: Ellipsoid Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact submodular minimization through the Lovász extension and ellipsoid separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a rational-valued submodular function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb Q\) through a value oracle and a known encoding bound. Normalize by subtracting \(f(\varnothing)\), form its Lovász extension \(\hat f\) on \([0,1]^V\), and use the greedy ordering at each query point to compute \(\hat f(z)\) and a subgradient. Apply the ellipsoid method to minimize \(\hat f\) over \([0,1]^V\), stopping once the encoding bound isolates the exact optimum. For an optimal \(z^*\), output a threshold set \(S_t=\{i:z_i^*\ge t\}\) attaining the least value among its coordinate thresholds. Then \(f(S_t)=\min_{S\subseteq V}f(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize the Lovász extension over the unit cube by ellipsoid subgradient cuts, then return the best threshold set of an exact optimal point.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is rational-valued and submodular on finite \(V\).
A value oracle and a polynomial encoding bound are available.
Exact rational arithmetic or equivalent bit-accurate separation is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{S\subseteq V}f(S)\).

notation.meaning: Lovász extension of the normalized submodular function.
An exact minimizer of the Lovász extension on the unit cube.

review_flags: The supplied network-flow locators do not support the Lovász-extension ellipsoid method.
An exact source is needed for the bit-complexity, stopping rule, and threshold-recovery formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind, but the available sources do not support Lovasz-extension ellipsoid minimization. The encoding assumptions and exact stopping criterion are not quantified, and 'among its coordinate thresholds' does not explicitly include the boundary threshold sets needed in degenerate cases; an authoritative algorithm and bit-complexity source is required before the formulation can be fixed reliably.

children.title: Separation-Based Minimization
children.top_down_role: Minimization frameworks organized around separation access.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Based Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional exact submodular minimization using strong separation over the base polyhedron and a lifted linear optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a normalized submodular function \(f\), the identity \(\min_{S\subseteq V}f(S)=\max_{x\in B(f)}\sum_{i\in V}\min\{x_i,0\}\) converts minimization into linear optimization over the lifted polyhedron \(Q=\{(x,z):x\in B(f),\ z_i\le x_i,\ z_i\le0\text{ for every }i\in V\}\). Given a strong separation oracle for \(B(f)\), separation for \(Q\) is immediate, so the ellipsoid method can maximize \(\sum_{i\in V}z_i\) exactly under the stated rational encoding bounds. If \(x^*\) is an optimal base, then \(S^- =\{i\in V:x_i^*<0\}\) is a minimizer of \(f\). This is a conditional separation-based method; it does not derive separation for \(B(f)\) from value-oracle access alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a strong separation oracle for the base polyhedron, a lifted linear program and the ellipsoid method recover an exact minimizing set; value-oracle access alone does not supply that separation oracle.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{Q}\) is normalized and submodular.
A strong separation oracle is available for \(B(f)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^V:x(A)\le f(A)\text{ for every }A\subseteq V,\ x(V)=f(V)\}\).
Polynomial rational encoding bounds are available for the oracle outputs and the relevant polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A set \(S^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{S\subseteq V}f(S)\) is recoverable using polynomially many strong-separation calls and bit operations.

notation.meaning: base polyhedron of the normalized submodular function
sum of the coordinates indexed by a set
lifted polyhedron that linearizes the sum of negative coordinates
negative-coordinate set of an optimal base

children.title: Ellipsoid–Separation Interface
children.top_down_role: Computational relationship between ellipsoid frameworks and separation oracles.

knowledge_statements.title: Ellipsoid–Separation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial oracle equivalence of strong separation and strong linear optimization for well-described rational polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty well-described rational polytope with known polynomial encoding and geometric size bounds. Given a strong separation oracle for \(P\), the ellipsoid method computes, for every \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\), a point \(x^*\in P\) satisfying \(c^\top x^*=\max\{c^\top x:x\in P\}\) using polynomially many oracle calls and bit operations. Conversely, a strong linear-optimization oracle for \(P\), together with the same description bounds, implements strong separation in polynomial time. Thus the two oracle problems are polynomial-time reducible to one another on this class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty well-described rational polytope, strong separation and exact linear optimization are polynomial-time equivalent through the ellipsoid framework.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty well-described rational polytope.
Polynomial bounds on the facet complexity, geometric size, and oracle-output encoding are known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong separation and strong linear optimization over \(P\) are polynomial-time oracle reducible to one another.

notation.meaning: an exact optimizer of the linear objective over the polytope

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes bit-polynomial ellipsoid guarantees from strongly polynomial value-oracle bounds.

source_refs.locator: Polynomial and Strongly Polynomial Computations, p. 32; Chapter 3, The Ellipsoid Method, p. 64

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard exact ellipsoid reduction for submodular minimization has running time polynomial in \(n\), the geometric encoding data, and \(L\). Consequently it is a polynomial-time algorithm in the bit model. It is not, merely from this analysis, strongly polynomial: the number or size of arithmetic operations may depend on \(L\). Any claimed strongly polynomial oracle bound must instead bound the number of value-oracle calls and arithmetic operations by a polynomial in \(n\), with intermediate encoding lengths polynomially controlled independently of the magnitudes of \(f(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ellipsoid minimization is polynomial in input bit length, but its standard analysis does not by itself give a strongly polynomial value-oracle algorithm.

Exchange capacities and residual arcs are computed consistently from \(f\) and \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination with no admissible improving exchange yields a minimizer of \(f\); otherwise an exchange or augmentation produces the next feasible base representation.

notation.meaning: current point in the base polyhedron
directed exchange graph associated with the current base representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic exchange-graph framework; the precise Cunningham variant requires source disambiguation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize an extreme base \(x\in B(f)\) from an ordering of \(V\). Construct a directed exchange graph \(D_x\) whose arc \((i,j)\) represents a positive feasible transfer \(x\mapsto x+\alpha(\chi_i-\chi_j)\), with \(0<\alpha\) not exceeding the corresponding exchange capacity. Search \(D_x\) for an admissible path from a coordinate requiring decrease to one permitting increase, augment by the path bottleneck, and update the base decomposition and capacities. Repeat until no admissible improving path exists; the terminal reachability set supplies a minimizer of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method maintains a base, augments along feasible paths in its exchange graph, and extracts a minimizing set when no improving path remains.
knowledge_statements.title: Cunningham Exchange-Graph Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation identifies the intended Cunningham algorithm or supports the stated exchange graph, augmentation direction, maintained decomposition, and terminal reachability certificate. These details vary across exchange-based frameworks and cannot be validated from the generic description.

assumptions_latex: \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{Z}\) is submodular and given by a value oracle.
\(M\ge \max_{S\subseteq V}|f(S)|\) is an available magnitude bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaling exchange method terminates after a number of phases logarithmic in \(M\), hence is weakly polynomial rather than strongly polynomial.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling-based Iwata–Fleischer–Fujishige variant with magnitude-dependent phase count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an initial scale \(\Delta\) comparable to a positive power-of-two upper bound on \(M\). At each scale, maintain a feasible convex combination of extreme bases, form the residual exchange graph using arcs with capacity at least \(\Delta\), and perform admissible augmentations until the scale-level optimality conditions hold. Replace \(\Delta\) by \(\Delta/2\) and repeat until integrality makes the residual error zero. The number of scaling phases is \(O(\log M)\); with polynomial work per phase in \(n\), the resulting oracle bound is polynomial in \(n\) and \(\log M\), but depends on numerical magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This exchange algorithm uses capacity scaling, requiring logarithmically many magnitude-dependent phases and therefore giving only weak polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Polynomial Exchange Variant

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The magnitude-dependent scaling claim is plausible, but no source identifies the precise Iwata–Fleischer–Fujishige variant or establishes its phase and per-phase bounds. A source is also needed to determine whether this method leaf should be represented primarily as an algorithm rather than only as a complexity bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weakly Polynomial IFF Scaling Algorithm for Submodular Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extracted exchange-and-flow delta-scaling procedure; correctness and complexity guarantees are not asserted by this algorithm block alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{Initialize }L,x,\delta,I,\varphi\text{ as prescribed. While }\delta\geq n^{-2},\text{ form }S=\{v\mid x(v)+\partial\varphi(v)\leq-\delta\},\ T=\{v\mid x(v)+\partial\varphi(v)\geq\delta\},\text{ and }W=\operatorname{Reach}_{G(\varphi)}(S).\text{ Apply Double-Exchange to active triples while applicable before reachability meets }T;\text{ when }W\cap T\neq\varnothing,\text{ augment }\varphi\text{ along a }\delta\text{-augmenting path and update }G(\varphi),S,T,W.\text{ Apply Reduce}(x,I),\text{ then set }\delta\leftarrow\delta/2\text{ and }\varphi\leftarrow\varphi/2.\text{ Return }W.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize the prescribed IFF data. In each scaling phase, form the negative-excess set S, positive-excess set T, and the vertices W reachable from S in the residual graph. Perform double exchanges on active triples, augment the flow along a delta-augmenting path when W reaches T, update the residual structures, and apply the reduction operation. Halve delta and the flow after each phase, and return W when the scaling loop terminates.
assumptions_latex: W\text{ is the set reachable from }S\text{ in }G(\varphi)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{When the loop condition }\delta\geq n^{-2}\text{ fails, return }W

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a feasible convex combination of extreme bases and an exchange graph encoding allowable transfers. Select augmentations and contractions by combinatorial progress measures, rather than by a scale initialized from \(\max_S|f(S)|\). Each augmentation changes the maintained representation or forces a structural event such as saturation, contraction, or deletion; a polynomial bound in \(n\) applies to the total number of such events. Consequently the total work has the form \(p(n)\mathrm{EO}+q(n)\) for polynomials \(p\) and \(q\), independent of the numerical magnitudes of oracle values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structural progress events replace magnitude scaling, yielding an exchange algorithm whose oracle and arithmetic counts depend only polynomially on the ground-set size.

A residual path admits simultaneous feasible exchanges in the participating bases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A multiple exchange preserves membership in \(B(f)\) while decreasing the chosen imbalance measure by the augmentation amount.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous augmentation variant within the Iwata–Fleischer–Fujishige framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a residual path, identify every extreme base in the convex representation of \(x\) that supports an exchange along an arc of that path. Let \(\delta\) be the minimum of the relevant exchange capacities and available convex weights. Apply all supported elementary transfers simultaneously, update the affected extreme bases and their weights, and merge duplicate bases. The aggregate coordinate change equals the path augmentation, every updated extreme base remains in \(B(f)\), and convexity therefore preserves \(x\in B(f)\). Repeat multiple exchanges until an arc saturates or a prescribed structural event occurs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple exchange performs compatible transfers across several extreme bases at once, preserving feasibility and advancing the residual augmentation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The assumptions never introduce f or its domain, and no source defines which multiple-exchange operation is intended. Simultaneous feasibility, the choice of delta, weight updates, and the asserted imbalance decrease require a precise algorithm and invariant from an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strongly polynomial combinatorial submodular minimization via greedy bases and exchange operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize greedy extreme bases \(y^k\in B(f)\), weights \(\lambda_k\ge0\) with \(\sum_k\lambda_k=1\), and \(x=\sum_k\lambda_k y^k\). Repeatedly use exchange capacities, reachability, and updates of the underlying permutations to alter the decomposition while preserving \(x\in B(f)\). Each iteration either performs an improving augmentation or makes irreversible combinatorial progress in the maintained orders and reachability relation. When no improving augmentation exists, output the terminal reachable set \(S^*\); the base-polyhedron optimality conditions give \(f(S^*)=\min_{S\subseteq V}f(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schrijver's family maintains greedy bases and uses combinatorial exchanges and reachability until the terminal set satisfies the base-polyhedron optimality conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Schrijver Algorithm for Submodular Function Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extracted high-level initialization, graph construction, stopping test, and update loop; the referenced graph and update rules require the surrounding construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a linear ordering \(L_1\) and set \(I:=\{1\}\), \(\lambda_1:=1\). Repeatedly construct the graph \(G=(V,A)\) prescribed by the algorithm, form \(x=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i y_i\), and set \(P:=\operatorname{supp}^+(x)\), \(N:=\operatorname{supp}^-(x)\). If no directed path from \(P\) to \(N\) exists, let \(W\) be the prescribed set of vertices reachable to \(N\) and stop; \(W\) is a minimizer of \(\rho\). Otherwise update \(\{(L_i,\lambda_i)\mid i\in I\}\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schrijver's method maintains an ordering-based representation of a base, constructs an associated directed graph, and tests for a directed path from the positive support to the negative support. When no such path exists, it returns the prescribed set of vertices reachable to the negative support as a minimizer; otherwise it updates the representation and repeats.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho:2^V\to\mathbf{R}\) is the submodular set function being minimized.
The graph, ordering-generated bases, reachability convention, and update operation are those of the referenced Schrijver construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At the stated stopping condition, the returned set \(W\) minimizes \(\rho\).
