children.title: Orlin Strongly Polynomial Method
children.top_down_role: The strongly polynomial minimization framework associated with Orlin.

assumptions_latex: \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is submodular and supplied by an exact evaluation oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimizer is computable in \(O(n^5\mathrm{EO}+n^6)\) time in the standard oracle-arithmetic accounting.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard value-oracle complexity attributed to Orlin's strongly polynomial algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Orlin's algorithm computes a set \(S^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{S\subseteq V}f(S)\) in \(O(n^5\mathrm{EO}+n^6)\) time. The algorithm combines strongly polynomial submodular-minimization primitives with contractions and a dimensional-reduction scheme: identified elements or blocks are fixed or contracted, and the remaining instance is solved recursively or by an exchange-based routine. The bound counts exact value-oracle evaluations at cost \(\mathrm{EO}\) and additional arithmetic operations separately, and neither count depends on the magnitudes or encoding lengths of the values \(f(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orlin's exact value-oracle algorithm minimizes a submodular function in strongly polynomial time, with the standard bound O(n^5 EO + n^6).
knowledge_statements.title: Orlin Strongly Polynomial Method

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated O(n^5 EO+n^6) bound is commonly attributed to Orlin, but the record has no source or locator confirming the exact model and separation of oracle from arithmetic costs. Because the terminal names a method, the source should also establish whether the primary record should be an algorithm rather than a bare complexity bound.

children.title: Post-Orlin Refinements
children.top_down_role: Later strongly polynomial refinements, simplifications, and related frameworks.

assumptions_latex: \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is submodular and accessed by an exact value oracle.
The refinement preserves exact minimization for unrestricted, possibly nonmonotone \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid refinement must retain magnitude-independent polynomial oracle complexity while improving a specified exponent, arithmetic term, or restricted-instance bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification criterion; the navigation label does not determine a unique post-Orlin result.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Call an algorithm a post-Orlin refinement only after specifying a bound \(T(n,\mathrm{EO})\) and a computational model in which it returns \(S^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{S\subseteq V}f(S)\). For an unrestricted strongly polynomial refinement, both the number of oracle calls and the number of arithmetic operations must be bounded by polynomials in \(n\) independent of \(\max_S|f(S)|\) and value encoding lengths. An improvement may reduce the exponent of \(n\), reduce non-oracle work, or apply to a stated restricted class; these claims are not interchangeable without their respective hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A post-Orlin refinement must state its model and exact bound, preserve exact minimization, and keep operation counts independent of function-value magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.title: Post-Orlin Refinements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is only a criterion for labeling a future result, not a post-Orlin refinement. It states no algorithm, author, bound, restricted class, or concrete improvement and substantially duplicates the sibling mechanism and boundary containers.

children.title: Strong-Polynomiality Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Structural devices supporting strongly polynomial complexity.

assumptions_latex: An exact value-oracle model is used for \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\).
Every iteration is assigned a combinatorial progress event from a finite family polynomially bounded in \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If each event occurs only polynomially many times and each iteration has polynomial cost, then the algorithm is strongly polynomial.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient mechanism for strong polynomiality in exchange, contraction, and decomposition algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an exact minimization algorithm performs at most \(N(n)\) iterations, where \(N\) is polynomial and does not depend on oracle-value magnitudes. Suppose further that each iteration uses polynomially many oracle calls and arithmetic operations, that intermediate numbers have polynomial encoding length, and that termination follows from irreversible combinatorial events such as arc saturation, contraction, deletion, rank reduction, or a bounded change of an ordering. Then the total oracle and arithmetic complexity is polynomial in \(n\) alone, so the algorithm is strongly polynomial in the oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality follows when magnitude-independent combinatorial events bound the iterations and each iteration has polynomial oracle, arithmetic, and encoding cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Polynomiality Mechanisms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The general progress-event mechanism fits the container, but the record combines an arbitrary real exact oracle with bit-encoding requirements that are meaningful only after specifying a rational computation model. A source is needed to state the applicable strong-polynomiality criterion precisely.

children.title: Refinement Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Differences in access assumptions, complexity guarantees, and applicable regimes.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm exactly minimizes \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{Q}\) in the value-oracle model.
Its analysis invokes a numerical scale, tolerance, or bit-length parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a magnitude-independent replacement for that parameter, the analysis proves at most weak polynomiality and cannot certify a strongly polynomial refinement.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between genuine strongly polynomial refinements and bit- or magnitude-dependent improvements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the iteration or operation bound contains \(L\), \(\log\max_S|f(S)|\), \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\), or another numerical magnitude parameter, then the bound is not strongly polynomial in \(n\), even when it improves an earlier bit-complexity estimate. Likewise, a faster result for symmetric, integer-valued, bounded-range, or otherwise restricted submodular functions does not automatically refine unrestricted minimization. To cross the strong-polynomiality boundary, the analysis must bound oracle calls and arithmetic operations by polynomials in \(n\) alone and control intermediate encoding lengths polynomially.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Magnitude-, precision-, or restriction-dependent speedups do not establish a strongly polynomial improvement for unrestricted exact submodular minimization.
knowledge_statements.title: Refinement Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between magnitude-dependent and strongly polynomial bounds is mathematically plausible and failure_boundary fits the leaf, but no cited source supports its application to post-Orlin submodular-minimization refinements or the listed restricted cases.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite ground set and \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is normalized and submodular.
The base polyhedron \(B(f)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^V:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for all }S\subseteq V,\ x(V)=f(V)\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_-\) is the unique inclusion-minimal minimizer of \(f\), and \(A_0\) is the unique inclusion-maximal minimizer of \(f\).

notation.meaning: Unique Euclidean minimum-norm point of the base polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimum-norm-point characterization for normalized finite submodular functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute the unique point \(x^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in B(f)}\|x\|_2\). Define \(A_-=\{i\in V:x_i^*<0\}\) and \(A_0=\{i\in V:x_i^*\le0\}\). Then \(A_-\) and \(A_0\) both minimize \(f\) over \(2^V\). Moreover, every minimizer \(A\) satisfies \(A_-\subseteq A\subseteq A_0\); consequently, \(A_-\) is the unique inclusion-minimal minimizer and \(A_0\) is the unique inclusion-maximal minimizer. An exact minimum-norm-point computation therefore returns an exact minimizer through coordinate thresholding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact minimum-norm point of the base polyhedron identifies the smallest and largest minimizers through its negative and nonpositive coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Norm-Point Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimum-norm-point characterization is mathematically plausible and fits the method container, but the theorem and threshold conclusions have no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Symmetric Submodular Minimization
children.top_down_role: Minimization restricted to symmetric submodular functions.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite with \(|V|\ge2\), and \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is submodular.
\(f\) is symmetric: \(f(S)=f(V\setminus S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The symmetric submodular minimization problem is \(\min\{f(S):\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\}\), with complementary sets having equal objective value.

notation.meaning: Complement of a set relative to the ground set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle formulation excluding the two trivial subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symmetric submodular minimization instance consists of a finite set \(V\) and a function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(f(A)+f(B)\ge f(A\cap B)+f(A\cup B)\) and \(f(S)=f(V\setminus S)\) for all \(A,B,S\subseteq V\). Its feasible family is \(\mathcal{F}=2^V\setminus\{\varnothing,V\}\), and its value is \(\min_{S\in\mathcal{F}}f(S)\). Symmetry identifies each feasible solution with its complement, so either side of an optimal bipartition represents the same objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a symmetric submodular function over all nonempty proper subsets; either side of a bipartition has the same value.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Submodular Minimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the symmetric-minimization container and is internally precise, but no source supports the stated formulation and exclusion of the trivial subsets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Legal order used in symmetric submodular minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy ordering primitive appearing in the recursive symmetric-minimization procedure; the definition and construction themselves require only value-oracle access to the set function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An ordering \((s_1,\ldots,s_n)\) of \(S\) is legal for \(f\) if, for each \(i=1,\ldots,n\), \(x=s_i\) minimizes \[f(\{s_1,\ldots,s_{i-1},x\})-f(\{x\})\] over \(x\in S\setminus\{s_1,\ldots,s_{i-1}\}\). Such an order can be found using \(O(|S|^2)\) calls to a value oracle for \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A legal order chooses each next element to minimize the stated expression relative to the current prefix. Greedy selection constructs one using quadratically many value-oracle calls.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalized symmetric submodular min-cut problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines symmetry and the associated nontrivial minimization problem under zero normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite with \(|V|=n\ge 2\), and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be submodular. The function is symmetric when \(f(X)=f(V\setminus X)\) for every \(X\subseteq V\). If additionally \(f(\varnothing)=f(V)=0\), then \(f(X)\ge 0\) for every \(X\subseteq V\), so \(\varnothing\) and \(V\) minimize \(f\) on \(2^V\). Symmetric submodular minimization therefore seeks a minimizer over \(2^V\setminus\{\varnothing,V\}\); such a minimizer is called a min-cut of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A submodular set function is symmetric if every set and its complement have equal value. Under zero normalization at the empty set and ground set, all values are nonnegative and those two trivial sets are minimizers. A min-cut is a minimum over the nonempty proper subsets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(X)\ge 0\ (\forall X\subseteq V),\qquad \operatorname{MinCut}(f)\in\arg\min_{X\in 2^V\setminus\{\varnothing,V\}}f(X)

notation.meaning: Accumulated prefix in a maximum-adjacency ordering.
Maximum-adjacency score of an unchosen element.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-oracle Queyranne contraction algorithm for finite symmetric submodular functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(v_1\in V\) arbitrarily. Given \(W_i=\{v_1,\ldots,v_i\}\), choose an unselected \(v_{i+1}\) maximizing \(q_i(v)=f(W_i)+f(\{v\})-f(W_i\cup\{v\})\). The last two elements \((v_{n-1},v_n)\) form a pendant pair. Record \(\{v_n\}\), contract \(v_{n-1}\) and \(v_n\) into one element, and repeat on the induced symmetric submodular function until one element remains. Expand every recorded set to original elements and output the recorded nonempty proper set of minimum value. The method uses \(O(|V|^3)\) value-oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Queyranne's method repeatedly finds a pendant pair by maximum-adjacency ordering, records one side, contracts the pair, and returns the best recorded set.
knowledge_statements.title: Queyranne Method Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the method-family container, but the pendant-pair guarantee, contraction details, and cubic oracle bound require an authoritative algorithm or theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cuts and auxiliary stage weights in Queyranne's construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Introduces the cut terminology and auxiliary symmetric functions used in the MA-ordering analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For distinct \(s,t\in V\), an \(s\)-\(t\) cut is a set \(U\subset V\) satisfying \(|\{s,t\}\cap U|=1\); a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut minimizes \(f(U)\) among such sets. Given an ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), let \(U_k=\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}\). For \(k=1,\ldots,n-1\), define \[w_k(C)=f(C)-\frac12\left(f(C\cap\overline U_{k-1})+f(\overline C\cap\overline U_{k-1})-f(\overline U_{k-1})\right).\] Then \(w_k(C)=w_k(V\setminus C)\) for every \(C\subseteq V\), but \(w_k\) need not be submodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An s-t cut contains exactly one of s and t, and a minimum s-t cut has least objective value among such cuts. The auxiliary function defined from an ordering prefix is symmetric, although it is not necessarily submodular.
assumptions_latex: f:2^V\to\mathbb R\text{ is symmetric and submodular}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w_k(C)=w_k(V\setminus C)\quad(\forall C\subseteq V),\qquad w_k\text{ need not be submodular}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Queyranne legal-order contraction recurrence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive method for minimizing a symmetric submodular function over nonempty proper subsets; trivial base cases must be handled directly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^S\to\mathbb R\) be symmetric and submodular, and suppose the recursive step is applied when \(|S|\ge3\). Find a legal order \((s_1,\ldots,s_n)\). By identifying \(s_{n-1}\) and \(s_n\), recursively obtain a nonempty proper set \(T\subset S\) minimizing \(f(T)\) among sets that do not split \(\{s_{n-1},s_n\}\). Then \[\min_{\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq S}f(U)=\min\{f(T),f(\{s_n\})\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute a legal order, contract its last two elements, recursively find the best nontrivial set keeping that pair together, and compare its value with the last-element singleton. The smaller value is the minimum over all nonempty proper subsets.
assumptions_latex: f:2^S\to\mathbb R\text{ is symmetric and submodular}
T\text{ minimizes }f\text{ among nonempty proper subsets not splitting }\{s_{n-1},s_n\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq S}f(U)=\min\bigl\{f(T),f(\{s_n\})\bigr\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singleton minimum-cut property of the stage weight
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stagewise cut-minimality lemma used in the analysis of Queyranne's ordering construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) be the ordering under construction, let \(U_k=\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}\), and let \(w_k\) be the associated stage function. For every \(k\in\{1,ldots,n-1\}\) and every \(u\in V\setminus U_k\), the singleton \(\{u\}\) minimizes \(w_k(C)\) over all \(u\)-\(v_k\) cuts \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each eligible stage, the singleton of any element outside the current prefix is a minimum cut separating that element from the current ordered element under the auxiliary stage function.

U_k=\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}\text{ and }w_k\text{ is the associated stage function}

children.title: Pendant-Pair Structure
children.top_down_role: Structural role of pendant pairs within the Queyranne family.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite with \(|V|\ge2\), and \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is symmetric and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordered pair \((t,u)\) is pendant exactly when \(f(\{u\})=\min\{f(X):u\in X,\ t\notin X\}\).

notation.meaning: Sets separating the ordered pair with the second element on the selected side.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered pendant-pair convention used in Queyranne's algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ordered pair \((t,u)\) is a pendant pair for \(f\) if the singleton \(\{u\}\) is a minimum-value set separating \(u\) from \(t\) with \(u\) on the selected side. Equivalently, with \(\mathcal{S}_{t,u}=\{X\subseteq V:u\in X,\ t\notin X\}\), the defining equality is \(f(\{u\})=\min_{X\in\mathcal{S}_{t,u}}f(X)\). For a maximum-adjacency ordering of a symmetric submodular function, its final ordered pair has this property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pendant pair is an ordered pair whose second singleton is cheapest among all sets containing the second element but excluding the first.
knowledge_statements.title: Pendant-Pair Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pendant-pair definition is coherent, but the additional claim about the final pair of a maximum-adjacency ordering is a nontrivial theorem with no cited source.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the minimum-cut property of the last two elements in the ordering produced by Queyranne's algorithm.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the ordering returned by Queyranne's algorithm, the final singleton is a minimum-value cut separating the last two ordered elements.
assumptions_latex: f:2^V\to\mathbb R\text{ is symmetric and submodular}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{v_n\}\in\arg\min\{f(C):C\text{ is a }v_{n-1}\text{-}v_n\text{ cut}\}

children.title: Symmetry Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of the method family outside exact symmetry regimes.

assumptions_latex: A maximum-adjacency ordering starts with \(a\) and resolves ties as \(a,b,c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The final pair \((b,c)\) is not pendant, demonstrating that submodularity without symmetry does not imply the pendant-pair theorem.

notation.meaning: A modular, hence submodular, but nonsymmetric function.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of the pendant-pair conclusion after removing symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(X)=-\mathbf{1}_{\{a\in X\}}\) is modular and therefore submodular, but it is not symmetric. Every maximum-adjacency score \(f(W)+f(\{v\})-f(W\cup\{v\})\) equals \(0\), so the ordering \(a,b,c\) is admissible. Its final ordered pair is \((b,c)\). However, \(f(\{c\})=0\), while \(f(\{a,c\})=-1\) and \(c\in\{a,c\}\), \(b\notin\{a,c\}\). Thus \((b,c)\) is not pendant. Symmetry is therefore essential to the general maximum-adjacency pendant-pair guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A three-element modular nonsymmetric function admits a maximum-adjacency ordering whose final pair is not pendant, so submodularity alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is internally consistent and the failure-boundary kind fits the container, but the record supplies no source or locator for the boundary claim.

children.title: Graph-Representable Functions
children.top_down_role: Submodular functions admitting direct graph-based representations.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite set of binary variables.
\(G=(\{s,t\}\cup V\cup U,E)\) is a directed graph with nonnegative arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function is graph-representable when \(f(S)=\kappa+\min_{T\subseteq U}c(\delta^+(\{s\}\cup S\cup T))\) for every \(S\subseteq V\).

notation.meaning: Auxiliary vertices whose cut sides are optimized out.
Arcs leaving a source-side vertex set.
Total capacity of an arc set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed nonnegative-capacity cut representation with auxiliary binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is graph-representable if there exist a finite auxiliary set \(U\), a directed graph \(G=(\{s,t\}\cup V\cup U,E)\), nonnegative capacities \(c_e\), and a constant \(\kappa\in\mathbb{R}\) such that, for every \(S\subseteq V\), \[f(S)=\kappa+\min_{T\subseteq U}c\bigl(\delta^+(\{s\}\cup S\cup T)\bigr).\] The prescribed variable vertices in \(S\) lie on the source side, those in \(V\setminus S\) lie on the sink side, and auxiliary vertices may choose either side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph-representable set function equals a constant plus the cheapest source-sink cut consistent with each variable assignment, after optimizing auxiliary vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Representable Functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The auxiliary-vertex cut definition is precise and fits Graph-Representable Functions, but this convention-sensitive definition has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Cut-Reducible Functions
children.top_down_role: Submodular functions reducible to graph-cut optimization.

assumptions_latex: \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is given on a finite ground set.
A reduction constructs a capacitated source-sink graph in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduction is valid when decoding any minimum cut yields an element of \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{S\subseteq V}f(S)\).

notation.meaning: Decoded subset represented by a cut.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization-preserving reduction, weaker than pointwise objective representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is cut-reducible if a polynomial-time transformation constructs a capacitated source-sink graph \(G_f\) and a polynomial-time decoder \(D\) such that every minimum source-sink cut \(C^*\) satisfies \(D(C^*)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{S\subseteq V}f(S)\). The definition requires preservation of optimal solutions, but it need not provide a cut whose capacity equals \(f(S)\) for every prescribed set \(S\). If graph size and capacities are polynomially encoded, one minimum-cut computation solves the resulting minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is cut-reducible when a polynomial graph construction and decoder turn every minimum cut into a minimizing subset, without necessarily representing every objective value.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Reducible Functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The optimizer-preserving reduction definition fits the container, but its distinction from pointwise graph representation and its encoding conditions are unsupported by a cited source.

children.title: Representation–Reduction Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between direct graph representation and cut reduction.

assumptions_latex: \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) has a nonnegative-capacity graph representation with polynomially many vertices and arcs.
The representation and its rational capacities are available explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact graph representation implies a value-preserving minimum-cut reduction and \(\min_{S\subseteq V}f(S)=\kappa+\min_C c(C)\).

notation.meaning: Source-side original variables decoded from a cut.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise representation implies an optimization-preserving cut reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f(S)=\kappa+\min_{T\subseteq U}c(\delta^+(\{s\}\cup S\cup T))\) for every \(S\subseteq V\). Minimizing both sides over \(S\) gives \[\min_{S\subseteq V}f(S)=\kappa+\min_{C\text{ an }s\text{-}t\text{ cut}}c(C).\] If \(C^*\) has source side \(W^*\), then \(S^*=V\cap W^*\) minimizes \(f\). Thus an explicit polynomial-size graph representation yields a polynomial minimum-cut reduction. Conversely, an arbitrary optimizer-preserving cut reduction need not imply the displayed pointwise equality; that converse requires value preservation for every prescribed assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointwise cut representation immediately yields a minimum-cut reduction; an optimizer-only reduction does not conversely guarantee pointwise representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation–Reduction Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation-to-reduction implication is coherent and the representation kind fits the correspondence container, but neither direction-related claim has source support.

children.title: Nonrepresentability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Function classes or interaction patterns that resist graph representation or cut reduction.

assumptions_latex: Graph representations use directed cuts with nonnegative capacities and allow arbitrary auxiliary vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(g\) is not graph-representable because it violates submodularity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Submodularity is a necessary boundary for nonnegative-capacity cut representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every nonnegative-capacity cut function is submodular, and minimizing such a function over auxiliary coordinates preserves submodularity on the remaining coordinates. Hence every graph-representable function is submodular. For the displayed \(g\), taking \(A=\{1\}\) and \(B=\{2\}\) gives \(g(A)+g(B)=0\), whereas \(g(A\cap B)+g(A\cup B)=1\). The submodular inequality fails, so no graph with nonnegative capacities and any number of auxiliary vertices can represent \(g\) in the stated cut sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative cut representations necessarily produce submodular functions; a two-variable positive conjunction violates submodularity and is therefore not representable.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonrepresentability Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example violates submodularity as stated and fits a failure-boundary container, but the essential claim that auxiliary minimization preserves submodularity lacks a source and locator.

assumptions_latex: \(P=(E,\preceq)\) is a finite partially ordered set.
\(f:\mathcal{I}(P)\to\mathbb{R}\) is submodular on the lattice of order ideals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distributive-lattice minimization is \(\min\{f(I):I\in\mathcal{I}(P)\}\) under lattice submodularity.

notation.meaning: Family of order ideals of the poset.
Meet and join in the ideal lattice.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Birkhoff representation by order ideals of a poset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An order ideal is a set \(I\subseteq E\) such that \(x\in I\) and \(y\preceq x\) imply \(y\in I\). The family \(\mathcal{I}(P)\), ordered by inclusion, is a distributive lattice with meet \(I\cap J\) and join \(I\cup J\). A function \(f:\mathcal{I}(P)\to\mathbb{R}\) is lattice-submodular when \(f(I)+f(J)\ge f(I\cap J)+f(I\cup J)\) for all \(I,J\in\mathcal{I}(P)\). Distributive-lattice minimization asks for an ideal \(I^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{I\in\mathcal{I}(P)}f(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a lattice-submodular function over the order ideals of a finite poset, whose meet and join are intersection and union.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributive-Lattice Minimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite order-ideal formulation is mathematically standard and fits the topic, but no cited source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Odd-Set Minimization
children.top_down_role: Submodular minimization restricted to feasible sets of odd cardinality.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite ground set and \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is submodular.
At least one odd-cardinality subset exists, equivalently \(V\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Odd-set minimization is \(\min\{f(S):S\subseteq V,\ |S|\equiv1\pmod 2\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-parity constrained submodular minimization problem.

source_refs.locator: Section 8.2, “Minimizing Submodular Functions Over Odd Sets,” p. 197
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{O}(V)=\{S\subseteq V:|S|\equiv1\pmod 2\}\). The odd-set minimization problem for \(f\) is to compute \[S^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{S\in\mathcal{O}(V)}f(S).\] Unlike unconstrained submodular minimization, the feasible family is not closed under union or intersection: two odd sets may have an even union or intersection. Thus the parity condition is part of the feasible-domain definition and cannot be discarded merely from submodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Odd-set minimization restricts a submodular objective to subsets of odd cardinality, a family not generally closed under union or intersection.
knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Set Minimization

children.title: Parity-Constrained Minimization
children.top_down_role: Submodular minimization under general parity-based feasibility restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite, \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is submodular, and \(T\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Parity-constrained minimization is \(\min\{f(S):S\subseteq V,\ |S\cap T|\equiv b\pmod 2\}\), provided the feasible family is nonempty.

notation.meaning: Subsets satisfying the prescribed intersection parity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection-parity formulation, specializing to odd cardinality when \(T=V\) and \(b=1\).

source_refs.locator: Section 8.2, “Minimizing Submodular Functions Over Odd Sets,” p. 197
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(T\subseteq V\) and \(b\in\{0,1\}\), define
\[
\mathcal F_{T,b}=\{S\subseteq V:|S\cap T|\equiv b\pmod 2\}.
\]
The parity-constrained submodular minimization problem is
\[
\min\{f(S):S\in\mathcal F_{T,b}\},
\]
provided \(\mathcal F_{T,b}\ne\varnothing\). When \(T=V\) and \(b=1\), this specializes to odd-cardinality submodular minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parity-constrained minimization restricts feasible subsets by the parity of their intersection with a specified set; odd-cardinality minimization is the case T equals V.
knowledge_statements.title: Parity-Constrained Minimization

source_witnesses.locator: Section 8.2, “Minimizing Submodular Functions Over Odd Sets,” p. 197
source_witnesses.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The supplied locator covers odd-cardinality sets, corresponding to T=V and b=1, but does not establish the broader intersection-parity formulation for arbitrary T and b.

children.title: Odd-Parity Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Placement of odd-set restrictions within broader parity-constrained regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{f(S):S\subseteq V,\ |S|\text{ odd}\}=\min\{f(\operatorname{supp}x):x\in\{0,1\}^{V},\ \sum_{i\in V}x_i\equiv1\pmod 2\}\).

notation.meaning: Incidence vector of a subset S.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-vector correspondence for unconstrained odd-set submodular minimization.

source_refs.locator: 8.2 Minimizing Submodular Functions Over Odd Sets p. 197
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(S\subseteq V\), its incidence vector \(\chi^S\in\{0,1\}^{V}\) satisfies
\[
|S|\equiv\sum_{i\in V}\chi_i^S\pmod 2.
\]
Hence the odd subsets of \(V\) are in bijection with binary vectors satisfying the odd-parity equation. Under this bijection, assigning the vector objective \(x\mapsto f(\operatorname{supp}x)\) preserves every objective value and every minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Odd subsets correspond exactly to binary incidence vectors whose coordinate sum is odd, so odd-set minimization and binary odd-parity minimization are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Parity Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: 8.2 Minimizing Submodular Functions Over Odd Sets p. 197
source_witnesses.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

children.title: Parity Feasibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limits caused by parity restrictions and feasible-family interactions.

assumptions_latex: Feasible sets must satisfy \(\ell\le |S|\le u\), where \(0\le\ell\le u\le n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An odd feasible set exists exactly when \([\ell,u]\cap\{1,3,5,\ldots\}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility boundary for odd parity under interval cardinality constraints.

source_refs.locator: 8.2 Minimizing Submodular Functions Over Odd Sets p. 197
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
\mathcal F_{\rm odd}=\{S\subseteq V:\ell\le |S|\le u,\ |S|\equiv1\pmod 2\}.
\]
Then \(\mathcal F_{\rm odd}\neq\varnothing\) if and only if the integer interval \([\ell,u]\) contains an odd integer. In particular, without cardinality restrictions an odd subset exists if and only if \(n\ge1\). Thus parity-constrained minimization is infeasible precisely beyond this boundary, independently of the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With interval cardinality bounds, odd-set feasibility holds exactly when the permitted interval contains an odd integer; unconstrained feasibility requires a nonempty ground set.
knowledge_statements.title: Parity Feasibility Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 8.2 Minimizing Submodular Functions Over Odd Sets p. 197

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\lambda\le\mu\), then the inclusion-minimal minimizers satisfy \(S^-_\lambda\subseteq S^-_\mu\).

notation.meaning: Inclusion-minimal minimizer of the parameterized objective.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone nesting for the linear modular-parameter convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\), let \(f_\lambda(S)=f(S)-\lambda w(S)\). The minimizers of \(f_\lambda\) are closed under union and intersection, so they possess a unique inclusion-minimal member \(S^-_\lambda\). For any \(\lambda\le\mu\),
\[
S^-_\lambda\subseteq S^-_\mu.
\]
Consequently the minimal optimal set changes along a nested chain as the reward parameter increases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting an increasing positive modular reward yields inclusion-minimal optimal sets that expand monotonically with the parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Submodular Minimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nesting claim is mathematically plausible for the stated positive modular weights, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the lattice-of-minimizers and parametric monotonicity assertions.

children.title: Weak Polynomiality
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured relative to numerical encoding length.

assumptions_latex: The submodular function and all numerical data are rationally encoded.
\(L\) denotes the total binary encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak polynomiality permits a running-time bound \(p(|V|,L)\) for some polynomial \(p\).

notation.meaning: Binary input length of numerical data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Turing-model weak polynomiality for explicitly encoded rational instances.

source_refs.locator: 6.3 Weak and Strong Problems p. 170
Time and Space Complexity p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A submodular-minimization algorithm is weakly polynomial when, for every explicitly encoded rational instance, its bit-operation count is bounded by
\[
p(n,L)
\]
for a fixed polynomial \(p\), where \(n=|V|\) and \(L\) is the input encoding length. Dependence on numerical magnitudes through their bit lengths is permitted; hence this classification alone does not establish strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly polynomial algorithm runs in time polynomial in both the ground-set size and the binary encoding length of all numerical data.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Polynomiality

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Weak and Strong Problems p. 170
Time and Space Complexity p. 23

children.title: Strong Polynomiality
children.top_down_role: Arithmetic-operation bounds independent of numerical magnitudes.

assumptions_latex: The algorithm operates on rationally encoded submodular-minimization instances.
Each elementary arithmetic operation and comparison is counted once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong polynomiality requires polynomially many operations in \(|V|\), with polynomially bounded intermediate encoding lengths.

notation.meaning: Number of arithmetic operations and comparisons.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic-model strong polynomiality with controlled intermediate bit lengths.

source_refs.locator: 6.3 Weak and Strong Problems p. 170

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An algorithm is strongly polynomial when there is a polynomial \(p\) such that
\[
T_{\rm arith}\le p(n)
\]
for every instance, independently of the magnitudes and encoding lengths of its numerical data, and every intermediate rational number has encoding length polynomial in the original input length. These two requirements imply a polynomial bit-operation bound while excluding iteration counts governed by numerical magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality bounds arithmetic steps solely by combinatorial dimension and also controls the bit lengths of intermediate numbers.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Polynomiality

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Weak and Strong Problems p. 170

children.title: Oracle Polynomiality
children.top_down_role: Complexity relative to value-oracle access.

assumptions_latex: \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{Q}\) is accessed only through an exact value oracle.
One oracle call returns \(f(S)\) for a queried \(S\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Oracle polynomiality requires at most \(p(|V|)\) oracle calls and \(p(|V|)\) additional elementary operations.

notation.meaning: Number of value-oracle calls made by algorithm A.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact value-oracle model with unit-cost oracle calls.

source_refs.locator: The Running Time of Oracle Algorithms p. 26
Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An exact value-oracle algorithm for submodular minimization is oracle-polynomial when some polynomial \(p\) satisfies
\[
Q_A(n)\le p(n)
\]
and its non-oracle work is also bounded by \(p(n)\) elementary operations. Oracle evaluation is assigned unit cost. Therefore this classification measures combinatorial access complexity and does not by itself bound the time or bit cost required to implement the oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle polynomiality means polynomially many exact value queries and polynomial additional work, treating each oracle response as a unit-cost operation.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Polynomiality

source_witnesses.locator: The Running Time of Oracle Algorithms p. 26
Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

children.title: Polynomiality Separation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Distinctions among the three complexity guarantees.

assumptions_latex: Explicit rational inputs are measured by Turing bit complexity.
Oracle inputs are measured with unit-cost exact function evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong polynomiality implies weak polynomiality, whereas oracle polynomiality requires an oracle-implementation bound before yielding a Turing-time guarantee.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of strong, weak, and unit-cost oracle complexity guarantees.

source_refs.locator: 6.3 Weak and Strong Problems p. 170
The Running Time of Oracle Algorithms p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For explicit rational instances, a strongly polynomial algorithm is weakly polynomial because polynomially many arithmetic operations on polynomial-length intermediates yield polynomial bit complexity. The converse does not follow from a bound polynomial in \(n\) and \(L\), since that bound may depend on \(L\). Likewise, an oracle-polynomial bound becomes a Turing-time bound only after the oracle's evaluation time and output encoding lengths are polynomially controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality entails weak polynomiality, but weak bounds may depend on bit length, and oracle bounds omit the cost of implementing value queries.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomiality Separation Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Weak and Strong Problems p. 170
The Running Time of Oracle Algorithms p. 26

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Oracle Query Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case adaptive query complexity in the deterministic exact value-oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be an \(n\)-element ground set, let \(\mathcal C_n\) be a specified class of submodular functions \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\), and let \(A\) be a deterministic adaptive algorithm that terminates with a minimizer for every \(f\in\mathcal C_n\). A value query selects \(S\subseteq V\) and returns the exact value \(f(S)\). If \(N_A(f)\) is the number of queries made on input oracle \(f\), then the worst-case query complexity of \(A\) is
\[
Q_A(n)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal C_n}N_A(f).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a specified class of submodular functions on n elements, the value-oracle query complexity of a terminating deterministic adaptive algorithm is the supremum, over functions in that class, of the number of exact set-value queries made before returning a minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C_n\) is a specified class of submodular functions \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\).
\(A\) is deterministic, may select queries adaptively, and terminates with a minimizer for every \(f\in\mathcal C_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_A(n)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal C_n}N_A(f)\).

notation.meaning: Specified class of submodular functions on n-element ground sets.
Number of value queries made by algorithm A when interacting with oracle f.
Worst-case value-oracle query complexity on n elements.

source_refs.locator: The Running Time of Oracle Algorithms p. 26

source_witnesses.locator: The Running Time of Oracle Algorithms p. 26

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact-cardinality submodular minimization is NP-hard because minimizing \(-|E(S)|\) solves the clique decision problem.

notation.meaning: Edges having both endpoints in S.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-hardness boundary created by an exact-cardinality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f_G(S)=-|E(S)|\), where \(E(S)\) contains the edges induced by \(S\). The function \(f_G\) is submodular. Moreover,
\[
\min_{|S|=k}f_G(S)=-\binom{k}{2}
\]
if and only if \(G\) contains a clique of size \(k\). Thus adding an exact-cardinality constraint makes general submodular minimization NP-hard, despite polynomial-time solvability of unconstrained submodular minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact-cardinality constraints destroy general tractability: minimizing the negative number of induced edges decides whether a graph contains a clique of the prescribed size.
knowledge_statements.title: Constrained-Minimization Intractability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The clique reduction and submodularity claim are plausible, but this nontrivial NP-hardness boundary has no cited source. An inspectable hardness or reduction reference is required.

children.title: Approximate-Value Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by deterministic value approximation.

assumptions_latex: The oracle returns \(\widetilde f(S)\) with \(|\widetilde f(S)-f(S)|\le\varepsilon\) for every query.
The algorithm must identify an exact minimizer of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform additive error cannot distinguish candidates whose true objective gap is at most \(2\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information boundary for exact recovery from uniformly approximate values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For two feasible sets \(A,B\), the error guarantee implies
\[
\widetilde f(A)-\widetilde f(B)\in[f(A)-f(B)-2\varepsilon,\ f(A)-f(B)+2\varepsilon].
\]
Hence when \(|f(A)-f(B)|\le2\varepsilon\), admissible oracle answers can reverse or erase their true ordering. Without an objective-gap promise exceeding \(2\varepsilon\), uniformly approximate values therefore do not suffice to guarantee identification of an exact minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Additive value errors can reverse comparisons across gaps up to twice the error, so exact minimizer recovery needs a sufficiently large objective gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Value Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison interval and the 2ε ambiguity threshold are mathematically plausible, but the information-theoretic exact-recovery conclusion has no cited source.

children.title: Noisy-Value Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by stochastic or adversarial value perturbations.

assumptions_latex: No distributional, independence, repetition, or deterministic magnitude bound is imposed on \(\xi(S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite-query algorithm can guarantee an exact minimizer uniformly over all admissible noise assignments.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability failure under unrestricted query-dependent noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(\xi(S)\) is unrestricted, any finite transcript \(Y(S_1),\ldots,Y(S_m)\) is compatible with distinct submodular objectives having different minimizers: for either objective, choose the queried noises to reproduce that transcript. Consequently the observations do not identify the underlying objective, and no algorithm can uniformly guarantee an exact minimizer. Recovery requires additional assumptions such as bounded noise, unbiased independent samples, or repeatable queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With unrestricted query-dependent noise, identical observations can arise from submodular functions having different minimizers, so exact recovery is impossible without further assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Noisy-Value Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the impossibility assertion, and the assumptions do not explicitly introduce a finite nonempty ground set or the domain and class of the underlying submodular objective.

children.title: Error-Amplification Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where small evaluation errors produce large optimization losses.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde f(A)+\widetilde f(B)\ge\widetilde f(A\cup B)+\widetilde f(A\cap B)-4\varepsilon\) for all \(A,B\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fourfold amplification of pointwise error in the submodularity inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(A,B\subseteq V\), pointwise error can affect each of the four terms in the submodularity inequality. Consequently
\[
\widetilde f(A)+\widetilde f(B)\ge
\widetilde f(A\cup B)+\widetilde f(A\cap B)-4\varepsilon.
\]
Thus an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate value table is necessarily \(4\varepsilon\)-approximately submodular. Exact submodularity of \(\widetilde f\) is not guaranteed, because the four perturbations may all act in the adverse direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform pointwise error can accumulate across all four terms of the submodularity inequality, producing a submodularity defect as large as four times the error.
knowledge_statements.title: Error-Amplification Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The 4ε inequality is correct, but no source is supplied. Moreover, the terminal title denotes an error boundary, so failure_boundary is more appropriate than property.

children.title: Submodular Function Maximization
children.top_down_role: Submodular-specific approximation structures for monotone and nonmonotone objectives; general approximation machinery and hardness techniques remain external.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: An Analysis of Approximations for Maximizing Submodular Set Functions
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: An Analysis of Approximations for Maximizing Submodular Set Functions

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Maximizing a Monotone Submodular Function Subject to a Matroid Constraint
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Maximizing a Monotone Submodular Function Subject to a Matroid Constraint

knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Nonmonotone Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the value-oracle regime without feasibility constraints or a monotonicity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a finite ground set and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) be submodular, meaning \(f(A)+f(B)\ge f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B)\) for all \(A,B\subseteq V\). The unconstrained nonmonotone maximization regime is
\[
\operatorname*{maximize}_{S\subseteq V} f(S),
\]
with no assumption that \(f(A)\le f(B)\) whenever \(A\subseteq B\). The feasible family is the entire power set \(2^V\); sign or normalization conditions on \(f\) are separate regime parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximize a submodular set function over every subset of the ground set, without assuming that adding elements cannot decrease its value.
assumptions_latex: No monotonicity condition is imposed on \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=2^V\) and \(\mathrm{OPT}=\max_{S\subseteq V}f(S)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the unconstrained nonmonotone regime, but the record has no citation. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required for candidate-review admission.

children.title: Cardinality-Constrained Regimes
children.top_down_role: Selection limits expressed through set cardinality.

knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality-Constrained Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers at-most and exact cardinality constraints for submodular maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite ground set \(V\), an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le |V|\), and a submodular function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\), the at-most-cardinality regime is
\[
\max\{f(S):S\subseteq V,\ |S|\le k\}.
\]
The exact-cardinality regime replaces \(|S|\le k\) by \(|S|=k\). Objective monotonicity, nonnegativity, and normalization are independent specifications and are not implied by the cardinality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cardinality regime maximizes a submodular function over subsets having either at most k elements or exactly k elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_{\le k}=\{S\subseteq V:|S|\le k\}\) or \(\mathcal F_{=k}=\{S\subseteq V:|S|=k\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two cardinality regimes are stated precisely and definition is the correct content kind, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Uniform-Budget Regimes
children.top_down_role: Equal-cost resource limits over selectable elements.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Budget Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies equal-cost knapsack feasibility with a cardinality bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let every element \(e\in V\) have the same positive cost \(c\), and let the available budget be \(B\ge0\). Then
\[
\left\{S\subseteq V:\sum_{e\in S}c\le B\right\}
=
\left\{S\subseteq V:|S|\le \left\lfloor B/c\right\rfloor\right\}.
\]
Thus a uniform-budget submodular maximization instance is precisely an at-most-cardinality instance with effective rank \(k=\min\{|V|,\lfloor B/c\rfloor\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every item has the same positive cost, a knapsack budget is equivalent to an at-most-cardinality constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{S\subseteq V:|S|\le k\}\), where \(k=\min\{|V|,\lfloor B/c\rfloor\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equal-cost knapsack representation is mathematically correct and representation fits the leaf, but the record lacks a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Exact-Size Versus At-Most-Size Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural differences between fixed-size and upper-bound feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Size Versus At-Most-Size Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when exact-size and at-most-size optima coincide and exhibits nonmonotone separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(0\le k\le |V|\). If \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is monotone nondecreasing, then every set of size below \(k\) can be extended without decreasing value, and hence
\[
\max_{|S|\le k}f(S)=\max_{|S|=k}f(S).
\]
Without monotonicity the equality can fail: for the cut function of a single edge on \(V=\{u,v\}\) and \(k=2\), the at-most optimum is \(1\), while the exact-size optimum is \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact-k and at-most-k optima agree for monotone objectives, but can differ for nonmonotone submodular objectives, as a single-edge cut demonstrates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) monotone implies \(\max_{|S|\le k}f(S)=\max_{|S|=k}f(S)\); without monotonicity, equality is not guaranteed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotone equality and single-edge cut separation are correctly stated, and property fits the comparison leaf. Neither claim has an inspectable citation, however.

children.title: Single-Knapsack Regimes
children.top_down_role: Submodular maximization under one weighted resource limit.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Knapsack Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines submodular maximization subject to one nonnegative additive budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be finite, let \(c:V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) assign nonnegative costs, and let \(B\ge0\). A single-knapsack regime maximizes a submodular function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) over
\[
\mathcal F=\left\{S\subseteq V:\sum_{e\in S}c(e)\le B\right\}.
\]
Zero-cost elements are permitted unless excluded explicitly. Monotonicity, nonnegativity, and normalization of \(f\) constitute separate objective regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-knapsack regime permits subsets whose total nonnegative item cost does not exceed one budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{S\subseteq V:\sum_{e\in S}c(e)\le B\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The single-knapsack feasible family is precise and definition fits the leaf, but no authoritative source is cited.

children.title: Multiple-Budget Regimes
children.top_down_role: Feasibility under several simultaneous resource limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Budget Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines simultaneous feasibility under several nonnegative additive budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be finite and let \(d\ge2\). For costs \(c_i:V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) and capacities \(B_i\ge0\), a \(d\)-budget regime maximizes a submodular function over
\[
\mathcal F=\left\{S\subseteq V:\sum_{e\in S}c_i(e)\le B_i\text{ for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\right\}.
\]
The budgets are simultaneous: a set is feasible only if it satisfies every coordinate inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple-budget regime requires the chosen subset to satisfy every one of several additive knapsack inequalities simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\mathcal F\Longleftrightarrow \sum_{e\in S}c_i(e)\le B_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simultaneous multiple-budget formulation is precise and definition fits the leaf, but no authoritative source is cited.

children.title: Budget-Dimensionality Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Behavior as the number of resource constraints varies.

knowledge_statements.title: Budget-Dimensionality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates constant-dimensional and variable-dimensional multiple-budget instance classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a multiple-budget instance encoded by \(d\) cost vectors and capacities, the fixed-dimensional regime requires a universal constant \(d_0\) such that \(d\le d_0\) for every instance in the class. The variable-dimensional regime permits \(d\) to grow with the input and includes its \(d\) inequalities in the encoding. Consequently, guarantees whose exponent or hidden constant depends on \(d\) are polynomial-time guarantees only in the fixed-dimensional regime unless that dependence is itself polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Budget dimension is fixed when uniformly bounded by a constant; it is variable when the number of encoded budget inequalities may grow with the input.
assumptions_latex: Each instance explicitly encodes \(d\) budget inequalities.
Running time is measured in the full binary input length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d=O(1)\) defines the fixed-dimensional regime, whereas input-dependent \(d\) defines the variable-dimensional regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is an appropriate content kind for this regime boundary, but the complexity qualification depends on the encoding and on the precise form of the running-time dependence on d. A specific complexity source is required.

children.title: Matroid-Constrained Regimes
children.top_down_role: Feasible sets governed by a single matroid.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid-Constrained Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines submodular maximization over the independent sets of one matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(V,\mathcal I)\) be a matroid: \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\), membership in \(\mathcal I\) is hereditary, and whenever \(A,B\in\mathcal I\) with \(|A|<|B|\), some \(e\in B\setminus A\) satisfies \(A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). A matroid-constrained submodular maximization regime is
\[
\max\{f(S):S\in\mathcal I\},
\]
where \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is submodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid-constrained regime maximizes a submodular set function over the independent sets of one matroid.
assumptions_latex: \((V,\mathcal I)\) satisfies the matroid independence axioms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=\mathcal I\) and \(\mathrm{OPT}=\max_{S\in\mathcal I}f(S)\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Matchoid-Constrained Regimes
children.top_down_role: Feasible sets governed by locally overlapping matroid restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Matchoid-Constrained Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the local-matroid definition of a matchoid, with overlap bounded by an element frequency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V_1,\ldots,V_m\subseteq V\), and for each \(i\) let \(M_i=(V_i,\mathcal I_i)\) be a matroid. The associated matchoid feasible family is
\[
\mathcal F=\{S\subseteq V:S\cap V_i\in\mathcal I_i\text{ for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\}.
\]
It is an \(\ell\)-matchoid when every element belongs to at most \(\ell\) local ground sets, namely \(\max_{e\in V}|\{i:e\in V_i\}|\le\ell\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matchoid requires every selected set’s restriction to each local ground set to be independent in the corresponding matroid.
assumptions_latex: \(M_i=(V_i,\mathcal I_i)\) is a matroid for every \(i\).
Each \(e\in V\) belongs to at most \(\ell\) sets \(V_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\mathcal F\Longleftrightarrow S\cap V_i\in\mathcal I_i\) for every \(i\), with overlap at most \(\ell\).

notation.meaning: maximum local-matroid frequency of an element

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-matroid formulation and overlap parameter are coherent, and definition fits the leaf. Because matchoid terminology varies, the exact convention requires an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Matroid-Intersection Multiplicity
children.top_down_role: Regimes distinguished by the number and overlap of constituent restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(M_j=(V,\mathcal I_j)\) is a matroid for each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\mathcal F\Longleftrightarrow S\in\mathcal I_j\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\).

notation.meaning: j-th matroid on the common ground set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines multiplicity as the number of simultaneous matroid independence constraints on a common ground set.

source_refs.locator: 3. Matroid Intersection p. 84
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_j=(V,\mathcal I_j)\) for \(j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\) be matroids on the same finite ground set \(V\). A \(p\)-matroid-intersection constraint has feasible family
\[
\mathcal F=\bigcap_{j=1}^{p}\mathcal I_j.
\]
Its multiplicity is \(p\). The case \(p=1\) is an ordinary matroid constraint, \(p=2\) is classical matroid intersection, and larger \(p\) records the number of simultaneously imposed independence systems rather than their ranks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid-intersection multiplicity is the number p of matroids whose independence constraints a feasible set must satisfy simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.title: Matroid-Intersection Multiplicity

source_witnesses.locator: 3. Matroid Intersection p. 84
source_witnesses.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

children.title: Packing-Constraint Regimes
children.top_down_role: Feasibility represented by nonnegative packing inequalities.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\mathcal F\Longleftrightarrow A\mathbf 1_S\le b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines set feasibility through nonnegative linear packing inequalities on incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{m\times |V|}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{m}\). For \(S\subseteq V\), let \(\mathbf 1_S\in\{0,1\}^{V}\) be its incidence vector. A packing-constraint regime maximizes a submodular function over
\[
\mathcal F=\{S\subseteq V:A\mathbf 1_S\le b\}.
\]
The inequality is componentwise. Nonnegativity of \(A\) ensures that deleting selected elements cannot increase any packing load.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A packing regime permits subsets whose incidence vectors satisfy a system of componentwise nonnegative linear capacity inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Packing-Constraint Regimes

children.title: Downward-Closed Feasibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Hereditary feasible families with no required packing representation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\mathcal F\) and \(T\subseteq S\) imply \(T\in\mathcal F\), and consequently \(\varnothing\in\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines hereditary feasibility independently of any particular constraint representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^V\) on a finite ground set \(V\) is downward closed if
\[
S\in\mathcal F\text{ and }T\subseteq S\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\in\mathcal F.
\]
A downward-closed feasibility regime maximizes a submodular function over such a family, customarily with \(\varnothing\in\mathcal F\). Every nonempty downward-closed family contains \(\varnothing\), but it need not admit a polynomial-size packing representation or satisfy a matroid exchange axiom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasibility family is downward closed when every subset of every feasible set is also feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Downward-Closed Feasibility Regimes

children.title: Packing-Representation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of transferring guarantees between explicit packing systems and abstract hereditary families.

knowledge_statements.title: Packing-Representation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact binary packing representations of downward-closed families may require exponentially many inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be finite and let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^V\) be nonempty and downward closed. For every inclusion-minimal excluded set \(C\notin\mathcal F\), impose \(\sum_{i\in C}x_i\le |C|-1\). Then
\[
\mathcal F=\left\{S\subseteq V:\mathbf 1_S\text{ satisfies every such inequality}\right\}.
\]
Thus every downward-closed family has a binary packing representation with nonnegative coefficients. Its number of minimal-exclusion inequalities can nevertheless be exponential in \(|V|\); downward closure alone therefore does not imply a polynomial-size explicit packing description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimal excluded sets give an exact nonnegative packing representation, but their number can be exponential, so downward closure does not guarantee compact representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\) has the displayed packing representation, potentially with exponentially many inequalities.

notation.meaning: an inclusion-minimal set outside the feasible family

review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports the minimal-exclusion representation and exponential-size boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically plausible and fits the failure-boundary container, but no citation or inspectable locator supports either the minimal-exclusion formulation or the exponential-size claim.

children.title: Nonnegative Objective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objectives restricted to nonnegative values.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative Objective Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise nonnegativity for set-function maximization, without requiring normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite ground set \(V\), a submodular maximization instance \(\max\{f(S):S\in\mathcal F\}\) lies in the nonnegative-objective regime precisely when
\[
f(S)\ge 0\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V.
\]
This condition is distinct from normalization: it permits \(f(\varnothing)>0\). If only feasible-set nonnegativity is intended, the weaker predicate is \(f(S)\ge0\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and that convention must be stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is nonnegative when every set has nonnegative value; this does not require the empty set to have value zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(S)\ge0\) for all \(S\subseteq V\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly documents the objective-sign taxonomy or its feasible-only variant.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the regime container and clearly distinguishes global from feasible-set nonnegativity, but the selected convention has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Nonnormalized Objective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objectives whose empty-set value need not vanish.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonnormalized Objective Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Submodular objectives whose empty-set value is not fixed to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) is nonnormalized when no condition \(f(\varnothing)=0\) is imposed; in particular, the strict nonnormalized case has \(f(\varnothing)\ne0\). Defining
\[
g(S)=f(S)-f(\varnothing)
\]
produces a normalized function \(g\) with exactly the same marginal differences and the same maximizers over every fixed feasible family. Submodularity and monotonicity are preserved by this translation, while multiplicative value guarantees need not be preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting the empty-set value normalizes the objective and preserves marginals and maximizers, but may alter multiplicative approximation statements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g=f-f(\varnothing)\) is normalized and has the same marginal differences and constrained maximizers as \(f\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the normalization convention and translation consequences.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The translation claims are standard, but “nonnormalized” may mean either normalization is not assumed or that f(empty set) is nonzero. A source is needed to establish the intended regime terminology and consequences.

children.title: Signed Objective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objectives permitted to take negative values.

knowledge_statements.title: Signed Objective Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Submodular maximization when negative objective values are permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A submodular maximization instance lies in the signed-objective regime when \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) is not assumed nonnegative; equivalently, the admissible class contains functions for which \(f(S)<0\) for some \(S\subseteq V\). Consequently, a multiplicative guarantee \(f(A)\ge\alpha f(O)\) is informative only under an additional sign convention, ordinarily \(f(O)\ge0\), where \(O\) is optimal. Additive-error or baseline-relative guarantees remain meaningful without global nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signed objectives may take negative values, so ordinary multiplicative ratios require a nonnegative optimum or another explicit baseline.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Multiplicative approximation requires an explicit sign or baseline convention when negative values are allowed.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the signed-objective regime or approximation-ratio boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the signed-objective regime, but the approximation-ratio boundary and proposed alternatives are nontrivial claims without a cited source or locator.

children.title: Normalization-Sensitivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Guarantees that change under shifts or sign variation.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalization-Sensitivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive normalization preserves optimization but not value ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g(S)=f(S)-c\) for a constant \(c\in\mathbb R\). For every feasible family \(\mathcal F\),
\[
\operatorname*{argmax}_{S\in\mathcal F}g(S)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{S\in\mathcal F}f(S),
\]
and all marginal differences are unchanged. However, from \(g(A)\ge\alpha g(O)\) one obtains only
\[
f(A)\ge\alpha f(O)+(1-\alpha)c.
\]
Hence an \(\alpha\)-multiplicative guarantee transfers unchanged only in shift-invariant formulations or when the additive term is otherwise controlled; normalization is not innocuous for raw approximation ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant shifts preserve maximizers and marginals but introduce an additive term into multiplicative guarantees, so raw approximation ratios are normalization-sensitive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(A)\ge\alpha g(O)\) implies \(f(A)\ge\alpha f(O)+(1-\alpha)c\), not generally \(f(A)\ge\alpha f(O)\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the normalization-sensitivity formula.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shift formula is algebraically correct and fits a failure-boundary container, but the record does not introduce the domain of f or explicitly quantify A, and no source supports the approximation-sensitivity claim.

children.title: Classical Greedy Families
children.top_down_role: Direct marginal-selection approaches for discrete maximization.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Greedy Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marginal-gain greedy maximization under a cardinality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) and an integer \(k\), initialize \(S_0=\varnothing\). For \(t=0,\ldots,k-1\), choose
\[
e_t\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{e\in V\setminus S_t}\bigl(f(S_t\cup\{e\})-f(S_t)\bigr)
\]
and set \(S_{t+1}=S_t\cup\{e_t\}\); stop earlier if no element is available. Output \(S_k\). If \(f\) is normalized, nonnegative, monotone, and submodular, then for an optimal set \(O\) with \(|O|\le k\), \(f(S_k)\ge(1-(1-1/k)^k)f(O)\ge(1-1/e)f(O)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly add the element with largest marginal gain; for monotone normalized submodular maximization under a cardinality bound, this gives a 1−1/e guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) is normalized, monotone, and submodular.

notation.meaning: optimal set of cardinality at most k

review_flags: The supplied locators do not directly support the classical submodular greedy theorem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and cardinality-constrained guarantee are standard and the algorithm content kind fits, but the nontrivial approximation theorem requires an authoritative theorem or section locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the float-maximization problem, Algorithm 2.2 achieves approximation ratio 1 minus 1/e.
