children.title: Mixed Network Interaction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interfaces where substitutive plus complementary behavior coexist.

assumptions_latex: The interaction graph is \(G=(V,E)\), and \(F\) is defined on an integer box \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z^V\).
The valuation convention is used, and all relevant cross-differences are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is mixed precisely when the admissible family \(\{\Delta_{ij}F(x)\}\) contains both a positive and a negative value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly mixed pairwise signs across edges or feasible network states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every edge \(ij\in E\) and feasible \(x\in B\), let
\[
\Delta_{ij}F(x)=F(x+e_i+e_j)-F(x+e_i)-F(x+e_j)+F(x),
\]
whenever all four arguments lie in \(B\). The network interaction regime of \(F\) is mixed if there exist admissible \((ij,x)\) and \((k\ell,y)\) such that
\[
\Delta_{ij}F(x)<0<\Delta_{k\ell}F(y).
\]
Thus the same model contains a substitution effect and a complementarity effect, possibly on different edges or at different feasible states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network regime is mixed when some admissible cross-difference is negative and another is positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Network Interaction Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement gives a coherent strict mixed-sign regime, but no source confirms that mixed network interactions must contain both a strictly negative and a strictly positive cross-difference rather than merely fail the uniform substitution and complementarity conditions.

children.title: Matroidal Domains
children.top_down_role: Matroid structures serving as domains for discrete convex models.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family \(\mathcal B\) is a matroidal domain exactly when it satisfies equicardinality and basis exchange.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: matroid bases are characterized by the basis-exchange axiom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matroidal domains represented as families of bases on a finite ground set.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty family \(\mathcal B\subseteq 2^E\) is a matroidal domain if all its members have the same cardinality and it satisfies basis exchange: for every \(X,Y\in\mathcal B\) and every \(i\in X\setminus Y\), there exists \(j\in Y\setminus X\) such that
\[
X-i+j=(X\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}\in\mathcal B.
\]
Equivalently, \(\mathcal B\) is the family of bases of a matroid on \(E\). Its incidence-vector realization is \(\{\chi_X:X\in\mathcal B\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^E\), whose vectors have a common coordinate sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroidal domain is a nonempty equicardinal family of subsets satisfying the basis-exchange axiom.
knowledge_statements.title: Matroidal Domains

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Valuated Matroids
children.top_down_role: Valued matroid structures within discrete convex analysis.

assumptions_latex: The effective domain \(\mathcal B=\{X:f(X)<+\infty\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(f\) is a valuated matroid when it satisfies the valuated basis-exchange inequality.

notation.meaning: Exchange of i for j in X

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real valuated matroids in the minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) with nonempty effective domain \(\mathcal B\) is a valuated matroid if, for all \(X,Y\in\mathcal B\) and each \(i\in X\setminus Y\), there exists \(j\in Y\setminus X\) such that
\[
f(X)+f(Y)\ge f(X-i+j)+f(Y-j+i).
\]
The inequality implies that both exchanged sets on the right belong to \(\mathcal B\); hence \(\mathcal B\) is a matroidal domain and all its sets have the same cardinality. Reversing the inequality gives the equivalent maximization convention for valuations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valuated matroid assigns extended-real weights to bases and satisfies a paired basis-exchange inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Valuated Matroids

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The extended-real minimization formulation and paired exchange inequality are mathematically coherent, but the precise valuated-matroid convention and its domain consequence require a direct authoritative citation.

children.title: Matroid Valuation Interface
children.top_down_role: The passage from unvalued matroid structure to valued exchange structure.

assumptions_latex: The function \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) has nonempty equicardinal effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Valuated matroids on \(E\) correspond exactly to \(M\)-convex functions supported on fixed-sum binary vectors.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary fixed-sum interface between valuated matroids and M-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), define \(g:\mathbb Z^E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) by
\[
g(\chi_X)=f(X)\quad(X\subseteq E),\qquad g(x)=+\infty\quad(x\notin\{0,1\}^E).
\]
Then \(f\) is a valuated matroid in the minimization convention if and only if \(g\) is \(M\)-convex and \(\operatorname{dom}g\) lies in a fixed-sum hyperplane. Under this correspondence, basis exchange of sets becomes the \(M\)-exchange operation \(x-e_i+e_j\), and the matroidal domain of \(f\) becomes the binary effective domain of \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incidence-vector encoding identifies valuated matroids with M-convex functions whose finite domain consists of fixed-sum binary vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Valuation Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary incidence-vector representation is the appropriate kind of interface claim, but the exact equivalence with M-convexity and the role of the fixed-sum condition need a direct discrete-convex-analysis source.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair has the integral-intersection property exactly when every nonempty face of \(P\cap Q\) contains an integer point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic integrality criterion for the common feasible region of two rational polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For rational polyhedra \(P,Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), call \((P,Q)\) an integral pair when their common feasible region is integral:
\[
P\cap Q=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((P\cap Q)\cap\mathbb Z^n\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, every nonempty face \(F\) of \(P\cap Q\) contains an integer point. If \(P\cap Q\) is pointed, this is also equivalent to every vertex of \(P\cap Q\) being integral. Integrality of \(P\) and \(Q\) separately is not part of this definition and, without an additional structural hypothesis, does not imply integrality of their intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two rational polyhedra form an integral pair when their intersection is the convex hull of its integer points.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality for Pairs of Polyhedra

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated face characterization is plausible for an integral rational intersection, but no source confirms that the taxonomy's 'pair' terminology means only integrality of the intersection. A source is also needed to determine whether this leaf should contain a definition, condition, or stronger structural theorem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity in Intersection and Minkowski Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Names two family-level discrete-convexity properties and records their applicability to the M-convex and L-convex set families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \(\mathcal F\) of subsets of \(\mathbb Z^n\) has convexity in intersection if, for all \(S_1,S_2\in\mathcal F\), \(S_1\cap S_2=\varnothing\) implies \(\operatorname{conv}(S_1)\cap\operatorname{conv}(S_2)=\varnothing\). It has convexity in Minkowski sum if, for all \(S_1,S_2\in\mathcal F\), \(S_1+S_2=\operatorname{conv}(S_1+S_2)\cap\mathbb Z^n\). The families of M-convex sets and L-convex sets have these properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity in intersection means that disjoint members have disjoint convex hulls. Convexity in Minkowski sum means that every pairwise sum is hole free. The M-convex and L-convex set families have these properties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F\text{ has intersection convexity}\iff\forall S_1,S_2\in\mathcal F:\ S_1\cap S_2=\varnothing\Rightarrow\operatorname{conv}(S_1)\cap\operatorname{conv}(S_2)=\varnothing;\quad\mathcal F\text{ has Minkowski-sum convexity}\iff\forall S_1,S_2\in\mathcal F:\ S_1+S_2=\operatorname{conv}(S_1+S_2)\cap\mathbb Z^n

children.title: Integrally Convex Sets
children.top_down_role: The set-level component of integral convexity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(S\) is integrally convex when every point of \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is generated by nearby points of \(S\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: local-neighborhood convex-hull definition is standard in discrete convex analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard local-neighborhood definition for subsets of the integer lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), define its integral neighborhood by
\[
N(x)=\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:|z_i-x_i|<1\text{ for every }i\}.
\]
A nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) is integrally convex if
\[
x\in\operatorname{conv}(S\cap N(x))
\]
for every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\). Thus each point of the global convex hull must admit a convex representation using only lattice points of \(S\) lying in the unit cell or cells incident to that point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lattice set is integrally convex when every point of its convex hull is a convex combination of neighboring set points.

children.title: Local Convex Hulls
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood-scale hull geometry for lattice sets.

assumptions_latex: The set \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) and point \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local convex hull at \(x\) is \(\operatorname{conv}(S\cap N(x))\), and it is contained in \(\operatorname{conv}S\).

notation.meaning: Local convex hull of S at x

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convex hull of lattice points in the integral neighborhood
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local hull generated by lattice points in the open unit coordinate neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), let
\[
N(x)=\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:|z_i-x_i|<1\text{ for all }i\}.
\]
The local convex hull of \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) at \(x\) is
\[
L_S(x)=\operatorname{conv}(S\cap N(x)).
\]
It is a polytope, possibly empty, generated by at most \(2^n\) lattice points and satisfies \(L_S(x)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}S\). When \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\), the strict inequalities give \(N(x)=\{x\}\), so \(L_S(x)=\{x\}\) if \(x\in S\) and is empty otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local hull at a point is the convex hull of set points lying in that point's integral neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Convex Hulls

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-hull definition and its elementary boundary cases are consistent, but no authoritative citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Local-Hull Characterization
children.top_down_role: The relationship between integral convexity plus local hull structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(S\) is integrally convex if and only if \(\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{x\in\operatorname{conv}S}\operatorname{conv}(S\cap N(x))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise and union forms of the local-hull characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be nonempty and set \(L_S(x)=\operatorname{conv}(S\cap N(x))\). The following are equivalent:
\[
\text{(i) }S\text{ is integrally convex};
\]
\[
\text{(ii) }x\in L_S(x)\text{ for every }x\in\operatorname{conv}S;
\]
\[
\text{(iii) }\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{x\in\operatorname{conv}S}L_S(x).
\]
Indeed, each local hull is automatically contained in \(\operatorname{conv}S\); the substantive condition is that every point of the global hull belongs to its own local hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral convexity is equivalent to every global-hull point lying in its own local hull, or to local hulls covering the global hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Hull Characterization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem content kind fits the characterization leaf, and the three formulations are presented consistently, but the equivalence—particularly the union formulation—requires a direct source with a specific locator.

children.title: Integrally Convex Functions
children.top_down_role: The function-level component of integral convexity.

assumptions_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) has nonempty effective domain.
The local convex extension is formed from finite convex combinations over each integral neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(f\) is integrally convex exactly when its local convex extension \(\widetilde f\) is convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convexity of the local convex extension is the standard definition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real lattice functions defined through convexity of their local convex extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(N(x)=\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:|z_i-x_i|<1\text{ for all }i\}\) and define
\[
\widetilde f(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{z\in N(x)}\lambda_z f(z):\lambda_z\ge0,\ \sum_z\lambda_z=1,\ \sum_z\lambda_z z=x\right\},
\]
with value \(+\infty\) when no finite feasible combination exists. The function \(f\) is integrally convex if its local convex extension \(\widetilde f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is convex. At every lattice point \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\), one has \(N(x)=\{x\}\) and therefore \(\widetilde f(x)=f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lattice function is integrally convex when interpolation by convex combinations within each integral neighborhood produces a globally convex extension.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrally Convex Functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected definition matches the standard role of integrally convex functions, but no direct source is cited. The infimum formula should also explicitly restrict positive-weight support to finite-valued lattice points, avoiding undefined products involving zero weights and +infinity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Convex Extension and Integral Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-neighborhood interpolation and the defining global-convexity condition for integrally convex lattice functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $x\in\mathbb R^n$, define $N(x)=\{y\in\mathbb Z^n\mid \lfloor x_i\rfloor\le y_i\le\lceil x_i\rceil\ (i=1,\ldots,n)\}$. For $f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ with nonempty effective domain, define
\[\widetilde f(x)=\sup\{\langle p,x\rangle+\alpha\mid \langle p,y\rangle+\alpha\le f(y)\ (\forall y\in N(x))\}.\]
Equivalently,
\[\widetilde f(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{y\in N(x)}\lambda_yf(y)\mid \lambda_y\ge0,\ \sum_y\lambda_y=1,\ \sum_y\lambda_yy=x\right\}.\]
It satisfies $\widetilde f(x)\ge\bar f(x)$ on $\mathbb R^n$ and $\widetilde f(x)=f(x)$ on $\mathbb Z^n$. Although $\widetilde f$ is convex on every unit integer box, it need not be convex on all of $\mathbb R^n$. The function $f$ is integrally convex precisely when $\widetilde f$ is convex on $\mathbb R^n$, equivalently when $\widetilde f=\bar f$ on $\mathbb R^n$; hence every integrally convex function is convex extensible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local convex extension interpolates a lattice function from the integer vertices of the unit box containing each point. It agrees with the function on lattice points and dominates the global convex closure. It is always convex within each unit box but may fail to be globally convex. Integral convexity means that it is globally convex, equivalently that it equals the convex closure everywhere, and therefore implies convex extensibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is integrally convex}\iff \widetilde f\text{ is convex on }\mathbb R^n\iff \widetilde f=\bar f\text{ on }\mathbb R^n;\qquad f\text{ integrally convex}\Rightarrow f\text{ convex extensible}.

assumptions_latex: For each \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), convex combinations are taken over the finite set \(N(x)=\{z\in\mathbb{Z}^n\mid \lfloor x_i\rfloor\le z_i\le\lceil x_i\rceil\ \text{for all }i\}\).

notation.meaning: integer points in the smallest coordinatewise unit box containing x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local convex closure over each coordinatewise unit cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the local convex extension of \(f\) is
\[
\widetilde f(x)=\min\left\{\sum_{z\in N(x)}\lambda_z f(z)\ \middle|\ \lambda_z\ge0,\ \sum_{z\in N(x)}\lambda_z=1,\ \sum_{z\in N(x)}\lambda_z z=x\right\}.
\]
Terms with \(\lambda_z=0\) contribute zero even when \(f(z)=+\infty\); equivalently, only points with finite function value may receive positive weight. If no admissible finite-valued convex combination exists, the minimum is \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local convex extension linearly convexifies the lattice values separately inside every coordinatewise unit cell.

children.title: Local-Extension Fidelity
children.top_down_role: How local extensions preserve or fail to preserve integral convexity.

assumptions_latex: The local convex extension \(\widetilde f\) is formed from \(f:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) using coordinatewise unit-cell neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), \(\widetilde f(x)=f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery of lattice data by the local convex extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an integer point \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), its unit-cell neighborhood is the singleton \(N(x)=\{x\}\). Consequently, the only coefficients satisfying \(\lambda_z\ge0\), \(\sum_z\lambda_z=1\), and \(\sum_z\lambda_z z=x\) have \(\lambda_x=1\). Hence the local convex extension preserves every original lattice value:
\[
\widetilde f(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb{Z}^n).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every lattice point, the local convex extension agrees exactly with the original function.

notation.meaning: indices where x is below y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer exchange-axiom definition of an M-convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) is M-convex if, for every \(x,y\in S\) and every \(i\in\operatorname{supp}^{+}(x-y)\), there exists \(j\in\operatorname{supp}^{-}(x-y)\) such that
\[
x-e_i+e_j\in S\quad\text{and}\quad y+e_i-e_j\in S.
\]
This exchange axiom implies that all vectors in \(S\) have the same component sum, because otherwise an excess coordinate could not always be paired with a deficit coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M-convex set permits every unit removed from an excess coordinate to be exchanged with some deficit coordinate in both compared vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: M-Convex Sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: M-Convex Domains, Sets, and Integral Base Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the base-exchange property of M-convex effective domains and characterizes M-convex sets through indicator functions and integral base polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f:\mathbf Z^V\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is M-convex, then \(\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbf Z}f\) satisfies the integer base-exchange axiom: for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbf Z}f\) and \(u\in\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y)\), there exists \(v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y)\) such that
\[
x-\chi_u+\chi_v,\quad y+\chi_u-\chi_v\in\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbf Z}f.
\]
For \(B\subseteq\mathbf Z^V\),
\[
\delta_B\text{ is M-convex}\iff B\text{ is the set of integer points of an integral base polyhedron}.
\]
Sets of integer points satisfying this base-exchange axiom are called M-convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain of an M-convex function satisfies the integer base-exchange axiom. A set has an M-convex indicator exactly when it is the integer-point set of an integral base polyhedron; such sets are called M-convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}_{\mathbf Z}f\text{ satisfies B-EXC}[\mathbf Z],\qquad \delta_B\text{ is M-convex}\iff B\text{ is the integer-point set of an integral base polyhedron}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete Separation of Disjoint M-Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict integral linear separation of two disjoint M-convex lattice sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $B_1,B_2\subseteq\mathbb Z^V$ be M-convex sets. If $B_1\cap B_2=\varnothing$, then there exists $p^*\in\{0,1\}^V\cup\{0,-1\}^V$ such that

\inf_{x\in B_1}\langle p^*,x\rangle-\sup_{x\in B_2}\langle p^*,x\rangle\geq 1.
\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of an M-convex set of integer vectors over a finite ground set.

assumptions_latex: The set \(S\) is a nonempty subset of \(\mathbb{Z}^n\).

notation.meaning: indices where x is below y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer exchange definition allowing transfer without a compensating coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) is M-natural-convex if, for every \(x,y\in S\) and every \(i\in\operatorname{supp}^{+}(x-y)\), either
\[
x-e_i\in S\quad\text{and}\quad y+e_i\in S,
\]
or there exists \(j\in\operatorname{supp}^{-}(x-y)\) such that
\[
x-e_i+e_j\in S\quad\text{and}\quad y+e_i-e_j\in S.
\]
Unlike M-convexity, this axiom permits component sums to vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M-natural-convex set allows either a direct unit transfer or a paired exchange through a deficit coordinate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection and Exchange Characterizations of M-Natural-Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines M-natural-convex sets, gives their exchange characterization, and records strict containment of the M-convex class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $0
otin V$ and $\widetilde V=\{0\}\cup V$. A set $Q\subseteq\mathbf Z^V$ is $M^
atural$-convex if and only if there exists an M-convex set $B\subseteq\mathbf Z^{\widetilde V}$ such that $Q=\{x\in\mathbf Z^V\mid \exists x_0\in\mathbf Z:\ (x_0,x)\in B\}$. Equivalently, for every $x,y\in Q$ and $u\in\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y)$, either $x-\chi_u,y+\chi_u\in Q$, or there exists $v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y)$ such that $x-\chi_u+\chi_v,y+\chi_u-\chi_v\in Q$. Every M-convex set is $M^
atural$-convex, and this inclusion of classes is strict.

atural	ext{-convex}\iff Q	ext{ has the stated projection representation}\iff Q	ext{ satisfies }(B^
atural	ext{-EXC}[\mathbf Z]),\quad \{	ext{M-convex sets}\}\subsetneq\{	ext{$M^
atural$-convex sets}\}.

assumptions_latex: A fixed integer \(r\) is used for the added coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(S\) is M-natural-convex if and only if \(\widehat S_r\) is M-convex.

notation.meaning: sum of the coordinates of x
constant-sum lift of S into one additional coordinate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-sum lifting equivalence between the two M-type set classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the constant-sum lift
\[
\widehat S_r=\{(r-x(N),x)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}\mid x\in S\}.
\]
Then \(S\) is M-natural-convex if and only if \(\widehat S_r\) is M-convex. An exchange involving the added coordinate corresponds exactly to the direct-transfer alternative in the M-natural exchange axiom; an exchange between two original coordinates corresponds to its paired-exchange alternative. The equivalence holds for every choice of \(r\in\mathbb{Z}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a coordinate that fixes the total sum converts M-natural-convex sets exactly into M-convex sets.
knowledge_statements.title: M-Type Set Translation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constant-sum lift is an appropriate representation, but the equivalence for every integer r and its exchange interpretation require an authoritative citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Box Reduction of an M-Type Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the extended-value restriction of an M-convex or M-natural-convex function to a coordinate box meeting its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f$ be an $M$-convex or $M^{\natural}$-convex function on $\mathbb{R}^V$. Given $\underline l:V\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}$ and $\overline l:V\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}$ such that $\operatorname{dom}f\cap[\underline l,\overline l]\neq\varnothing$, define
\[f_{\underline l}^{\overline l}(x)=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap[\underline l,\overline l],\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}\]
This function is called a box reduction of $f$. Every coordinate box $[\underline l,\overline l]$ is a generalized polymatroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box reduction restricts an M-convex or M-natural-convex function to a coordinate box that intersects its domain and assigns positive infinity elsewhere. Every coordinate box is a generalized polymatroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_{\underline l}^{\overline l}(x)=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap[\underline l,\overline l],\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\quad\text{is the box reduction of }f,\qquad [\underline l,\overline l]\text{ is a generalized polymatroid}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is M-convex if, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(i\in\operatorname{supp}^{+}(x-y)\), there exists \(j\in\operatorname{supp}^{-}(x-y)\) such that

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hierarchy of M-exchange and quasi M-exchange conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the strong-to-weak implication diagram and characterizes M-exchange by weak quasi M-convexity under every linear tilt.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $f:\mathbb Z^V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, $\mathrm{M\text{-}EXC}[\mathbb Z]\Rightarrow\mathrm{SSQM}\Rightarrow\mathrm{QM}$ and $\mathrm{M\text{-}EXC}_w[\mathbb Z]\Rightarrow\mathrm{SSQM}_w\Rightarrow\mathrm{QM}_w$. In addition, $\mathrm{M\text{-}EXC}[\mathbb Z]\Rightarrow\mathrm{M\text{-}EXC}_w[\mathbb Z]$, $\mathrm{SSQM}\Rightarrow\mathrm{SSQM}_w$, and $\mathrm{QM}\Rightarrow\mathrm{QM}_w$. The same chain holds for the weak variants, and every strong condition implies its corresponding weak condition. M-exchange is also equivalent to weak quasi M-convexity of every linear tilt.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: M-Convex Function Exchange Axiom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines M-convexity on the integer lattice and records its equivalent discrete-increment formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function f:\mathbf Z^V\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\} with \operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing is M-convex if, for every x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f and every u\in\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y), there exists v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y) such that f(x)+f(y)\ge f(x-\chi_u+\chi_v)+f(y+\chi_u-\chi_v). The inequality entails that both exchanged points lie in \operatorname{dom}f. Equivalently, with \Delta f(z;v,u)=f(z+\chi_v-\chi_u)-f(z), one has \max_{u\in\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y)}\min_{v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y)}[\Delta f(x;v,u)+\Delta f(y;u,v)]\le0 for all x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f, where a maximum and minimum over an empty set are respectively -\infty and +\infty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty-domain extended-real function on the integer lattice is M-convex when every surplus coordinate between two domain points can be paired with a deficit coordinate so that exchanging one unit does not increase their total function value. The stated maximum-minimum increment inequality is equivalent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exchange Directional Derivative of an M-Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional derivative along feasible base-polyhedron exchange directions, with finite-step and infeasible-direction conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be M-convex, B_f=\operatorname{dom}f, x\in B_f, and u,v\in V. If v\in\operatorname{dep}_{B_f}(x,u)\setminus\{u\}, define f'(x;u,v)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha(\chi_u-\chi_v))-f(x)}{\alpha}. By local polyhedral convexity, this derivative equals the displayed difference quotient for sufficiently small \alpha>0. If f is domain-integral and x\in\mathbb{Z}^{V}, \alpha=1 may be chosen. If v\notin\operatorname{dep}_{B_f}(x,u)\setminus\{u\}, define f'(x;u,v)=+\infty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exchange directional derivative of an M-convex function is the right derivative along a feasible transfer from coordinate v to coordinate u. Local polyhedrality permits an exact sufficiently small finite difference, and domain-integrality at an integral point permits a unit difference. Infeasible exchange directions are assigned positive infinity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exchange-decomposition lower bound for an M-convex function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds the value difference between two domain points using integral decompositions into unit exchanges evaluated at the initial point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\mathcal M[\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R]\) and \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Then
\[

\]

\[
\check f(x,y)=\inf_{\lambda}\left\{\sum_{u,v\in V}\lambda_{uv}\bigl[f(x-\chi_u+\chi_v)-f(x)\bigr]\;\middle|\;\sum_{u,v\in V}\lambda_{uv}(\chi_v-\chi_u)=y-x,\ \lambda_{uv}\in\mathbb Z_+\ (u,v\in V)\right\}.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: M-Convex Functions and the Exchange Axiom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines integer-lattice M-convexity by the two-point unit-exchange inequality, including its domain implication, marginal-difference form, empty-set conventions, and sign-reversed concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(f:\mathbf Z^V\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}\) with \(\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbf Z}f\ne\varnothing\) is M-convex if, for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbf Z}f\) and every \(u\in\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y)\), there exists \(v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y)\) such that
\[
f(x)+f(y)\ge f(x-\chi_u+\chi_v)+f(y+\chi_u-\chi_v).
\]
The finiteness of the right-hand side implies that both exchanged points lie in \(\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbf Z}f\). With
\[
\Delta f(z;v,u)=f(z+\chi_v-\chi_u)-f(z),
\]
the axiom is equivalently
\[
\max_{u\in\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y)}\min_{v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y)}\bigl[\Delta f(x;v,u)+\Delta f(y;u,v)\bigr]\le0,
\]
where the maximum over an empty set is \(-\infty\) and the minimum over an empty set is \(+\infty\). A function \(h\) is M-concave if \(-h\) is M-convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real function on the integer lattice is M-convex when every positively imbalanced coordinate between two domain points can be paired with a negatively imbalanced coordinate so that exchanging one unit between the points does not increase their total value. The exchanged points remain in the domain. The axiom also has the stated max-min marginal form, and M-concavity is defined by sign reversal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y):\ f(x)+f(y)\ge f(x-\chi_u+\chi_v)+f(y+\chi_u-\chi_v).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: M-Natural-Convex Functions and Their Exchange Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-variable formulation including projection, M-convex lifting, and the exchange characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an M-convex function has effective domain in \(\{x\in\mathbb R^V\mid x(V)=r\}\), fixing \(v_0\in V\) and writing \(V'=V\setminus\{v_0\}\) gives the projection \(f'(x')=f(r-x'(V'),x')\). A function \(f:\mathbb Z^V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is M\(^{\natural}\)-convex exactly when its lift \(\widetilde f(x_0,x)=f(x)\) for \(x_0=-x(V)\), and \(+\infty\) otherwise, is M-convex. Equivalently, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbb Z}f\) and \(u\in\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y)\), \[f(x)+f(y)\geq\min\!\left\{f(x-\chi_u)+f(y+\chi_u),\ \min_{v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y)}\left[f(x-\chi_u+\chi_v)+f(y+\chi_u-\chi_v)\right]\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M-natural-convex function is obtained by projecting an M-convex function along a coordinate subject to its constant-sum domain, or equivalently by requiring its constant-sum lift to be M-convex. Its exchange inequality permits either a one-coordinate transfer or a compensating exchange with a negative-support coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is M}^{\natural}\text{-convex iff its constant-sum lift is M-convex, equivalently iff it satisfies }(\mathrm M^{\natural}\text{-EXC}[\mathbb Z]).

children.title: M-Type Function Translation
children.top_down_role: Structural passage between the two M-type function classes.

assumptions_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) has nonempty effective domain.
A fixed integer \(r\) is used for the added coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(f\) is M-natural-convex if and only if \(\widehat f_r\) is M-convex.

notation.meaning: sum of the coordinates of x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-sum lifting equivalence between M-natural-convex and M-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(\widehat f_r:\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) by
\[
\widehat f_r(x_0,x)=
\begin{cases}
f(x),&x_0+x(N)=r,\\+\infty,&x_0+x(N)\ne r.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\) is M-natural-convex if and only if \(\widehat f_r\) is M-convex. Exchanges through coordinate \(0\) encode direct unit transfers, while exchanges among coordinates \(1,\ldots,n\) encode paired exchanges. This equivalence is independent of the chosen \(r\in\mathbb{Z}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant-sum auxiliary coordinate translates M-natural-convex functions exactly into M-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.title: M-Type Function Translation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lifted-function representation is plausible and correctly classified, but its equivalence and independence of r have no inspectable supporting citation.

children.title: Local Exchange Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Local neighborhoods generated by M-type exchange structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local exchange neighborhood of \(x\) is \(\mathcal N_f(x)\) as displayed.

notation.meaning: standard unit vector in coordinate i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible unit exchanges for an M-convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), its local exchange neighborhood is
\[
\mathcal N_f(x)=\{x-e_i+e_j\mid i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\ f(x-e_i+e_j)<+\infty\}.
\]
Allowing \(i=j\) includes \(x\) itself. A strict descent move is any \(y\in\mathcal N_f(x)\) satisfying \(f(y)<f(x)\); thus every local move preserves the component sum and changes at most two coordinates by one unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local neighborhood consists of all feasible vectors obtained by moving one unit from one coordinate to another.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Exchange Neighborhoods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the neighborhood leaf, but inclusion of the center via i=j is convention-dependent and no source is supplied to establish the intended convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local exchange axiom for M-convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The integer-lattice local exchange condition restricted to effective-domain points at l1-distance four.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The condition $(\mathrm{M\text{-}EXC}_{\mathrm{loc}}[\mathbf Z])$ requires that, for every $x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f$ with $\lVert x-y\rVert_1=4$, there exist $u\in\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y)$ and $v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y)$ such that
\[
f(x)+f(y)\geq f(x-\chi_u+\chi_v)+f(y+\chi_u-\chi_v).
\]
If $y=x-\chi_{u_1}-\chi_{u_2}+\chi_{v_1}+\chi_{v_2}$ with $\{u_1,u_2\}\cap\{v_1,v_2\}=\varnothing$, this condition can be written as
\[
f(y)-f(x)\geq\min\left\{\Delta f(x;v_1,u_1)+\Delta f(x;v_2,u_2),\;\Delta f(x;v_2,u_1)+\Delta f(x;v_1,u_2)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every pair of effective-domain points at l1-distance four, there is a positive-difference coordinate and a negative-difference coordinate whose exchange satisfies the M-convex exchange inequality. Under the displayed two-unit representation, this is expressed by the minimum over the two possible pairings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists u\in\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y)\;\exists v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y):\ f(x)+f(y)\geq f(x-\chi_u+\chi_v)+f(y+\chi_u-\chi_v)

children.title: Descent Certificates
children.top_down_role: Local descent information used to assess improvement or optimality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities \(f(x)\le f(x-e_i+e_j)\) for all feasible exchanges certify that \(x\) is a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local optimality certificate for unconstrained M-convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) is a global minimizer of \(f\) if and only if
\[
f(x)
\le f(x-e_i+e_j)
\]
for every \(i,j\in\{1,
\ldots,n\}\) with \(x-e_i+e_j\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Equivalently,
\[
f(x)=\min\{f(y)\mid y\in\mathcal N_f(x)\}.
\]
Because each displayed inequality compares two explicitly given lattice points, the complete list of feasible local comparisons is a verifiable certificate of global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an M-convex function, absence of an improving feasible unit exchange certifies global optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Descent Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate content kind is appropriate, but the local-to-global optimality equivalence is a nontrivial theorem and requires an authoritative source with a theorem or section locator.

children.title: Exchange–Descent Link
children.top_down_role: The structural connection between local exchanges plus descent behavior.

assumptions_latex: The point \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) is not a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist coordinates \(i,j\) such that \(f(x-e_i+e_j)<f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-to-global descent principle for M-convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) is not a global minimizer, then its exchange neighborhood contains a strict descent point:
\[
\exists\,i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\quad x-e_i+e_j\in\operatorname{dom}f
\quad\text{and}\quad
f(x-e_i+e_j)<f(x).
\]
Consequently, repeatedly selecting a strictly improving feasible unit exchange can terminate only at a global minimizer, provided the generated sublevel set contains no infinite strictly descending sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: M-convex exchange structure guarantees an improving unit exchange at every nonoptimal point.
knowledge_statements.title: Exchange–Descent Link

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exchange–descent principle fits the node, but both the strict local-descent conclusion and the added termination claim require authoritative support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edge-direction characterizations of M-convex and M-natural-convex polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes both M-type polyhedral classes by their permitted edge directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron $B\subseteq\mathbb R^V$, $B$ is M-convex if and only if every edge of $B$ is parallel to $\chi_u-\chi_v$ for some $u,v\in V$. For a nonempty polyhedron $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^V$, $Q$ is M$^\natural$-convex if and only if every edge of $Q$ is parallel to $\chi_u-\chi_v$ for some $u,v\in V\cup\{0\}$, where $\chi_0=0$.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The base polyhedron associated with \(p\) is
\[
B(p)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid x(A)\ge p(A)\ \text{for every }A\subseteq N,\ x(N)=p(N)\}.
\]
A polyhedron representable in this form is called an M-convex polyhedron. If \(p\) is integer-valued wherever finite, then \(B(p)\) is integral, and \(B(p)\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\) satisfies the M-convex set exchange axiom. Conversely, the convex hull of an M-convex set is an integral M-convex polyhedron under the usual boundedness assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: M-convex polyhedra are supermodular base polyhedra; their integer points satisfy the M-convex exchange axiom.
knowledge_statements.title: M-Convex Polyhedra

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exchange and base-polyhedron characterizations of M-convex polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines real M-convex polyhedra by exchange and records the equivalent one-sided axiom, submodular base-polyhedron representations, and integral correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty polyhedron $B\subseteq\mathbb R^V$ is M-convex if, for every $x,y\in B$ and $u\in\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y)$, there exist $v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y)$ and $\alpha_0>0$ such that $x-\alpha(\chi_u-\chi_v),y+\alpha(\chi_u-\chi_v)\in B$ for all $\alpha\in[0,\alpha_0]$. For nonempty polyhedra this two-sided axiom is equivalent to the one-sided axiom requiring only the latter inclusion. Moreover, $B$ is M-convex if and only if $B=\mathbf B(\rho)$ for some $\rho\in\mathcal S[\mathbb R]$, and it is integral M-convex if and only if $B=\mathbf B(\rho)$ for some $\rho\in\mathcal S[\mathbb Z]$. An integral polyhedron $B$ is M-convex if and only if $B\cap\mathbb Z^V$ is an M-convex set; for integer $x,y\in B\cap\mathbb Z^V$, one may take $\alpha_0=1$ in the exchange axiom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron is M-convex when it satisfies the two-sided local exchange axiom, which is equivalent to its one-sided form. These polyhedra are precisely submodular base polyhedra, with integer-valued submodular functions characterizing the integral case. An integral polyhedron is M-convex exactly when its lattice points form an M-convex set, and lattice points admit a unit exchange interval.
assumptions_latex: B\subseteq\mathbb R^V\text{ is a nonempty polyhedron}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mathrm{B\!-EXC}[\mathbb R])\Longleftrightarrow(\mathrm{B\!-EXC}_+[\mathbb R]),\quad B\in\mathcal M_0[\mathbb R]\Longleftrightarrow B=\mathbf B(\rho)\text{ for some }\rho\in\mathcal S[\mathbb R],\quad B\in\mathcal M_0[\mathbb Z\mid\mathbb R]\Longleftrightarrow B=\mathbf B(\rho)\text{ for some }\rho\in\mathcal S[\mathbb Z].

knowledge_statements.title: M-Convex Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-closure extension of a finite-domain M-convex function from the integer lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be M-convex with finite effective domain. Its polyhedral convex extension is
\[\bar f(x)=\min\left\{\sum_{k=1}^m\lambda_k f(y^k)\;\middle|\;m\geq1,\ y^k\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \lambda_k\geq0,\ \sum_k\lambda_k=1,\ \sum_k\lambda_k y^k=x\right\}.\]
The value is \(+\infty\) when no such representation exists. Then \(\bar f\) is convex and polyhedral, \(\operatorname{dom}\bar f=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), and \(\bar f(x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex closure of a finite-domain M-convex function is a polyhedral convex function on the convex hull of its domain and preserves all integer values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar f\) is a polyhedral convex extension of \(f\) with domain \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).

notation.meaning: The set of integer points where f is finite.

knowledge_statements.title: Extension–Polyhedron Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph and domain correspondence for finite-domain M-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be M-convex with finite effective domain, and let \(\bar f\) be its convex closure. There is an integral base polyhedron \(B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) such that
\[\operatorname{dom}f=B\cap\mathbb Z^n,\qquad \operatorname{dom}\bar f=B.\]
Moreover,
\[\operatorname{epi}\bar f=\operatorname{conv}\{(x,t)\in\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R\mid x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ t\geq f(x)\}.\]
Consequently, minimizing \(f\) over its integer domain and minimizing \(\bar f\) over \(B\) have the same optimal value, and every integral minimizer of \(\bar f\) minimizes \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M-convex domain is the integer-point set of an integral base polyhedron, while the convex extension has that polyhedron as its domain and the convexified epigraph.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is M-convex with finite effective domain.
\(\bar f\) is the convex closure of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\bar f=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{dom}f)=B\) and \(\operatorname{epi}\bar f\) is the convex hull of the discrete epigraph.

notation.meaning: The integral base polyhedron associated with the M-convex domain.
The epigraph of an extended-real-valued function g.

review_flags: An exact source is needed to certify the intended finite-domain polyhedral-interface formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the interface container, but the base-polyhedron domain theorem, convexified-epigraph identity, and optimization consequences have no inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Closure Characterizations of M-Convexity and M-Natural-Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizations using convex extensibility and the polyhedral structure of every nonempty minimizer set under linear perturbation of the convex closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:\mathbf Z^V\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}$ satisfy $\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing$, and let $\bar f$ be its convex closure. Then
\[
f\text{ is }M\text{-convex}\iff\left[f\text{ is convex extensible and }\forall p\in\mathbf R^V,\ \operatorname*{argmin}\bar f[-p]\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}\bar f[-p]\text{ is an }M\text{-convex polyhedron}\right],
\]
and
\[
f\text{ is }M^{\natural}\text{-convex}\iff\left[f\text{ is convex extensible and }\forall p\in\mathbf R^V,\ \operatorname*{argmin}\bar f[-p]\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}\bar f[-p]\text{ is an }M^{\natural}\text{-convex polyhedron}\right].
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty-domain extended-real function on the integer lattice, M-convexity is equivalent to convex extensibility plus the requirement that every nonempty minimizer set of every linearly perturbed convex closure be an M-convex polyhedron. The corresponding equivalence holds for M-natural-convexity and M-natural-convex polyhedra.
assumptions_latex: \bar f\text{ is the convex closure of }f

knowledge_statements.title: Valuated-Matroid Valuations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization-sign convention for valuated matroids on equicardinal feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite, let \(\mathcal B\subseteq2^E\) be nonempty, and suppose all members of \(\mathcal B\) have the same cardinality. A map \(v:\mathcal B\to\mathbb R\) is a valuated-matroid valuation if, for every \(X,Y\in\mathcal B\) and every \(i\in X\setminus Y\), there exists \(j\in Y\setminus X\) such that \(X-i+j,Y-j+i\in\mathcal B\) and
\[v(X)+v(Y)\leq v(X-i+j)+v(Y-j+i).\]
Equivalently, extending \(v\) by \(-\infty\) outside \(\mathcal B\) gives an M-concave function on incidence vectors of fixed coordinate sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valuated matroid assigns values to equicardinal feasible sets and satisfies a value-improving symmetric exchange inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal B\) is a nonempty equicardinal family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is valuated-matroid precisely when it satisfies the displayed valuated exchange axiom.

notation.meaning: The set obtained from X by deleting i and adding j.

knowledge_statements.title: Gross-Substitutes Valuations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Demand-correspondence definition for finite indivisible goods and quasilinear prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite set of goods and \(v:2^E\to\mathbb R\). For \(p\in\mathbb R^E\), define
\[D_v(p)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{X\subseteq E}\left(v(X)-\sum_{i\in X}p_i\right).\]
The valuation \(v\) satisfies gross substitutes if, whenever \(p,q\in\mathbb R^E\) obey \(p\leq q\) componentwise and \(X\in D_v(p)\), there exists \(Y\in D_v(q)\) such that
\[\{i\in X\mid p_i=q_i\}\subseteq Y.\]
Thus every previously demanded good whose price did not rise can be retained in some demand at the new prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When some prices rise, a gross-substitutes buyer has a new optimal bundle retaining every previously demanded good whose price stayed fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is gross substitutes exactly when its demand correspondence satisfies the stated price-monotonicity condition.

notation.meaning: Bundles maximizing quasilinear utility at price vector p.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the standard demand-based gross-substitutes condition.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The demand-correspondence definition is precise and appropriate, but it has no inspectable citation supporting the selected gross-substitutes convention.

children.title: Economic–Combinatorial Correspondence

knowledge_statements.title: Economic–Combinatorial Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of gross substitutes, M-natural concavity, and dummy-good valuated-matroid lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite and \(v:2^E\to\mathbb R\). Then \(v\) is gross substitutes if and only if, for all \(X,Y\subseteq E\) and \(i\in X\setminus Y\), either
\[v(X)+v(Y)\leq v(X-i)+v(Y+i),\]
or there exists \(j\in Y\setminus X\) such that
\[v(X)+v(Y)\leq v(X-i+j)+v(Y-j+i).\]
Equivalently, \(v\) is M-natural-concave. If \(D\) is a disjoint set of \(|E|\) dummy goods, the equicardinal lifting \(\widehat v(B)=v(B\cap E)\) for \(|B|=|E|\) is then a valuated-matroid valuation, and conversely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gross substitutes are exactly M-natural-concave valuations; after adding enough dummy goods and fixing bundle size, they become valuated-matroid valuations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is gross substitutes if and only if it is M-natural-concave, equivalently if and only if its dummy-good homogenization is a valuated matroid.

notation.meaning: A set of zero-value dummy goods.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The exchange characterization and dummy-good homogenization are standard discrete-convex formulations of gross substitutes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the correspondence leaf, but the equivalence among gross substitutes, M-natural concavity, and the stated dummy-good homogenization requires an authoritative source with a theorem or section locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L-Convex and L-Natural-Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Difference-constraint representations and the coordinate-section relationship between the two set classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A polyhedron $P\subseteq\mathbb R^V$ is $L$-convex if there exist $A\subseteq V	imes V$ and $b_{uv}\in\mathbb R$ such that $P=\{x\in\mathbb R^V\mid x(u)-x(v)\le b_{uv}\ ((u,v)\in A)\}$. Such a set satisfies $x+\alpha\mathbf 1\in P$ for every $x\in P$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb R$. If $w\in V$, the section $P^{\swarrow}=\{x\in P\mid x(w)=0\}$, viewed in $\mathbb R^{V\setminus\{w\}}$, is called $L^
atural$-convex. Equivalently, an $L^
atural$-convex set in $\mathbb R^V$ is representable using coordinate lower bounds $x(u)\ge b_u^-$, coordinate upper bounds $x(u)\le b_u^+$, and difference constraints $x(u)-x(v)\le b_{uv}$ over specified index sets. Every $L$-convex set in $\mathbb R^V$ is also $L^
atural$-convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An L-convex polyhedron is described by difference constraints and is invariant under common translation of all coordinates. Fixing one coordinate to zero gives an L-natural-convex set in the remaining coordinates. L-natural-convex sets equivalently admit coordinate bounds together with difference constraints, and every L-convex set is L-natural-convex.
assumptions_latex: V\text{ is the coordinate index set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is classified as }L\text{-convex or }L^\natural\text{-convex by the corresponding representation and coordinate-section construction.}

knowledge_statements.title: L-Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-lattice definition using sublattice closure and all-ones translation invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) is L-convex if, for all \(x,y\in S\) and every \(\alpha\in\mathbb Z\),
\[x\wedge y\in S,\qquad x\vee y\in S,\qquad x+\alpha\mathbf1\in S,\]
where the meet and join are taken componentwise. Thus an L-convex set is a sublattice of \(\mathbb Z^n\) invariant under translation in the all-ones direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An L-convex set is a nonempty integer sublattice closed under every integer translation along the all-ones vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is L-convex exactly when it has the displayed meet, join, and translation closures.

notation.meaning: The all-ones vector in the ambient lattice.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines integer-lattice L-convex sets through the referenced sublattice and translation conditions and states their indicator-function characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty set \(D\subseteq\mathbf Z^V\) is L-convex if
\[
p,q\in D\implies p\vee q,\ p\wedge q\in D

\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intersection structure and feasibility of L-convex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull compatibility, difference-constraint representation, feasibility, and preservation of L-convexity under nonempty intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D_1,D_2\subseteq\mathbf Z^V be L-convex sets. Then \overline{D_1}\cap\overline{D_2}=\overline{D_1\cap D_2}. If D_i=\mathbf D(\gamma_i)\cap\mathbf Z^V with \gamma_i\in\mathcal T[\mathbf Z] for i=1,2 and \gamma_{12}(u,v)=\min\{\gamma_1(u,v),\gamma_2(u,v)\}, then D_1\cap D_2=\mathbf D(\gamma_{12})\cap\mathbf Z^V and D_1\cap D_2\ne\varnothing if and only if G_{\gamma_{12}} has no negative cycle. If D_1\cap D_2 is nonempty, it is L-convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The barred sets commute with intersection for two L-convex sets. Under difference-constraint representations, their intersection is represented using the pointwise minimum of the two parameter functions and is nonempty exactly when the associated graph has no negative cycle. A nonempty intersection is L-convex.

knowledge_statements.title: L-Natural-Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-lattice definition by closure under rounded coordinatewise midpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) is L-natural-convex if, for every \(x,y\in S\),
\[\left\lfloor\frac{x+y}{2}\right\rfloor\in S
\quad\text{and}\quad
\left\lceil\frac{x+y}{2}\right\rceil\in S,\]
where floor and ceiling are applied componentwise. The two rounded midpoints coincide when every coordinate of \(x+y\) is even.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An L-natural-convex set contains both componentwise rounded midpoints of every pair of its points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is L-natural-convex exactly when it is closed under both rounded midpoint operations.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Rounded-midpoint closure is the standard definition of an L-natural-convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: L-Type Set Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogenization and zero-coordinate slicing between L-natural-convex and L-convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\), define its homogenization by
\[\widetilde S=\{(x_0,x)\in\mathbb Z^{n+1}\mid x-x_0\mathbf1\in S\}.\]
Then \(S\) is L-natural-convex if and only if \(\widetilde S\) is L-convex. Moreover,
\[S=\{x\in\mathbb Z^n\mid(0,x)\in\widetilde S\}.\]
Conversely, if \(T\subseteq\mathbb Z^{n+1}\) is L-convex, its normalized slice \(S_T=\{x\mid(0,x)\in T\}\) is L-natural-convex and reconstructs \(T\) through the same homogenization formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a translation coordinate converts an L-natural-convex set into an L-convex set; fixing that coordinate to zero reverses the construction.
assumptions_latex: \(T\subseteq\mathbb Z^{n+1}\) is nonempty when the converse is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is L-natural-convex if and only if \(\widetilde S\) is L-convex, with zero-coordinate slicing as the inverse normalization.

notation.meaning: The all-ones vector in n dimensions.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Translation-coordinate homogenization is the standard normalization connecting the two L-type set classes.

knowledge_statements.title: L-Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real lattice definition with submodularity and affine all-ones translation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper function \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is L-convex if there exists \(r\in\mathbb R\) such that, for all \(x,y\in\mathbb Z^n\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb Z\),
\[f(x)+f(y)\geq f(x\wedge y)+f(x\vee y),\qquad
f(x+\alpha\mathbf1)=f(x)+\alpha r.\]
The first condition is lattice submodularity; the second specifies affine behavior along the all-ones direction. Extended-real arithmetic is understood whenever the displayed terms are defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An L-convex function is lattice-submodular and changes affinely, with a fixed slope, under integer all-ones translations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is L-convex exactly when it satisfies lattice submodularity and the displayed translation law for some \(r\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the standard submodularity-plus-translation definition of an L-convex function.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the L-convex-function leaf and consistently states the translation-slope convention, but no authoritative source with a precise locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shifted Lattice Inequality for Polyhedral L-Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The shifted lattice inequality holds for every real shift, including negative shifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(g\in\mathcal L[\mathbb R\to\mathbb R]\) is polyhedral L-convex, then
\[
g(p)+g(q)\ge g((p-\alpha\mathbf1)\vee q)+g(p\wedge(q+\alpha\mathbf1))
\]
for every \(p,q\in\mathbb R^V\) and every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every polyhedral L-convex function satisfies the shifted lattice inequality for all pairs of real vectors and every real shift.
assumptions_latex: g\in\mathcal L[\mathbb R\to\mathbb R]\text{ is polyhedral L-convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(p)+g(q)\ge g((p-\alpha\mathbf1)\vee q)+g(p\wedge(q+\alpha\mathbf1))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Properties of Polyhedral L-Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation under the six operations listed in the source, subject to their individual qualification conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g,g_1,g_2\in\mathcal L[\mathbb R\to\mathbb R]\) be polyhedral L-convex. Then: (1) \(\lambda g\) is polyhedral L-convex for \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_{++}\); (2) \(p\mapsto g(a+\beta p)\) is polyhedral L-convex for \(a\in\mathbb R^V\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\); (3) \(g[-x]\) is polyhedral L-convex for \(x\in\mathbb R^V\); (4) for \(U\subseteq V\), the projection \(g^U\) is polyhedral L-convex provided \(g^U>-\infty\); (5) if \(\psi_v\in\mathcal C[\mathbb R\to\mathbb R]\) for every \(v\in V\), then
\[
\widetilde g(p)=\inf_{q\in\mathbb R^V}\left[g(q)+\sum_{v\in V}\psi_v(p(v)-q(v))\right]
\]
is polyhedral L-convex provided \(\widetilde g>-\infty\); and (6) \(g_1+g_2\) is polyhedral L-convex provided \(\operatorname{dom}(g_1+g_2)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyhedral L-convexity is preserved by positive scaling, the stated nondegenerate affine argument change, the bracket operation, projection when it never takes minus infinity, the stated separable infimal convolution when it never takes minus infinity, and addition when the summed function has nonempty domain.
assumptions_latex: g,g_1,g_2\in\mathcal L[\mathbb R\to\mathbb R]\text{ are polyhedral L-convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda g,\ p\mapsto g(a+\beta p),\ g[-x],\ g^U,\ \widetilde g,\text{ and }g_1+g_2\text{ are polyhedral L-convex under the respective stated conditions}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L-Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition on the integer lattice, including translation linearity and the integer-valued consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(g:\mathbf Z^V\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}\) with \(\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing\) is L-convex if \(g(p)+g(q)\ge g(p\vee q)+g(p\wedge q)\) for all \(p,q\in\mathbf Z^V\), and there exists \(r\in\mathbf R\) such that \(g(p+\mathbf1)=g(p)+r\) for all \(p\in\mathbf Z^V\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty-domain extended-real-valued function on an integer lattice is L-convex when it is lattice-submodular and changes by a fixed additive constant under translation by the all-ones vector. If the function is integer-valued, that constant is an integer.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integer-Lattice L-Convex and L-Concave Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines L-convexity on the integer lattice through lattice submodularity and translation-linearity in the all-ones direction, with L-concavity defined by sign reversal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(g:\mathbf Z^V\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}\) with \(\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbf Z}g\ne\varnothing\) is L-convex if
\[
g(p)+g(q)\ge g(p\vee q)+g(p\wedge q)\qquad(\forall p,q\in\mathbf Z^V)
\]
and
\[
\exists r\in\mathbf R\;\forall p\in\mathbf Z^V:\quad g(p+\mathbf1)=g(p)+r.
\]
A function \(k\) is L-concave if \(-k\) is L-convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty-domain extended-real function on the integer lattice is L-convex when it is submodular with respect to coordinatewise join and meet and changes by a fixed constant under translation by the all-ones vector. L-concavity is defined by sign reversal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is L-convex}\iff\left[\forall p,q\in\mathbf Z^V,\ g(p)+g(q)\ge g(p\vee q)+g(p\wedge q)\right]\land\left[\exists r\in\mathbf R\ \forall p\in\mathbf Z^V,\ g(p+\mathbf1)=g(p)+r\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain-integral L-convex proximity theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided proximity from subset-direction local optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f$ be a domain-integral L-convex function on $\mathbb R^V$ such that $f(x)=f(x+\lambda\mathbf 1)$ for all $x\in\mathbb R^V$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$. Let $y\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\mathbb Z^V$ and $\alpha>0$. If $$f(y)\le f(y+\alpha\chi_X)\qquad(X\subseteq V),$$ then, writing $n=|V|$, there exists $x^*\in\operatorname{argmin}f$ such that $$y\le x^*\le y+(n-1)\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf 1.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a translation-invariant, domain-integral L-convex function, subset-direction local optimality at an integral point guarantees a global minimizer between that point and the stated coordinatewise upper bound.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is domain-integral and L-convex on }\mathbb R^V
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^*\in\operatorname{argmin}f:\ y\le x^*\le y+(|V|-1)\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf 1

knowledge_statements.title: L-Natural-Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real definition by the global discrete midpoint inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper function \(g:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is L-natural-convex if, for every \(x,y\in\mathbb Z^n\),
\[g(x)+g(y)\geq g\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{x+y}{2}\right\rfloor\right)+g\!\left(\left\lceil\frac{x+y}{2}\right\rceil\right),\]
where floor and ceiling are componentwise. The inequality is interpreted in the extended-real sense; in particular, the effective domain of \(g\) is closed under both rounded midpoint operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An L-natural-convex function dominates the sum of its values at the two componentwise rounded midpoints of every pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is L-natural-convex exactly when it satisfies the global rounded-midpoint inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L-Natural-Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition by homogenization into an L-convex function; the displayed generalized inequality is named translation submodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0\notin V\), let \(\widetilde V=\{0\}\cup V\), and let \(g:\mathbf Z^V\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}\). Define \(\widetilde g:\mathbf Z^{\widetilde V}\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}\) by \(\widetilde g(p_0,p)=g(p-p_0\mathbf1)\). Then \(g\) is L-natural-convex if \(\widetilde g\) is L-convex. The function \(\widetilde g\) satisfies translation linearity with constant \(r=0\). The condition \(g(p)+g(q)\ge g((p-\alpha\mathbf1)\vee q)+g(p\wedge(q+\alpha\mathbf1))\) for all \(p,q\in\mathbf Z^V\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbf Z_+\) is called translation submodularity; for \(\alpha=0\) it reduces to lattice submodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is L-natural-convex when its homogenization obtained by adding one integer coordinate is L-convex. The homogenized function is invariant under simultaneous all-ones translation. Translation submodularity permits nonnegative integer shifts and reduces to ordinary lattice submodularity at shift zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is L-natural-convex}\iff\widetilde g\text{ is L-convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L-Natural-Convex Functions by Restriction and Lift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines integer L-natural-convexity through a coordinate-plane restriction of an L-convex function and its equivalent homogenizing lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(v_0\in V\), put \(V'=V\setminus\{v_0\}\), and write \(p=(p_0,p')\). If \(G\) is L-convex, then
\[
g'(p')=G(0,p')\qquad(p'\in\mathbf Z^{V'})
\]
is called L\(^{\natural}\)-convex; its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbf Z}G\cap\{p_0=0\}\), expressed in the remaining coordinates. Equivalently, with a new element \(0\notin V\), a function \(g:\mathbf Z^V\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is L\(^{\natural}\)-convex if
\[
\widetilde g(p_0,p)=g(p-p_0\mathbf1)
\]
is L-convex on \(\mathbf Z^{\{0\}\cup V}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting an L-convex function to a coordinate plane that removes its all-ones translation direction produces an L-natural-convex function. Formally, a function is L-natural-convex when the lift obtained by adjoining a coordinate and evaluating g(p−p0·1) is L-convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is L}^{\natural}\text{-convex}\iff\widetilde g(p_0,p)=g(p-p_0\mathbf1)\text{ is L-convex on }\mathbf Z^{\{0\}\cup V}.

knowledge_statements.title: L-Type Function Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation-coordinate homogenization between L-natural-convex and zero-slope L-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper function \(g:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), define
\[\widetilde g(x_0,x)=g(x-x_0\mathbf1),\qquad (x_0,x)\in\mathbb Z^{n+1}.\]
Then \(g\) is L-natural-convex if and only if \(\widetilde g\) is L-convex with translation slope zero, and \(g(x)=\widetilde g(0,x)\). More generally, if an L-convex function \(f\) has translation slope \(r\), its normalized slice \(g(x)=f(0,x)\) satisfies
\[f(x_0,x)=g(x-x_0\mathbf1)+x_0r.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenizing with a translation coordinate turns an L-natural-convex function into a zero-slope L-convex function; slicing and restoring the slope invert the construction.
assumptions_latex: For the converse formula, \(f\) is L-convex with translation slope \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is L-natural-convex if and only if \(\widetilde g\) is zero-slope L-convex, with the displayed slice reconstruction.

notation.meaning: The all-ones translation slope of f.
The all-ones vector in n dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Midpoint Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global discrete midpoint convexity for extended-real functions on the integer lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper function \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is globally discrete-midpoint-convex if, for every \(x,y\in\mathbb Z^n\) with \(\lVert x-y\rVert_\infty\geq2\),
\[f(x)+f(y)\geq f\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{x+y}{2}\right\rfloor\right)+f\!\left(\left\lceil\frac{x+y}{2}\right\rceil\right).\]
The rounding is componentwise. Requiring the inequality only when \(\lVert x-y\rVert_\infty=2\) defines local discrete midpoint convexity; the local and global predicates must not be conflated without additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global discrete midpoint convexity requires the rounded-midpoint inequality for every pair at sup-norm distance at least two; distance exactly two gives the local condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) satisfies global discrete midpoint convexity precisely when the displayed inequality holds for all pairs with \(\lVert x-y\rVert_\infty\geq2\).

notation.meaning: The maximum norm on the integer lattice.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The distance-qualified rounded-midpoint inequality is the standard global discrete midpoint convexity condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete midpoint convexity and the L-natural averaging property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two lattice inequalities introduced in the discrete-midpoint characterization of L-natural convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(g\) on \(\mathbf Z^V\) satisfies discrete midpoint convexity if, for every \(p,q\in\mathbf Z^V\), \[g(p)+g(q)\geq g\!\left(\left\lceil\frac{p+q}{2}\right\rceil\right)+g\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{p+q}{2}\right\rfloor\right),\] with componentwise rounding. It satisfies \(\mathrm L^{\natural}\!\operatorname{-APR}[\mathbf Z]\) if, for every \(p,q\in\mathbf Z^V\) such that \(\operatorname{supp}^{+}(p-q)\neq\varnothing\), \[g(p)+g(q)\geq g(p-\chi_X)+g(q+\chi_X),\qquad X=\arg\max_{v\in V}\{p(v)-q(v)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete midpoint convexity says that the sum of the values at two integer points is at least the sum at their componentwise rounded midpoints. The L-natural averaging property says that this sum does not increase when one unit is transferred from p to q in every coordinate attaining the maximum difference p(v)−q(v), provided p exceeds q somewhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(p)+g(q)\geq g\!\left(\left\lceil\frac{p+q}{2}\right\rceil\right)+g\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{p+q}{2}\right\rfloor\right),\qquad g(p)+g(q)\geq g(p-\chi_X)+g(q+\chi_X).

knowledge_statements.title: L-Convex Distance Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed constraint-distance associated with an integral L-convex difference-bound polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\gamma:V\times V\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) satisfy \(\gamma_{ii}=0\) and \(\gamma_{ik}\leq\gamma_{ij}+\gamma_{jk}\). For \(x\in\mathbb Z^V\), define
\[
d_\gamma(x)=\max_{i,j\in V}\bigl(x_j-x_i-\gamma_{ij}\bigr)_+.
\]
Then \(d_\gamma(x+\alpha\mathbf 1)=d_\gamma(x)\) for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb Z\), its zero set is \(P(\gamma)\cap\mathbb Z^V\), and
\[
d_\gamma(x)=\min\{\lambda\in\mathbb Z_+:x_j-x_i\leq\gamma_{ij}+\lambda\text{ for all }i,j\in V\}.
\]
Thus the directed violation distance is an integer-valued translation-invariant L-convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum positive violation of consistent difference constraints is translation invariant, vanishes exactly on the associated L-convex integer set, and equals the least uniform constraint relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma\) is integer-valued where finite and satisfies the directed triangle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_\gamma\) is an integer-valued translation-invariant L-convex distance function with zero set \(P(\gamma)\cap\mathbb Z^V\).

notation.meaning: The polyhedron defined by all inequalities \(x_j-x_i\leq\gamma_{ij}\).

knowledge_statements.title: L-Convex Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Difference-bound characterization of translation-invariant L-convex polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite set \(V\), let \(\gamma_{ij}\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) satisfy \(\gamma_{ii}=0\) and \(\gamma_{ik}\leq\gamma_{ij}+\gamma_{jk}\) for all \(i,j,k\in V\). The associated L-convex polyhedron is
\[
P(\gamma)=\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x_j-x_i\leq\gamma_{ij}\text{ for all }i,j\in V\}.
\]
It is closed under componentwise minimum and maximum and under translations \(x\mapsto x+\alpha\mathbf 1\), where \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). Conversely, every nonempty polyhedron having these three closure properties admits such a difference-bound representation, allowing redundant infinite bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An L-convex polyhedron is exactly a nonempty polyhedron described by consistent pairwise difference bounds, equivalently one closed under coordinatewise minimum, maximum, and all-ones translations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(\gamma)\) is L-convex, and every nonempty L-convex polyhedron has a difference-bound representation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The difference-bound characterization and its converse are specialized, nontrivial claims. No cited source or inspectable locator supports the equivalence between the closure properties and the representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L-Convex and Integral L-Convex Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines real L-convex polyhedra, their integral subclass, and the corresponding lattice-set criterion for integral polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty polyhedron \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^V\) is L-convex if \(p,q\in D\Rightarrow p\vee q,p\wedge q\in D\) and \(p\in D\Rightarrow p+\alpha\mathbf 1\in D\) for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). An L-convex polyhedron is integral L-convex when \(D=\overline{D\cap\mathbb Z^V}\). If \(D\) is an integral polyhedron, then \(D\) is L-convex if and only if \(D\cap\mathbb Z^V\) is an L-convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron is L-convex when it is closed under componentwise maximum and minimum and under translation by every real multiple of the all-ones vector. Such a polyhedron is integral L-convex when it is generated from its integer points as indicated. For an integral polyhedron, L-convexity is equivalent to L-convexity of its integer-point set.
assumptions_latex: D\subseteq\mathbb R^V\text{ is a nonempty polyhedron}
D\text{ is assumed integral only for the final lattice-set equivalence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is L-convex}\iff\left[\forall p,q\in D:\ p\vee q,p\wedge q\in D\right]\land\left[\forall p\in D,\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R:\ p+\alpha\mathbf1\in D\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L-Convex Cones and the Tangent-Cone Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines L-convex cones, gives their ring-family representation, and characterizes L-convex polyhedra through their tangent cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An L-convex cone is a cone that is an L-convex polyhedron. A cone \(D\) is L-convex if and only if there exists a ring family \(\mathcal D\subseteq2^V\) with \(V\in\mathcal D\) such that \[D=\left\{\sum_{X\in\mathcal D}c_X\chi_X\ \middle|\ c_X\geq0\text{ for every }X\in\mathcal D\setminus\{V\}\right\}.\] In addition, a polyhedron \(D\) is L-convex if and only if its tangent cone at every point of \(D\) is an L-convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An L-convex cone is an L-convex polyhedron that is also a cone. These cones are exactly those represented using incidence vectors of a ring family, with nonnegative coefficients except for the coefficient associated with the whole ground set. A polyhedron is L-convex exactly when its tangent cone at every one of its points is L-convex.
assumptions_latex: D\text{ is a cone for the ring-family representation}
D\text{ is a polyhedron for the tangent-cone characterization}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[D\text{ is an L-convex cone}\iff\exists\mathcal D\subseteq2^V\text{ a ring family},\ V\in\mathcal D:\ D=\left\{\sum_{X\in\mathcal D}c_X\chi_X\mid c_X\geq0\ (X\ne V)\right\}\right]
