knowledge_statements.title: Metric–Polyhedral Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-path closure identifies directed metrics with canonical difference-bound descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) have arc lengths \(c:A\to\mathbb R\) and no negative directed cycle. Let \(\gamma_{ij}\) be the shortest-path length from \(i\) to \(j\), with \(+\infty\) when no path exists. Then
\[
\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x_v-x_u\leq c_{uv}\text{ for every }uv\in A\}
=
\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x_j-x_i\leq\gamma_{ij}\text{ for all }i,j\in V\}.
\]
The matrix \(\gamma\) satisfies the directed triangle inequalities and is the componentwise least transitively closed system equivalent to the arc constraints. If \(c\) is integral, the resulting polyhedron is integral modulo its lineality generated by componentwise constants on unconstrained components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking all-pairs shortest-path distances converts graph arc constraints into the canonical directed-metric description of the same L-convex polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The arc-potential polyhedron equals \(P(\gamma)\), where \(\gamma\) is the shortest-path directed metric.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shortest-path closure equality is standard, but the canonical-minimality, integrality, and lineality claims need an authoritative locator. The phrase “unconstrained components” must also be tied to a precise graph decomposition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Correspondence Between L-Convex Sets and Integer-Valued Distance Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization by distance polyhedra and mutually inverse mappings between the explicitly named classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set D\subseteq\mathbf{Z}^{V} is L-convex if and only if D=\mathbf{D}(\gamma)\cap\mathbf{Z}^{V} for an integer-valued distance function \gamma\in\mathcal{T}[\mathbf{Z}]. More precisely, the mappings \Phi:\mathcal{L}_{0}[\mathbf{Z}]\to\mathcal{T}[\mathbf{Z}] and \Psi:\mathcal{T}[\mathbf{Z}]\to\mathcal{L}_{0}[\mathbf{Z}] given by \Phi(D)(u,v)=\sup\{p(v)-p(u)\mid p\in D\} and \Psi(\gamma)=\mathbf{D}(\gamma)\cap\mathbf{Z}^{V} are inverse to each other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: L-convex sets are exactly the integer-point sets of polyhedra defined by integer-valued distance functions. On the stated classes, the coordinate-difference and integer-point constructions are mutually inverse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is L-convex}\Longleftrightarrow D=\mathbf{D}(\gamma)\cap\mathbf{Z}^{V}\text{ for some }\gamma\in\mathcal{T}[\mathbf{Z}],\qquad \Psi\circ\Phi=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal{L}_{0}[\mathbf{Z}]},\quad\Phi\circ\Psi=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal{T}[\mathbf{Z}]}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance-Function Representation of L-Convex Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the correspondence between distance functions and real or integral L-convex polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every distance function \(\gamma\) with \(\mathbf D(\gamma)\ne\varnothing\), the polyhedron \(\mathbf D(\gamma)\) is L-convex; if \(\gamma\) is also integer-valued, then \(\mathbf D(\gamma)\) is integral L-convex. Moreover, \(D\) is an L-convex polyhedron if and only if \(D=\mathbf D(\gamma)\) for some \(\gamma\in\mathcal T[\mathbb R]\), while \(D\) is an integral L-convex polyhedron if and only if \(D=\mathbf D(\gamma)\) for some \(\gamma\in\mathcal T[\mathbb Z]\).

knowledge_statements.title: L-Convex Convex Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical piecewise-linear extension on the standard triangulation of the integer lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Triangulate each unit cube of \(\mathbb R^n\) into simplices whose vertices are
\[
z,\quad z+e_{\pi(1)},\quad z+e_{\pi(1)}+e_{\pi(2)},\ldots,\quad z+\mathbf 1,
\]
where \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\) and \(\pi\) is a permutation. For \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), let \(\bar f\) be affine on every such simplex and agree with \(f\) at lattice points. Then \(f\) is L-natural-convex, equivalently it satisfies
\[
f(x)+f(y)\geq f(\lceil(x+y)/2\rceil)+f(\lfloor(x+y)/2\rfloor),
\]
if and only if \(\bar f\) is convex on \(\mathbb R^n\). Translation-linear L-convex functions arise as the corresponding invariant subclass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear interpolation over the standard lattice triangulation is globally convex exactly when the lattice function satisfies discrete midpoint convexity.
assumptions_latex: The effective domain of \(f\) is compatible with the stated extended-real interpolation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is L-natural-convex if and only if its canonical simplicial extension \(\bar f\) is convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed equivalence involves a specialized extension theorem. A source must confirm the L-natural-convex convention and specify how simplexwise interpolation is defined when some vertex values are infinite. The final relationship to translation-linear L-convex functions is also insufficiently precise.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar g\in\mathcal L[\mathbf R\to\mathbf R]

knowledge_statements.title: M2-Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The two-summand enlargement of the M-convex function class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper function \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is M2-convex if there exist proper M-convex functions \(f_1,f_2:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) such that
\[
f(x)=f_1(x)+f_2(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb Z^n).
\]
Consequently, \(\operatorname{dom}f=\operatorname{dom}f_1\cap\operatorname{dom}f_2\). The representation by \(f_1,f_2\) need not be unique, and the sum generally need not satisfy the single-function M-convex exchange axiom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M2-convex function is a pointwise sum of two proper M-convex functions; its domain is the intersection of their effective domains.
assumptions_latex: Their effective domains have nonempty intersection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=f_1+f_2\) is M2-convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise-sum definition is plausible and fits the leaf, but the record supplies no authoritative locator for the M2-convex terminology or the accompanying nonuniqueness and strict-enlargement assertions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximity of a scaled cyclic-exchange point to a minimizer of the sum of two M-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f_1,f_2\in\mathcal M[\mathbb Z^V\to\mathbb R], \alpha\in\mathbb Z_{++}, and n=|V|. Suppose x^\alpha\in\operatorname{dom}f_1\cap\operatorname{dom}f_2 and, for every k\geq1 and u_1,\ldots,u_k,v_1,\ldots,v_k\in V with \{u_1,\ldots,u_k\}\cap\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}=\varnothing and u_{k+1}=u_1, \[\sum_{i=1}^k\left[f_1\!\left(x^\alpha-\alpha(\chi_{u_i}-\chi_{v_i})\right)-f_1(x^\alpha)\right]+\sum_{i=1}^k\left[f_2\!\left(x^\alpha+\alpha(\chi_{u_{i+1}}-\chi_{v_i})\right)-f_2(x^\alpha)\right]\geq0.\] Then \(\operatorname*{argmin}(f_1+f_2)\neq\varnothing\), and there exists \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}(f_1+f_2)\) such that \[\|x^\alpha-x^*\|_\infty\leq\frac{n^2}{2}(\alpha-1).\]

children.title: L2-Convex Functions
children.top_down_role: The L2-convex branch of related discrete convex classes.

knowledge_statements.title: L2-Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The two-factor infimal-convolution enlargement of the L-convex class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper function \(g:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is L2-convex if there exist proper L-convex functions \(g_1,g_2:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) such that
\[
g(p)=(g_1\mathbin{\square}g_2)(p):=\inf\{g_1(p_1)+g_2(p_2):p_1,p_2\in\mathbb Z^n,\ p_1+p_2=p\}.
\]
The infimum is required to be finite somewhere and attained whenever finite. This decomposition need not be unique, and an L2-convex function need not itself be L-convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An L2-convex function is the proper infimal convolution of two L-convex functions, with the infimum attained wherever its value is finite.
assumptions_latex: The displayed infimal convolution is proper and attained on its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g=g_1\mathbin{\square}g_2\) is L2-convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An authoritative source is required to confirm that this is the intended L2-convex definition and whether attainment is part of the definition, an automatic consequence under standard hypotheses, or an additional assumption.

children.title: M2–L2 Class Boundary
children.top_down_role: Shared structure plus distinctions between M2-convex and L2-convex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: M2–L2 Class Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete witness that the two-summand class strictly exceeds ordinary M-convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E=\{1,2,3,4\}\), and let
\[
B_1=\{\{1,3\},\{1,4\},\{2,3\},\{2,4\}\},\qquad
B_2=\{\{1,2\},\{1,4\},\{2,3\},\{3,4\}\}.
\]
Each \(B_k\) is the base family of a partition matroid, so its indicator \(\delta_{B_k}\) is M-convex on incidence vectors. Their sum is finite exactly on \(B_1\cap B_2=\{\{1,4\},\{2,3\}\}\). This two-element family violates basis exchange: no exchange from \(\{1,4\}\) toward \(\{2,3\}\) remains in the intersection. Hence \(\delta_{B_1}+\delta_{B_2}\) is M2-convex but not M-convex, showing that the M2 boundary is genuine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two partition-matroid base indicators have an M2-convex sum whose two-point domain violates basis exchange, so M2-convexity is strictly broader than M-convexity.
assumptions_latex: Indicators take value \(0\) on the stated incidence vectors and \(+\infty\) elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_{B_1}+\delta_{B_2}\) is M2-convex but not M-convex.

notation.meaning: The extended-real indicator of the incidence vectors of members of \(B\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly targets a separation between M2-convexity and ordinary M-convexity, but the terminal container is the M2–L2 class boundary. The record makes no statement about L2-convexity or the relationship between the M2 and L2 classes, so it does not match the exact local sense of the title.

knowledge_statements.title: Multimodular Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition through the cumulative-sum transformation to L-natural-convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), define \(g:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) by
\[
g(p_1,\ldots,p_n)=f(p_1,p_2-p_1,\ldots,p_n-p_{n-1}).
\]
The function \(f\) is multimodular if \(g\) is L-natural-convex; equivalently, \(g\) satisfies
\[
g(p)+g(q)\geq g(\lceil(p+q)/2\rceil)+g(\lfloor(p+q)/2\rfloor)
\]
for all \(p,q\in\mathbb Z^n\). Thus multimodularity is discrete midpoint convexity after changing from increments to cumulative coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is multimodular when expressing its arguments as successive differences transforms it into an L-natural-convex function.
assumptions_latex: Ceilings and floors are taken componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is multimodular if and only if the transformed function \(g\) is L-natural-convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cumulative-coordinate characterization is plausible and fits the leaf, but multimodular transformations appear in several coordinate conventions. A specific authoritative definition or theorem locator is required.

children.title: Jump Systems
children.top_down_role: Support structures governed by jump exchanges.

knowledge_statements.title: Jump Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-step axiom for subsets of the integer lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in\mathbb Z^n\), a step from \(x\) toward \(y\) is a vector \(s\in\{\pm e_1,\ldots,\pm e_n\}\) satisfying \(\|x+s-y\|_1=\|x-y\|_1-1\). A nonempty set \(J\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) is a jump system if, whenever \(x,y\in J\), \(s\) is a step from \(x\) toward \(y\), and \(x+s\notin J\), there exists a step \(t\) from \(x+s\) toward \(y\) such that \(x+s+t\in J\). This is the two-step jump axiom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A jump system allows every blocked unit move toward another feasible point to be completed by a second unit move reaching feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J\) is a jump system exactly when it satisfies the displayed two-step jump axiom.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-step axiom is stated precisely and matches the definition container, but no source or locator is supplied for this specialized definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure of Jump Systems under Minkowski Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure property for jump systems in a common integer lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(J_1,J_2\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) are jump systems, then their Minkowski sum \(J_1+J_2:=\{x_1+x_2:x_1\in J_1,\ x_2\in J_2\}\) is a jump system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If J1 and J2 are jump systems in the same integer lattice, then their Minkowski sum is also a jump system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J_1+J_2\text{ is a jump system}

children.title: Jump M-Convex Functions
children.top_down_role: Valuated structures over jump-system domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Jump M-Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valuated symmetric two-step exchange on an integer jump system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper function \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is jump M-convex if, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every step \(s\) from \(x\) toward \(y\), there exists a step \(t\) from \(x+s\) toward \(y\) such that
\[
x+s+t,\ y-s-t\in\operatorname{dom}f
\]
and
\[
f(x)+f(y)\geq f(x+s+t)+f(y-s-t).
\]
The selected pair of steps transfers the same displacement from \(y\) to \(x\); the effective domain therefore satisfies the corresponding symmetric two-step exchange property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jump M-convexity assigns values to a jump-system domain so every directed unit step can be completed by a symmetric two-step exchange that does not increase total value.
assumptions_latex: A step is defined by one-unit decrease of the one-norm distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) satisfies the valuated symmetric two-step exchange axiom.

notation.meaning: The integer vectors where \(f\) is finite.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Jump M-convexity has closely related exchange variants, often distinguished by constant-parity or natural-convex analogues. A source is needed to determine whether the stated symmetric two-step axiom is correct without an additional domain hypothesis.

children.title: Support–Valuation Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The interface between jump-system supports plus jump M-convex valuations.

knowledge_statements.title: Support–Valuation Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between jump-system supports and extended-real jump M-convex valuations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is jump M-convex, then its support \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is a jump system. Conversely, for a nonempty set \(J\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\), define
\[
\delta_J(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in J,\\+\infty,&x\notin J.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(\delta_J\) is jump M-convex if and only if \(J\) satisfies the symmetric two-step exchange axiom. Under the standard equivalence between the jump axiom and its symmetric exchange form, this is equivalent to \(J\) being a jump system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite domain of a jump M-convex valuation is a jump system, while zero-infinity indicators recover jump systems from their symmetric exchange form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Jump M-convex supports are jump systems, and jump systems correspond to jump M-convex indicator valuations.

notation.meaning: The support on which \(f\) is finite.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The correspondence depends on the exact jump M-convex convention and on an equivalence between ordinary and symmetric exchange axioms. Without a source, it is unclear whether all jump systems or only a constant-parity subclass admit the asserted indicator valuation.

children.title: Quasi M-Convexity
children.top_down_role: The quasi-M branch of weakened discrete convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi M-Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Max-type ordinal relaxation of the M-convex exchange inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper function \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) with constant coordinate sum on \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is quasi M-convex in the max-exchange sense if, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(i\) with \(x_i>y_i\), there exists \(j\) with \(x_j<y_j\) such that, writing \(x'=x-e_i+e_j\) and \(y'=y+e_i-e_j\),
\[
x',y'\in\operatorname{dom}f,
\qquad
\max\{f(x'),f(y')\}\leq\max\{f(x),f(y)\}.
\]
Unlike M-convexity, this condition depends only on the ordering of function values and is preserved by strictly increasing scalar transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasi M-convexity replaces the additive exchange inequality by a maximum-value inequality, preserving feasibility and the ordinal ranking of values.
assumptions_latex: All points in \(\operatorname{dom}f\) have the same coordinate sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every directed surplus coordinate admits a feasible exchange whose two new values do not exceed the former maximum.

notation.meaning: The pair obtained by a symmetric unit exchange.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The max-exchange formulation is coherent, but quasi M-convexity has multiple literature variants. An authoritative locator is necessary to establish that this definition, including the constant-sum hypothesis and transformation-invariance claim, is the intended one.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasi M-convex sets and their exchange axioms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines quasi M-convexity of an integer set through its indicator and records the corresponding strong and weak set-exchange conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $B\subseteq\mathbb Z^V$, quasi M-convexity is defined through the indicator $\delta_B:\mathbb Z^V\to\{0,+\infty\}$. The condition $(\mathrm{Q\text{-}EXC})$ requires that, for all $x,y\in B$ and every $u\in\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y)$, there exist $v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y)$ such that $x-\chi_u+\chi_v\in B$ or $y+\chi_u-\chi_v\in B$. The condition $(\mathrm{Q\text{-}EXC}_w)$ requires that, for every distinct $x,y\in B$, there exist $u\in\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y)$ and $v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y)$ satisfying the same disjunction. These correspond respectively to QM and $\mathrm{QM}_w$ for $\delta_B$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is quasi M-convex through its indicator function. The strong exchange condition requires a compensating coordinate for every positive discrepancy coordinate; the weak condition requires only some positive and negative discrepancy coordinates. In either case at least one exchanged endpoint remains in the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta_B\text{ satisfies QM respectively }\mathrm{QM}_w\text{ exactly when }B\text{ satisfies Q-EXC respectively Q-EXC}_w.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasi-M optimality criteria by unit exchanges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict and non-strict global optimality criteria under two distinct weak quasi-M exchange assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbf{Z}^{V}\to\mathbf{R}\cup\{+\infty\} and x\in\operatorname{dom}f. If f satisfies (\mathrm{QM}_{\mathrm w}), then
\[
f(x)<f(y)\quad(\forall y\in\mathbf{Z}^{V}\setminus\{x\})
\iff
\Delta f(x;v,u)>0\quad(\forall u,v\in V,\ u\ne v).
\]
If f satisfies (\mathrm{SSQM}_{\mathrm w}^{\ne}), then
\[
f(x)\le f(y)\quad(\forall y\in\mathbf{Z}^{V})
\iff
\Delta f(x;v,u)\ge 0\quad(\forall u,v\in V).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the weak quasi-M condition, a feasible point is the unique global minimizer exactly when every unit exchange between distinct indices has positive increment. Under the weak strict-semi-strict quasi-M condition, it is a global minimizer exactly when every unit exchange increment is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[f(x)<f(y)\ (\forall y\in\mathbf{Z}^{V}\setminus\{x\})\iff\Delta f(x;v,u)>0\ (\forall u,v\in V,\ u\ne v)\right],\quad\left[f(x)\le f(y)\ (\forall y\in\mathbf{Z}^{V})\iff\Delta f(x;v,u)\ge0\ (\forall u,v\in V)\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Level sets of a quasi M-convex function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the level-set notation used for weak quasi-M convexity and records its domain and minimizer special cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbf Z^V\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}\), \[L(f,\alpha)=\{x\in\mathbf Z^V\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\}.\] In particular, \(L(f,+\infty)=\operatorname{dom}f\); if \(\alpha_0=\min f\), then \(L(f,\alpha_0)=\arg\min f\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasi M-convexity and semistrict quasi M-convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records only the discrete exchange definitions owned by the Quasi M-Convexity node; the extract's continuous quasi-convexity discussion has different ownership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function $f:\mathbb Z^V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ with $\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing$ is quasi M-convex (QM) if, for all $x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f$ and every $u\in\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y)$, there exists $v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y)$ such that $\Delta f(x;v,u)\leq0$ or $\Delta f(y;u,v)\leq0$. It is semistrictly quasi M-convex (SSQM) if such a $v$ exists with $\Delta f(x;v,u)<0$, or $\Delta f(y;u,v)<0$, or $\Delta f(x;v,u)=\Delta f(y;u,v)=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasi M-convexity requires every positive discrepancy coordinate between two domain points to admit a compensating exchange that does not increase at least one endpoint. The semistrict version requires a strict decrease at one endpoint unless both exchange increments vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists v\in\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y)\text{ satisfying the stated QM or SSQM alternatives.}

children.title: Quasi L-Convexity

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi L-Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sublevel-set formulation relative to the chosen class of L-convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). For \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), define \(L_\alpha(f)=\{x\in\mathbb Z^n\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\}\). The function \(f\) is quasi L-convex if every nonempty \(L_\alpha(f)\) is an L-convex set. Equivalently, whenever \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(f(x),f(y)\leq\alpha\), all points required from \(x,y\) by the defining closure axioms of L-convex sets also belong to \(L_\alpha(f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is quasi L-convex when each of its nonempty lower level sets is an L-convex set.
assumptions_latex: The term \(\mathrm{L\text{-}convex\ set}\) uses the ambient chapter convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is quasi L-convex}\iff (\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R)\,[L_\alpha(f)=\varnothing\text{ or }L_\alpha(f)\text{ is L-convex}]\).

notation.meaning: lower level set of f at level alpha
effective domain where f is finite

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indicator-function characterization of quasi-submodular sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates quasi-submodularity conditions for an indicator function to lattice properties of its underlying set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D\subseteq\mathbf Z^V$ and let $\delta_D:\mathbf Z^V\to\{0,+\infty\}$ be its indicator function. Then $\delta_D$ satisfies $(\mathrm{QSB})$ if and only if $D$ satisfies $(\mathrm{QDL})$: for every $p,q\in D$, $p\wedge q\in D$ or $p\vee q\in D$. Moreover, $\delta_D$ satisfies $(\mathrm{SSQSB})$ if and only if $D$ satisfies $(\mathrm{SBS}[\mathbf Z])$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of a set is quasi-submodular exactly when every pair of points has either its meet or its join in the set. Semistrict quasi-submodularity of the indicator is equivalent to the SBS integer-lattice property of the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta_D\text{ satisfies }(\mathrm{QSB})\iff\forall p,q\in D:\ p\wedge q\in D\ \lor\ p\vee q\in D,\qquad \delta_D\text{ satisfies }(\mathrm{SSQSB})\iff D\text{ satisfies }(\mathrm{SBS}[\mathbf Z]).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasi-submodularity and quasi L-convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines quasi-submodularity, semistrict quasi-submodularity, and the corresponding translation-invariant quasi L-convex classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function $g:\mathbf Z^V\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}$ is quasi-submodular if, for every $p,q\in\mathbf Z^V$, $g(p\wedge q)\le g(p)$ or $g(p\vee q)\le g(q)$. It is semistrictly quasi-submodular if, for every $p,q\in\mathbf Z^V$, both $g(p\vee q)\ge g(q)\Rightarrow g(p\wedge q)\le g(p)$ and $g(p\wedge q)\ge g(p)\Rightarrow g(p\vee q)\le g(q)$ hold. A function with $\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing$ is quasi L-convex if it satisfies $(\mathrm{QSB})$ and $(\mathrm{TRF}[\mathbf Z])$, and semistrictly quasi L-convex if it satisfies $(\mathrm{SSQSB})$ and $(\mathrm{TRF}[\mathbf Z])$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasi-submodularity requires at least one specified meet-or-join comparison for every pair. Semistrict quasi-submodularity imposes both conditional comparisons. Together with the integer translation property and a nonempty effective domain, these conditions define quasi and semistrictly quasi L-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is quasi L-convex}\iff (\mathrm{QSB})\land(\mathrm{TRF}[\mathbf Z]),\qquad g\text{ is semistrictly quasi L-convex}\iff(\mathrm{SSQSB})\land(\mathrm{TRF}[\mathbf Z]).

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi M–L Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates sublevel-set quasi M- and quasi L-convexity in dimension two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adopt the sublevel-set definitions of quasi M- and quasi L-convexity. In \(\mathbb Z^2\), the indicator \(\delta_{\{(1,0),(0,1)\}}\) is quasi M-convex because its only nontrivial sublevel set is M-convex, but it is not quasi L-convex. Conversely, \(\delta_{\{(k,k)\mid k\in\mathbb Z\}}\) is quasi L-convex but not quasi M-convex: its effective domain is invariant in the all-ones direction and lattice closed, whereas it is not contained in a constant-sum hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasi M- and quasi L-convexity are incomparable: indicator functions of suitable two-dimensional M- and L-convex sets separate them.
assumptions_latex: Quasi classes are defined through their nonempty lower level sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{quasi M-convex}\not\subseteq\text{quasi L-convex}\) and \(\text{quasi L-convex}\not\subseteq\text{quasi M-convex}\).

children.title: Function Restriction
children.top_down_role: Restriction of discrete convex functions to smaller domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Function Restriction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction to a subset, represented as an extended-real function on the original lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and let \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\). The restriction of \(f\) to \(S\), viewed on the original ambient lattice, is the function \(f|_S:\mathbb Z^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) defined by \[f|_S(x)=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in S,\\+\infty,&x\notin S.\end{cases}\] Hence \(\operatorname{dom}(f|_S)=\operatorname{dom}f\cap S\). Fixing coordinates is the special case in which \(S=\{x\mid x_J=a\}\) for an index set \(J\) and prescribed vector \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restriction keeps a function unchanged on a chosen set and assigns positive infinity outside that set; coordinate fixing is a special case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}(f|_S)=\operatorname{dom}f\cap S\).

notation.meaning: restriction represented on the original ambient lattice

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the standard extended-real restriction convention.
A discrete-convex-analysis source locator is still required.

children.title: Function Projection
children.top_down_role: Projection of discrete convex functions onto retained variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Function Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection is partial minimization over coordinates removed from the argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) and \(J\) be disjoint finite coordinate sets, and let \(f:\mathbb Z^{I}\times\mathbb Z^{J}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). Assume that \(\inf_{y\in\mathbb Z^J}f(x,y)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in\mathbb Z^I\). The projection of \(f\) onto the \(I\)-coordinates is the function \(g:\mathbb Z^I\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) defined by \[g(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb Z^J}f(x,y).\] If this infimum is attained whenever it is finite, it may be written as a minimum. Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}g=\{x\in\mathbb Z^I\mid \exists y\in\mathbb Z^J:(x,y)\in\operatorname{dom}f\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection partially minimizes over the eliminated coordinates. When negative-infinite infima are excluded, its finite domain is the coordinate projection of the original finite domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb Z^J}f(x,y)\) and \(\operatorname{dom}g=\{x\in\mathbb Z^I\mid \exists y\in\mathbb Z^J:(x,y)\in\operatorname{dom}f\}\).

notation.meaning: retained and eliminated finite coordinate sets
projection of f onto the retained coordinates
set on which f is finite

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Partial minimization is the standard function-projection operation.
A discrete-convex-analysis source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Variable Elimination
children.top_down_role: Removal of variables through value optimization or marginalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination of one integer variable by partial minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\geq1\) and let \(f:\mathbb Z^{n-1}\times\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). Assume that \(\inf_{t\in\mathbb Z}f(x,t)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in\mathbb Z^{n-1}\). Eliminating the variable \(t\) produces the value function \(g:\mathbb Z^{n-1}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) defined by \[g(x)=\inf_{t\in\mathbb Z}f(x,t).\] When the infimum is attained, a minimizer \(t^*(x)\in\arg\min_{t\in\mathbb Z}f(x,t)\) may be retained for reconstruction. Several variables may be eliminated by joint partial minimization over their product lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable elimination partially minimizes over the removed integer variable; an attained minimizer may be stored for reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)=\inf_{t\in\mathbb Z}f(x,t)\).

notation.meaning: an attained minimizing value retained for reconstruction

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Exact variable elimination is partial minimization.
No computational algorithm or complexity guarantee is asserted.

children.title: Restriction–Projection Closure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Class-specific preservation limits across these domain-reduction operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Restriction–Projection Closure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary restriction need not preserve lattice submodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Closure under restriction requires structure in the restricting set. Let \(f\equiv0\) on \(\mathbb Z^2\), which is submodular, and let \(S=\{(1,0),(0,1)\}\). For \(g=f|_S\), take \(x=(1,0)\) and \(y=(0,1)\). Then \(g(x)+g(y)=0\), while \(g(x\wedge y)+g(x\vee y)=+\infty\). Thus the lattice-submodular inequality fails. Consequently, closure statements for restriction or projection must specify the function class, admissible domain, and attainment or boundedness conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary restriction can destroy discrete convexity; closure requires compatible restricting sets and, for projection, appropriate finiteness or attainment assumptions.
assumptions_latex: Extended-real lattice submodularity means \(h(x)+h(y)\geq h(x\wedge y)+h(x\vee y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ submodular}\centernot\implies f|_S\text{ submodular for arbitrary }S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The displayed values directly witness failure of the submodular inequality.
A source is needed for the broader class-specific closure taxonomy.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed restriction counterexample is correct, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. The broader statement about projection closure and required conditions is class-dependent and lacks a source.

children.title: Discrete Convolution
children.top_down_role: Convolution operations within discrete convex function classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infimal convolution on an integer lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f,g:\mathbb Z^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), their discrete infimal convolution is \[(f\mathbin{\square}g)(x)=\inf\{f(y)+g(z)\mid y,z\in\mathbb Z^n,\ y+z=x\}=\inf_{y\in\mathbb Z^n}\{f(y)+g(x-y)\}.\] If the infimum is attained, it may be replaced by a minimum. The effective domain satisfies \(\operatorname{dom}(f\mathbin{\square}g)=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g\), provided no value \(-\infty\) is created by an unbounded infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete convolution assigns each lattice point the least sum of two function values over all integer decompositions of that point.
assumptions_latex: The infimum is well-defined and does not equal \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f\mathbin{\square}g)(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb Z^n}\{f(y)+g(x-y)\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the standard infimal-convolution definition on a lattice.
A discrete-convex-analysis source locator is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The infimal-convolution definition and qualified domain identity are mathematically coherent, but no inspectable discrete-convex-analysis source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure of domain-integral M-natural convexity under convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure and integer-lattice representation of the convolution of two domain-integral M-natural-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let g_1 and g_2 be domain-integral M^{\natural}\text{-convex functions on }\mathbb{R}^V. If (g_1\circ g_2)(x)>-\infty for every x\in\mathbb{Z}^V, then g_1\circ g_2 is a domain-integral M^{\natural}\text{-convex function. Moreover, (g_1\circ g_2)(x)=\inf\{g_1(y)+g_2(x-y)\mid y\in\mathbb{Z}^V\} for every x\in\mathbb{Z}^V.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the convolution of two domain-integral M-natural-convex functions is greater than minus infinity at every integer point, it is again domain-integral and M-natural-convex. On the integer lattice it equals the infimum over integer decompositions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_1\circ g_2\text{ is domain-integral and }M^{\natural}\text{-convex, and }\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}^V,\ (g_1\circ g_2)(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{Z}^V}\{g_1(y)+g_2(x-y)\}.

children.title: Function Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Aggregation of discrete convex functions or variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Function Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise aggregation of extended-real discrete functions with strictly positive weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\geq1\), let \(f_i:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and let \(\lambda_i>0\). Their weighted pointwise aggregation is the function \(F:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) defined by \[F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x).\] Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}F=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i\). Whether \(F\) remains in a specified discrete-convex class is a separate class-specific closure property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly positive weighted pointwise aggregation sums the component functions, and its finite domain is the intersection of their finite domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)\) and \(\operatorname{dom}F=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i\).

children.title: Discrete-Convex Composition

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Convex Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition with an integer-lattice map, without asserting unconditional class preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb Z^m\to\mathbb Z^n\) be an integer-lattice map and let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\). The pullback composition of \(f\) by \(T\) is \[g=f\circ T,\qquad g(x)=f(T(x))\quad(x\in\mathbb Z^m).\] Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}g=T^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Preservation of a particular discrete-convex class is not automatic; it depends on the structural compatibility of \(T\), such as coordinate permutations or translations for classes invariant under those transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete composition pulls a function back through a lattice map; discrete convexity is preserved only for maps compatible with the chosen class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)=f(T(x))\) and \(\operatorname{dom}g=T^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The pullback formula is the standard notion of function composition.
Admissible maps differ among discrete-convex classes and need class-specific sourcing.

children.title: Composite Closure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Preservation limits across convolution, aggregation, plus composition.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Closure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinear scalar composition can destroy submodularity even when the inner function is modular.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\{0,1\}^2\), let \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1+x_2\), which is modular and hence submodular, and let \(\phi(t)=t^2\). For \(g=\phi\circ f\), one has \(g(1,0)+g(0,1)=2\), whereas \(g(0,0)+g(1,1)=4\). Therefore \(g(1,0)+g(0,1)<g(0,0)+g(1,1)\), violating submodularity. Thus even increasing convex scalar composition does not generally preserve submodularity; valid composition rules require stronger hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing a modular function with the increasing convex square function can violate submodularity, so unrestricted nonlinear composition is not closed.
assumptions_latex: Submodularity on \(\{0,1\}^2\) uses \(g(x)+g(y)\geq g(x\wedge y)+g(x\vee y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ modular and }\phi\text{ increasing convex}\centernot\implies\phi\circ f\text{ submodular}\).

notation.meaning: scalar composition of phi with f

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Direct evaluation supplies a concrete counterexample.
A source is needed for the complete closure-boundary classification.

children.title: Network Transformations

knowledge_statements.title: Network Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-preserving parallel-arc replacement represents an arc cost by discrete infimal convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an arc \(a=(u,v)\) carry an integer flow \(q\) with cost \(c(q)\), and suppose \(c=c_1\mathbin{\square}c_2\) on its feasible integer-flow domain. Replace \(a\) by two parallel arcs from \(u\) to \(v\), carrying integer flows \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) with costs \(c_1(q_1)\) and \(c_2(q_2)\). In every node-balance constraint, the two new arcs contribute the aggregate flow \(q_1+q_2\) in place of \(q\). For each fixed aggregate flow \(q\), their minimum cost is \[\inf_{q_1,q_2\in\mathbb Z:\,q_1+q_2=q}\{c_1(q_1)+c_2(q_2)\}=c(q).\] If no other constraint or objective term refers separately to \(q\), \(q_1\), or \(q_2\), minimizing the new internal flows preserves the network boundary value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing an arc by two parallel arcs whose costs infimally convolve to the original cost preserves every boundary value, provided only their aggregate flow enters the rest of the network model.
assumptions_latex: \(a=(u,v)\) is replaced by two parallel arcs with the same endpoints.
Only the aggregate \(q_1+q_2\) enters the remaining constraints and objective terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{transformed}}(b)=F_{\mathrm{original}}(b)\) for every boundary vector \(b\).

notation.meaning: original aggregate flow and the two parallel-arc flows

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Flow-Type and Potential-Type Network Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-valued network transformations from entrance-set functions to exit-set functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A;S,T)\) be a directed graph with \(S\cap T=\varnothing\). Given \(f,g:\mathbb Z^S\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(f_a,g_a:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) for \(a\in A\), define
\[
\widetilde f(y)=\inf_{\substack{\xi\in\mathbb Z^A,\ x\in\mathbb Z^S\\ \partial\xi=(x,-y,\mathbf 0)}}\left(f(x)+\sum_{a\in A}f_a(\xi(a))\right),\qquad y\in\mathbb Z^T,
\]
and
\[
\widetilde g(q)=\inf_{\substack{\eta\in\mathbb Z^A,\ p\in\mathbb Z^S,\ r\in\mathbb Z^{V\setminus(S\cup T)}\\ \eta=-\delta(p,q,r)}}\left(g(p)+\sum_{a\in A}g_a(\eta(a))\right),\qquad q\in\mathbb Z^T.
\]
These are respectively the flow-type and potential-type transformations induced by \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The flow-type transformation minimizes entrance and arc-flow costs subject to flow conservation for a prescribed exit demand. The potential-type transformation minimizes entrance and arc-tension costs subject to the tension being the negative coboundary of entrance, exit, and internal vertex potentials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widetilde f,\widetilde g:\mathbb Z^T\to\mathbb Z\cup\{\pm\infty\}\text{ are defined by the displayed flow-type and potential-type infima.}

children.title: Network-Induction Closure

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Induction Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite directed-network induction for M-convex functions with separable discrete-convex arc costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with incidence matrix \(B\), let \(f:\mathbb Z^V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper M-convex, and let each \(\varphi_a:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper discrete convex. Define
\[F(z)=\inf\left\{f(x)+\sum_{a\in A}\varphi_a(\xi_a)\mid x\in\mathbb Z^V,\ \xi\in\mathbb Z^A,\ z=x+B\xi\right\}.\]
If \(F\) is proper and every finite value is attained, then \(F\) is M-convex. Thus composition of finitely many such network inductions remains M-convex whenever each intermediate function is proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing an M-convex function plus separable convex arc costs over integral network flows preserves M-convexity, provided the induced function is proper and minima are attained.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is finite and \(B\) is its node-arc incidence matrix.
\(f\) is proper M-convex and every \(\varphi_a\) is proper discrete convex.
The defining infimum is attained and \(F\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is M-convex, and finite compositions of proper network inductions retain this property.

notation.meaning: Node-arc incidence matrix of the directed network.
Function induced by eliminating the network-flow variables.

children.title: Network-Transformation Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Transformation Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by replacing convex arc costs with a nonconvex integral cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the two-node network with one arc directed from node \(1\) to node \(2\), incidence vector \(b=(-1,1)\), and the M-convex indicator \(f=\delta_{\{(0,0)\}}\). Let \(\varphi(0)=\varphi(2)=0\), \(\varphi(1)=1\), and \(\varphi(t)=+\infty\) otherwise. The induced function satisfies \(F(tb)=\varphi(t)\). For \(x=0\) and \(y=2b\), the only M-exchange produces the two copies of \(b\), but
\[F(0)+F(2b)=0<2=F(b)+F(b).\]
Hence \(F\) is not M-convex; discrete convexity of every eliminated arc cost is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single nonconvex arc cost can destroy M-convexity: two zero-cost endpoint flows have an intermediate exchanged flow of positive cost.
assumptions_latex: The arc cost has values \(\varphi(0)=\varphi(2)=0\) and \(\varphi(1)=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The induced function \(F\) violates the M-exchange inequality and is not M-convex.

children.title: Function Scaling
children.top_down_role: Scaling operations applied to discrete convex functions or domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Function Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes value scaling from dilation of lattice arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a function \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and a scalar \(\lambda>0\), its value-scaled function is
\[ (\lambda f)(x)=\lambda f(x), \]
with the convention \(\lambda(+\infty)=+\infty\). For a positive integer \(k\), its lattice-argument scaling is
\[ f^{[k]}(x)=f(kx)\qquad(x\in\mathbb Z^n). \]
These are different operations: value scaling preserves the effective domain, whereas argument scaling replaces it by \(\{x\in\mathbb Z^n\mid kx\in\operatorname{dom}f\}\). Closure claims must therefore specify which scaling is intended.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Value scaling multiplies function values; lattice scaling evaluates the function on integer multiples. The operations have different domains and different closure behavior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}(\lambda f)=\operatorname{dom}f\), while \(\operatorname{dom}f^{[k]}=\{x\mid kx\in\operatorname{dom}f\}\).

notation.meaning: Positive value scaling of the function.
Scaling of lattice arguments by the positive integer k.
Set on which f is finite.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulas are coherent definitions, but an inspectable source is needed to establish that both operations, particularly the notation f^{[k]}, match the intended discrete-convex-analysis terminology.

children.title: Variable Splitting

knowledge_statements.title: Variable Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-coefficient splitting of each original coordinate into a block of integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I_1,\ldots,I_n\) be pairwise disjoint nonempty index sets, let \(m=\sum_i|I_i|\), and define the aggregation map \(A:\mathbb Z^m\to\mathbb Z^n\) by
\[(Ay)_i=\sum_{j\in I_i}y_j.\]
For \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), the variable-split lift of \(f\) is the function \(S_Af:\mathbb Z^m\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) given by
\[(S_Af)(y)=f(Ay).\]
Bounds or auxiliary costs imposed on split variables are additional operations and are not part of this bare splitting definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable splitting replaces each original coordinate by the sum of a nonempty block of new integer coordinates and composes the function with that aggregation.
assumptions_latex: The blocks \(I_1,\ldots,I_n\) are finite, nonempty, and pairwise disjoint.
\(f\) is an extended-real-valued function on \(\mathbb Z^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The split lift is \((S_Af)(y)=f(Ay)\) with \((Ay)_i=\sum_{j\in I_i}y_j\).

notation.meaning: Block of split variables representing coordinate i.

children.title: Scaling Closure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Discrete convex classes preserved under scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Closure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive value scaling is universal; argument scaling requires class-specific hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(\lambda>0\). Every defining inequality of M-convexity, L-convexity, integral convexity, or separable discrete convexity is preserved after multiplication by \(\lambda\); consequently, if \(f\) belongs to any one of these classes, then \(\lambda f\) belongs to the same class. By contrast, the implication from \(f\) to \(f^{[k]}(x)=f(kx)\) is not a class-independent closure rule. It is valid for separable discrete-convex functions because restriction of each univariate convex sequence to an arithmetic progression remains convex, but other classes require separate hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive multiplication preserves the standard discrete-convex classes. Scaling lattice arguments is automatically safe for separable convex functions but is not a universal closure operation.
assumptions_latex: All functions are proper whenever the class definition requires properness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive value scaling preserves M-, L-, integrally, and separably convex functions; lattice-argument scaling has only class-specific closure guarantees.

notation.meaning: Function obtained by scaling lattice arguments by k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Positive value scaling is standard, but the asserted boundary for lattice-argument scaling and its coverage across the named classes require an authoritative class-specific closure reference.

children.title: Splitting Closure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Splitting Closure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted aggregation is outside unit-coefficient variable-splitting closure rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Unit-coefficient block aggregation cannot be replaced by an arbitrary integer linear map. Let \(f=\delta_{\{0\}}\) on \(\mathbb Z\), which is integrally convex, and let \(A(y_1,y_2)=y_1+2y_2\). Then \(g=f\circ A\) has effective domain
\[S=\{(y_1,y_2)\in\mathbb Z^2\mid y_1+2y_2=0\}.\]
The points \((0,0)\) and \((2,-1)\) belong to \(S\), but their midpoint \((1,-1/2)\) is outside the convex hull of \(S\cap N(1,-1/2)\), where \(N(x)=\{z\in\mathbb Z^2\mid |z_i-x_i|<1\}\). Hence \(S\) and \(g\) are not integrally convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing unit splitting by weighted aggregation can lose integral convexity; the kernel of y1 plus 2y2 already supplies a concrete counterexample.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composition \(g=f\circ A\) is not integrally convex.

notation.meaning: Effective domain of the composed indicator function.

knowledge_statements.title: Class-Specific Closure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure under a discrete operation must be asserted separately for each convexity class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is no class-independent closure calculus for discrete-convex functions. Positive value scaling preserves M-convexity, L-convexity, and integral convexity because it preserves their defining inequalities. Arbitrary integral linear precomposition does not: with \(f=\delta_{\{0\}}\) and \(A(y_1,y_2)=y_1+2y_2\), the integrally convex function \(f\) yields \(f\circ A\) whose domain \(\{y\mid y_1+2y_2=0\}\) is not integrally convex. Therefore a closure statement must identify both the function class and the permitted structural form of the operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete-convex classes share some closures, such as positive value scaling, but arbitrary linear transformations can fail; every closure rule must name its class and operation.
assumptions_latex: Function classes are interpreted with their standard lattice definitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Closure for one discrete-convex class or one transformation form cannot be transferred automatically to another.

notation.meaning: Integer linear transformation used in the counterexample.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral M–L Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous polyhedral conjugacy between closed M-convex and L-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper closed polyhedral function and define its Legendre-Fenchel conjugate by
\[f^*(p)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)\}.\]
Then \(f\) is polyhedral M-convex if and only if \(f^*\) is polyhedral L-convex. In this correspondence, conjugation is involutive:
\[f^{**}=f.\]
Equivalently, closed polyhedral M-convex functions and closed polyhedral L-convex functions form mutually conjugate classes under the standard pairing on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Legendre-Fenchel conjugation maps closed polyhedral M-convex functions exactly to closed polyhedral L-convex functions, and double conjugation recovers the original function.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and polyhedral on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is polyhedral M-convex exactly when \(f^*\) is polyhedral L-convex, and \(f^{**}=f\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Argmin Difference Inequality for Polyhedral L-Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A quantified minimizer-ordering property on the polyhedral L-convex side of M–L conjugacy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\in\mathcal L[\mathbf R\to\mathbf R]\) be a polyhedral \(L\)-convex function. For \(x,y\in\mathbf R^V\) with \(\inf g[-x]>-\infty\) and \(\inf g[-y]>-\infty\), and for every \(u\in\operatorname{supp}^{+}(x-y)\), there exists \(v\in\operatorname{supp}^{-}(x-y)\) such that \[p(v)-p(u)\le q(v)-q(u)\qquad\left(\forall p\in\arg\min g[-x],\ \forall q\in\arg\min g[-y]\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedral L-convex function, each positive-support coordinate of x−y admits a negative-support coordinate satisfying the stated inequality simultaneously for every minimizer in the two specified argmin sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral M–L Conjugacy Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Legendre–Fenchel bijections between the polyhedral M/L classes and between their natural variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Legendre–Fenchel transformation gives a one-to-one correspondence between the classes \(\mathcal M=\mathcal M[\mathbf R\to\mathbf R]\) of polyhedral \(M\)-convex functions and \(\mathcal L=\mathcal L[\mathbf R\to\mathbf R]\) of polyhedral \(L\)-convex functions. knowledge_statements.title: Integral M–L Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-lattice conjugacy and biconjugacy for integer-valued M-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper M-convex and define
\[f^{\bullet}(p)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb Z^n}\{\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)\}\qquad(p\in\mathbb Z^n).\]
Whenever this conjugate is proper, \(f^{\bullet}\) is integer-valued L-convex. Conversely, the integral conjugate of a proper integer-valued L-convex function is M-convex. Moreover, integral biconjugacy holds:
\[f(x)=\sup_{p\in\mathbb Z^n}\{\langle p,x\rangle-f^{\bullet}(p)\}\qquad(x\in\mathbb Z^n).\]
Thus integral conjugation gives the lattice counterpart of polyhedral M–L conjugacy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral conjugation sends proper integer-valued M-convex functions to L-convex functions, reverses the correspondence, and satisfies lattice biconjugacy.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and M-convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\bullet}\) is L-convex and the displayed integral biconjugacy formula holds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral M–L discrete conjugacy theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-to-one discrete Legendre–Fenchel correspondences between the integer-valued M-convex/L-convex classes and between their natural variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the integer-restricted discrete Legendre–Fenchel transform, the classes $\mathcal M[\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Z]$ and $\mathcal L[\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Z]$ are in one-to-one correspondence: for $f\in\mathcal M[\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Z]$ and $g\in\mathcal L[\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Z]$, one has $f^\bullet\in\mathcal L[\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Z]$, $g^\bullet\in\mathcal M[\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Z]$, $f^{\bullet\bullet}=f$, and $g^{\bullet\bullet}=g$. Likewise, $\mathcal M^\natural[\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Z]$ and $\mathcal L^\natural[\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Z]$ are in one-to-one correspondence under the same transform.

knowledge_statements.title: Submodularity under Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Submodularity of the L-convex conjugate produced from an M-convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper M-convex and suppose its integral conjugate \(g=f^{\bullet}\) is proper. Since \(g\) is L-convex, it is submodular on the integer lattice: for all \(p,q\in\mathbb Z^n\),
\[g(p)+g(q)\ge g(p\wedge q)+g(p\vee q),\]
where the meet and join are taken componentwise. Thus M-convex exchange structure becomes lattice submodularity after integral conjugation; the accompanying L-convex translation law supplies the additional structure beyond submodularity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integral conjugate of an M-convex function is L-convex and therefore satisfies the componentwise lattice submodularity inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a proper integer-valued M-convex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(p)+g(q)\ge g(p\wedge q)+g(p\vee q)\) for every \(p,q\in\mathbb Z^n\).

notation.meaning: Integral conjugate of the M-convex function.

knowledge_statements.title: M–L Fenchel Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong integral Fenchel duality for an M-convex and an L-convex summand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper M-convex and \(g:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper L-convex. Define integral conjugates by \(h^{\bullet}(p)=\sup_x\{\langle p,x\rangle-h(x)\}\). If \(\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing\) and the primal minimum is finite and attained, then
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb Z^n}\{f(x)+g(x)\}=\max_{p\in\mathbb Z^n}\{-f^{\bullet}(p)-g^{\bullet}(-p)\}.\]
Under the standard properness conditions for the dual functions, the maximum is attained by an integral dual vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For compatible M-convex and L-convex functions, minimizing their sum over integer points equals an attained maximization involving their integral conjugates.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper integer-valued M-convex and \(g\) is proper integer-valued L-convex.
The primal value is finite and attained, with the dual conjugates proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_x(f(x)+g(x))=\max_p(-f^{\bullet}(p)-g^{\bullet}(-p))\), with an integral dual maximizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrally Convex–Separable Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete Fenchel duality for an integrally convex function and a separable convex summand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper integrally convex and let \(\Psi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_i(x_i)\), where every \(\psi_i:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper discrete convex. Define \(h^{\bullet}(p)=\sup_x\{\langle p,x\rangle-h(x)\}\). Under the discrete Fenchel constraint qualification that the effective domains intersect in a point belonging to the relative interior of the corresponding continuous convex extensions, and assuming a finite primal value,
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb Z^n}\{f(x)+\Psi(x)\}=\max_{p\in\mathbb Z^n}\{-f^{\bullet}(p)-\Psi^{\bullet}(-p)\}.\]
When the primal minimum is attained, an integral dual maximizer exists under the same qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrally convex function and a separable convex function satisfy integral Fenchel strong duality under the standard relative-interior domain qualification.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper integer-valued and integrally convex.
The continuous extensions satisfy the stated relative-interior qualification and the primal value is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_x(f(x)+\Psi(x))=\max_p(-f^{\bullet}(p)-\Psi^{\bullet}(-p))\) over integer primal and dual vectors.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Separation Theorems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict affine separation for disjoint finite M-convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S,T\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be nonempty finite M-convex sets. If \(S\cap T=\varnothing\), then their integral base-polyhedral convex hulls are disjoint. Consequently, there exist \(p\in\mathbb Q^n\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb Q\) such that
\[
\langle p,x\rangle<\alpha<\langle p,y\rangle
\quad(x\in S,\ y\in T).
\]
After multiplying by a common denominator, \(p\) and \(\alpha\) may be chosen integral while preserving strict separation after an appropriate rescaling of the gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two disjoint finite M-convex sets admit a strict rational affine separator, which can be rescaled to integral data.
assumptions_latex: \(S,T\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) are nonempty finite M-convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists(p,\alpha)\in\mathbb Q^n\times\mathbb Q\) with \(\langle p,x\rangle<\alpha<\langle p,y\rangle\) for all \(x\in S\), \(y\in T\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean pairing of the separating price vector and a lattice point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the leaf, but the claim that disjoint finite M-convex sets have disjoint base-polyhedral convex hulls—and hence an integral strict separator—requires an authoritative theorem-level citation.

knowledge_statements.title: General Discrete Lagrangian Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak Lagrange duality for equality-constrained lattice optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\), let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), and consider \(v_P=\inf\{f(x)\mid x\in X,\ Ax=b\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\). For \(p\in\mathbb R^m\), define
\[
L(x,p)=f(x)+\langle p,Ax-b\rangle,
\qquad q(p)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,p).
\]
The Lagrange dual value is \(v_D=\sup_{p\in\mathbb R^m}q(p)\), and weak duality always gives \(v_D\le v_P\). Equality and dual attainment require additional discrete-convex regularity or an exact penalty/separation condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing lattice equality constraints by prices produces a concave dual function whose supremum is always a lower bound on the primal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_D=\sup_{p\in\mathbb R^m}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,p)\le v_P\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weak-duality formulation is mathematically standard and the duality kind fits, but no cited source supports its placement as a discrete Lagrangian framework.

knowledge_statements.title: M-Convex Lagrangian Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of M-convexity under Lagrangian linear perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper M-convex function and impose \(Ax=b\). For every multiplier \(p\in\mathbb R^m\), define
\[
L_p(x)=f(x)+\langle A^{\mathsf T}p,x\rangle-\langle p,b\rangle.
\]
Then \(L_p\) is M-convex, because adding an affine function preserves the M-exchange inequality. Hence \(q(p)=\inf_xL_p(x)\) can be evaluated by M-convex minimization whenever its infimum is finite, and \(q\) is concave. Strong Lagrange duality is not asserted without an appropriate integral separation or constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every multiplier produces an M-convex subproblem; its minimum defines a concave dual function, while strong duality needs extra hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a proper M-convex function on \(\mathbb Z^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_p\) is M-convex for every \(p\), and \(q(p)=\inf_xL_p(x)\) is concave.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Affine perturbation preserves M-convexity and the dual value is concave, but a precise source is needed for the M-convex formulation and its extended-real finiteness conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Primal–Dual Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate symmetry for a proper closed discrete-convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper closed discrete-convex function \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), define its discrete conjugate on admissible price vectors by
\[
f^{\bullet}(p)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb Z^n}\{\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)\}.
\]
Whenever the selected M/L-convex conjugacy theorem applies, biconjugacy gives
\[
f(x)=\sup_p\{\langle p,x\rangle-f^{\bullet}(p)\}.
\]
Thus primal lattice points and dual prices enter symmetrically: \(p\in\partial f(x)\) if and only if \(x\in\partial f^{\bullet}(p)\), equivalently \(f(x)+f^{\bullet}(p)=\langle p,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete conjugacy exchanges lattice points and prices; equality in the conjugate inequality is equivalent to either mutual subgradient condition.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and closed in a discrete-convex class admitting biconjugacy.
\(x\) and \(p\) belong to the corresponding primal and price domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\in\partial f(x)\Longleftrightarrow x\in\partial f^{\bullet}(p)\Longleftrightarrow f(x)+f^{\bullet}(p)=\langle p,x\rangle\).

notation.meaning: Discrete conjugate of the primal function.
Discrete subdifferential at the primal point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record blends M- and L-convex conjugacy without fixing the function class, admissible price domain, or matching subdifferential definitions. An exact conjugacy theorem and locator are needed before the displayed equivalences can be assessed.

knowledge_statements.title: M-Convex Steepest-Descent Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-exchange descent for finite-valued M-convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an M-convex function \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(x^0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), at iteration \(k\) choose
\[
(i_k,j_k)\in\arg\min_{i,j}\ f(x^k-e_i+e_j)
\]
over feasible unit exchanges. If the minimum is at least \(f(x^k)\), stop and output \(x^k\); otherwise set \(x^{k+1}=x^k-e_{i_k}+e_{j_k}\). The M-exchange axiom implies that the stopping condition is equivalent to global optimality. With steepest choices, the number of iterations equals the minimum exchange distance from \(x^0\) to the minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly take the best feasible unit exchange. Absence of an improving exchange certifies global M-convex optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is M-convex and has a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm terminates at \(x^*\in\arg\min f\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-exchange algorithm and local-optimality conclusion fit the leaf, but the exact iteration-count assertion depends on the definition of exchange distance and the applicable steepest-descent theorem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Steepest-Descent Scaling Algorithm for M-Convex Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximity-based scaling method for an M-convex function with bounded effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be M-convex with bounded effective domain and K_\infty=\max\{\lVert p-q\rVert_\infty:p,q\in\operatorname{dom}f\}. Choose x\in\operatorname{dom}f, set \alpha=2^{\lceil\log_2(K_\infty/(4n))\rceil} and B=\operatorname{dom}f. At each scale, use steepest descent initialized at 0 to find an integer vector y locally minimizing \widetilde f(y)=f(x+\alpha y) when x+\alpha y\in B and +\infty otherwise, and set x\leftarrow x+\alpha y. If \alpha=1, return x. Otherwise set B\leftarrow B\cap\{z\in\mathbf{Z}^{V}:\lVert z-x\rVert_\infty\leq(n-1)(\alpha-1)\}, set \alpha\leftarrow\alpha/2, and repeat. The returned x is a minimizer of f.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each scale, solve a rescaled restricted problem by exchange steepest descent, update the current point, restrict the retained domain to the prescribed proximity box, and halve the scale. At scale one, the current point is a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha=1\Longrightarrow x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain-reduction scaling algorithm for M-convex minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling algorithm that maintains a domain point and a coordinatewise lower bound whose upper orthant contains a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f$ be M-convex and $S(\ell)=\{y\in\mathbf Z^V\mid y\ge\ell\}$. Maintain $x\in S(\ell)\cap\operatorname{dom}f$ and $S(\ell)\cap\arg\min f\ne\varnothing$. Starting from $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, set $\ell=x-K_\infty\mathbf1$ and $\alpha=2^{\lceil\log_2(K_\infty/(2n))\rceil}$. During each $\alpha$-scaling phase, update $(x,\ell)$ by scaled exchanges and lower-bound increases until $\ell\le x\le\ell+(n-1)(\alpha-1)\mathbf1$. If $\alpha>1$, replace $\alpha$ by $\alpha/2$ and repeat. When $\alpha=1$, the bound gives $x=\ell$, and the maintained invariants imply $x\in\arg\min f$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method combines domain reduction with halving-scale exchange phases. Each phase preserves a current domain point and an upper orthant containing a minimizer while tightening the coordinatewise gap. At scale one the current point equals the lower bound and is optimal.
assumptions_latex: K_\infty\text{ is as defined for the algorithm}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha=1\implies x=\ell\quad\text{and}\quad x\in\arg\min f

knowledge_statements.title: M-Convex Domain-Reduction Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certified shrinking of a box containing an M-convex minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Maintain an integral box \(B^k=[\ell^k,u^k]_{\mathbb Z}\) known to contain at least one minimizer of an M-convex function \(f\). Solve prescribed exchange or price-perturbed subproblems on \(B^k\) to obtain a valid certificate that some slab \(H^k\subset B^k\) contains no minimizer. Set \(B^{k+1}=B^k\setminus H^k\), represented by the certified smaller box, and continue until the remaining box is a singleton or direct exchange minimization is invoked. Correctness requires each reduction certificate to preserve
\[
B^{k+1}\cap\arg\min f\ne\varnothing.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain-reduction methods repeatedly remove certified minimizer-free coordinate slabs while retaining at least one M-convex minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is M-convex and has a minimizer in the initial finite box \(B^0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain-Reduction Algorithm for M-Convex Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested-domain method based on central points, improving exchanges, and M-minimizer cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be M-convex with bounded effective domain. For a bounded nonempty set B\subseteq\mathbf{Z}^{V}, define \ell_B(v)=\min_{y\in B}y(v), u_B(v)=\max_{y\in B}y(v), \ell_B^{\circ}=\lfloor(1-1/n)\ell_B+(1/n)u_B\rfloor, u_B^{\circ}=\lceil(1/n)\ell_B+(1-1/n)u_B\rceil, and B^{\circ}=\{y\in B:\ell_B^{\circ}\leq y\leq u_B^{\circ}\}. Initialize B=\operatorname{dom}f. Choose x\in B^{\circ} and distinct u,v minimizing f(x-\chi_u+\chi_v). If f(x)\leq f(x-\chi_u+\chi_v), return x; otherwise set B\leftarrow B\cap\{y\in\mathbf{Z}^{V}:y(u)\leq x(u)-1,\ y(v)\geq x(v)+1\} and repeat. The returned x is a minimizer of f. Moreover, B^{\circ}\neq\varnothing when B is M-convex, and the algorithm runs in time polynomial in n and \log_2K_\infty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a nested subset of the bounded effective domain. Choose a point in its central region and test the best unit exchange. A nonimproving best exchange certifies global optimality; an improving exchange determines a coordinate cut before repetition. The central region is nonempty for an M-convex working set, and the method has polynomial running time in n and log K-infinity.
assumptions_latex: B\text{ is bounded and nonempty when }B^{\circ}\text{ is formed}
B\text{ is M-convex for the assertion }B^{\circ}\neq\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)\leq f(x-\chi_u+\chi_v)\Longrightarrow x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f,\qquad T=\operatorname{poly}(n,\log_2K_\infty)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood descent for L-natural-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be L-natural-convex and start from \(x^0\in\operatorname{dom}f\). At iteration \(k\), minimize \(f\) over
\[
N(x^k)=\bigl(x^k+\{0,1\}^n\bigr)\cup\bigl(x^k-\{0,1\}^n\bigr).
\]
If a minimizer \(y^k\in N(x^k)\) satisfies \(f(y^k)<f(x^k)\), set \(x^{k+1}=y^k\); otherwise stop. L-natural-convex local optimality implies that the output is globally minimizing. Each neighborhood subproblem is a submodular set-function minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize over the upward and downward unit cubes around the current point; no local improvement certifies global L-natural-convex optimality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Steepest-Descent Scaling Algorithm for L-Convex Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling algorithm for an L-convex function satisfying the source-referenced condition (10.31).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\in\mathcal L[\mathbf Z\to\mathbf R]\) satisfy (10.31), and define \(\widehat K_\infty=\max\{\|p-q\|_\infty\mid p,q\in\operatorname{dom}g,\ p(v)=q(v)\text{ for some }v\in V\}\). Choose \(p\in\operatorname{dom}g\) and set \(\alpha=2^{\lceil\log_2(\widehat K_\infty/(2n))\rceil}\). At each scale, apply steepest descent with initial vector \(0\) to find an integer vector \(q\) such that, for \(\widetilde g(q)=g(p+\alpha q)\), \(\widetilde g(q)\leq\widetilde g(q+\chi_X)\) for every \(X\subseteq V\), and then set \(p\leftarrow p+\alpha q\). If \(\alpha=1\), stop and return \(p\), a minimizer of \(g\); otherwise set \(\alpha\leftarrow\alpha/2\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a domain point and initialize a power-of-two scale from the specified domain parameter. At each scale, run steepest descent from zero to obtain the stated local minimum of the scaled function, update the current point, and halve the scale. At scale one, the returned point is a global minimizer of the L-convex function.
assumptions_latex: g\in\mathcal L[\mathbf Z\to\mathbf R]\text{ satisfies the source-referenced condition (10.31)}
\widehat K_\infty=\max\{\|p-q\|_\infty\mid p,q\in\operatorname{dom}g,\ p(v)=q(v)\text{ for some }v\in V\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{When the algorithm reaches }\alpha=1,\quad p\in\operatorname*{argmin} g.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction to Submodular Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean-neighborhood subproblems represented as submodular set functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be L-natural-convex and fix \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Define set functions on \(2^{[n]}\) by
\[
h_x^+(S)=f(x+\mathbf 1_S),
\qquad h_x^-(S)=f(x-\mathbf 1_S).
\]
The discrete midpoint inequality implies that both \(h_x^+\) and \(h_x^-\) are submodular on their effective domains. Therefore minimizing \(f\) over the upward or downward Boolean neighborhood of \(x\) reduces exactly to submodular set-function minimization; comparing the two minima produces an L-natural-convex steepest-descent step or a local-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting an L-natural-convex function to either Boolean neighborhood yields a submodular set function, enabling exact local minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_x^+\) and \(h_x^-\) are submodular, and their minima equal the corresponding neighborhood minima of \(f\).

notation.meaning: Incidence vector of the subset S.
Upward and downward Boolean restrictions of f.
